title: CYTOKINETIC BOTTLENECKS OF HEAT WAVES
title_norm: cytokinetic bottlenecks of heat waves
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain encompasses plant cell biology, focusing on the unknown molecular mechanisms and genetic components that govern cytokinetic robustness under heat stress across different plant species. Although cytokinesis is known to be heat-sensitive in temperate plants and heat-resilient in tropical plants, comprehensive cytokinetic gene networks and specific molecular bottlenecks causing these differential responses remain incomplete. The primary objective is to predict these molecular bottlenecks by comparing multi-omics data between heat-susceptible and heat-resilient species, which will provide insights into evolutionary adaptation and enable the breeding of heat-resilient crops.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves a systematic comparative analysis of single-cell and whole-tissue omics data from heat-stressed and control plants to construct and compare multilayer cytokinetic networks. Key analytical methods include orthology inference, single-cell transcriptomics reprocessing, count normalization, dimensionality reduction, trajectory analysis, differential expression, and multiplex network construction. Analytical results will be internally benchmarked using known mitotic-specific transcripts to identify co-expressing genes and yield theoretical predictions that guide future functional validation experiments.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will utilize publicly available single-cell and whole-organ transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics datasets from species including Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, Sorghum bicolor, and Nicotiana tabacum. These datasets will be integrated by initially performing single-layer analysis within individual omics types before constructing a multiplex network representing inter-layer relationships. Limitations arising from varied plant growth conditions and differing initial normalizations will be addressed by standardizing the reprocessing pipeline and using a large sample size to mitigate noise.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The project spans a two-year timeline, culminating in the primary milestone of submitting a manuscript detailing the predicted cytokinetic bottlenecks towards the end of the second year. Successful execution requires collaboration to combine the domain expertise of the principal investigators in plant cell biology with external professional expertise in bioinformatics and complex multi-omics data analysis.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The research team comprises domain experts in plant cell biology, membrane trafficking, physiology, and biochemistry, supported by requested staff scientists with bioinformatics expertise. Although the project uses publicly available datasets and will disseminate findings through published manuscripts, the proposal does not specify open science plans for sharing newly generated code or data."
}

abstract_original: The lack of motility makes plants highly vulnerable to environmental anomalies such as periods of extreme high temperature known as heat waves. Plants can search for better habitats by exploiting seed mobility, which relies on completing the life cycle and producing seeds. Formation of reproductive organs and seed development requires the production of cells through cell division. The last stage of cell division, cytokinesis, encompasses many key cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signaling. While cytokinesis is highly sensitive to heat stress in plants adapted to temperate climates, cytokinesis is more resilient in species adapted to tropical zones. However, how heat stress affects cytokinesis and the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness across different plant species remains unknown. This project aims to compare changes in cytokinetic components under heat stress in susceptible and hardy species to characterize differential responses of genetic circuits responsible for specific cellular events during cytokinesis. The long term goal is to harness this data for identifying the bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness. The experimental approach here will be systematic analysis of publicly available data from single-cell and whole-organ omics data collected under control and high-temperature conditions including transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics. Predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks will inform future experimental design for their functional characterization leading to better understanding of cellular adaptation mechanisms to heat stress. This knowledge may provide insight into evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to different climates and improve predictions for heat resiliency at the level of individual plants and populations.
target_proposal_title: CYTOKINETIC BOTTLENECKS OF HEAT WAVES

title: Transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
title_norm: transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain is vertebrate genomics and evolutionary biology, specifically studying how transposable elements generate novel functional genomic elements and drive species diversification. The primary scientific gap is the underexplored functional role of transposable element-rich genome regions, which are typically discarded or ambiguously mapped in existing short-read sequencing pipelines. The objective is to determine how transposable elements generate new regulatory and coding sequences to connect molecular-level insertions to the evolution of higher-order regulatory networks and phenotypic diversity.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves reprocessing large-scale public genomic datasets with repeat-aware pipelines, followed by multi-omic integration to identify transposable element-derived functional elements. Key methods encompass telomere-to-telomere and pangenome assembly alignments, probabilistic read allocation tools, hidden Markov models, multi-species alignments, and tensor decomposition to recover signals from ambiguous multi-mapped short reads. Regarding further methodological details, the proposal does not specify that information.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The data sources comprise over 75,000 publicly available genomic, transcriptomic, and ribosome profiling datasets from consortia such as ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, FAANG, and GTEx. These datasets encompass multiple experimental modalities, including ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq. The synthesis plan involves intersecting repeat-aware genomic activity maps with transposable element annotations and employing tensor decomposition to identify higher-order dependencies between data modalities, transcription factors, and transposable element families.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The project timeline spans exactly two years. The first year focuses on pipeline finalization and large-scale data reprocessing, whereas the second year is dedicated to integrated data analysis, biological interpretation, and the publication of data resources.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The project requires collaboration due to the massive scale of data processing and involves a multidisciplinary team of computational staff scientists and researchers specializing in transposon biology, regulatory genomics, evolutionary biology, and computational data integration. Open science practices will be upheld by producing a publicly accessible collection of reprocessed datasets and releasing reproducible analysis pipelines for repeat-aware genomics."
}

abstract_original: Our working group aims to comprehensively investigate how transposable elements (TEs) contribute to genomic innovation and species diversification in vertebrates through the generation of novel functional elements. While TEs comprise nearly half of the human genome and are increasingly recognized as sources of regulatory innovation, their repetitive nature has complicated their analysis using short-read sequencing technologies. We propose a two-phase approach: First, we will reprocess tens of thousands of publicly available genomic datasets (including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq) using repeat-aware analysis pipelines and new telomere-to-telomere and pangenome assemblies. Second, we will synthesize this reprocessed data to understand how TEs generate new transcription factor binding sites, cell-specific and species-specific enhancers, novel transcripts, and protein-coding sequences. The project combines multidisciplinary expertise from multiple labs and will leverage advanced computational approaches to uncover complex relationships between TEs and regulatory networks. Our investigation represents a quintessential mesoscale emergence phenomenon, bridging molecular-level TE insertions with emergent regulatory networks and phenotypic innovations. The project will produce both a comprehensive public data resource of repeat-aware genomic analyses and new insights into how TEs drive biological innovation through regulatory network evolution.
target_proposal_title: Transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation

title: Searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new protein-protein interactions
title_norm: searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new proteinprotein interactions
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "Within the domain of structural proteomics, existing protein-protein interaction networks often lack residue-level structural evidence, and public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets in PRIDE are difficult to reuse due to inconsistent formats and metadata. The objective of this research is to standardize and reprocess public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets, validate interactions using structural predictions, and integrate the findings into the EBI Complex Portal. This approach provides physical, residue-level spatial evidence to discover or validate protein-protein interactions, thereby improving upon current models that lack structural confirmation.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves filtering and re-annotating datasets, reprocessing the data with modern algorithms, pooling crosslink data, and computationally validating interactions against network predictions. The analytical approach utilizes crosslinking mass spectrometry, the Scout search algorithm, huMAP for interaction prediction, and AlphaFold3 for structural modeling. The resulting data will be validated by determining whether the crosslinked residues demonstrate spatial proximity within the structural models generated by AlphaFold.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "Data sources for this project include crosslinking datasets from the PRIDE repository, the huMAP database, and the EBI Complex Portal. The synthesis plan involves reprocessing raw PRIDE data, pooling crosslink pairs, mapping them to huMAP networks, and subsequently uploading the structurally validated pairs into the EBI Complex Portal. The limitation of inconsistent metadata in legacy datasets will be resolved by re-annotating and reprocessing the raw data using modern search algorithms.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The project follows a fifteen-month timeline that allocates the first six months for dataset reannotation and reprocessing, months seven through twelve for structural validation and portal integration, and the final three months for exploring uncharacterized proteins and publication. The feasibility of this project relies on a collaboration that merges expertise in crosslinking mass spectrometry and structural biology with database engineering and data standards infrastructure.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "Reprocessed data will be openly deposited into a dedicated PRIDE Crosslinking database, and validated interactions will be made public via the EBI Complex Portal. The research team is composed of Dr. Fried's research group, database collaborators from the European Bioinformatics Institute, and dedicated data scientists."
}

abstract_original: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a powerful structural proteomics method that can provide high-resolution structural information about complex mixtures of proteins in their native physiological context.1,2,3 The method works by chemically crosslinking two reactive amino acid residues that are close to one another in 3-D space, thereby freezing this spatial information into a covalent bond, and then retrieving this information by sequencing crosslinked peptides following enzymatic digest of the constituent proteins (like Hi-C,4 but for proteins). Initially developed in the 2000s to interrogate purified proteins, by the late-2010s, methods became available to interrogate protein-protein interactions (PPIs) on the proteome-scale and in the cellular environment.5 This project seeks to standardize, combine, and integrate existing publicly available crosslinking datasets from PRIDE to make these data more re-usable and useful for integrative and hybrid modeling. We will also create a meta-dataset to catalogue PPIs in human and other model organisms. Because XL-MS encodes information about both protein identity and interacting residues, these findings can be cross-validated to structural predictions of protein complexes using AlphaFold3, thereby providing stronger evidence for their existence compared to huMAP3.0, which predicts protein complexes without structural evidence. We will integrate these findings into the EBI Complex Portal to make it accessible to the life science community.
target_proposal_title: Searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new protein-protein interactions

title: Intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data
title_norm: intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometrybased proteomics data
authors: Wout Bittremieux; Iddo Friedberg
abstract_original: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics generates vast amounts of data, yet the effective reuse and discovery of these datasets remain challenging due to incomplete and inconsistent metadata. Metadata, which provides critical contextual information such as experimental conditions, sample characteristics, and data processing details, is essential for making data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable). To address these challenges, our working group aims to develop intelligent, automated workflows for comprehensive metadata extraction, harmonization, and integration into PRIDE, the largest public proteomics data repository. We will develop powerful bioinformatics and natural language processing tools to extract metadata directly from raw mass spectrometry files and scientific publications. By leveraging structured data standards, metadata will be enriched with controlled vocabulary terms, enhancing dataset transparency and usability. Community engagement through a machine-learning challenge will further drive innovation in metadata extraction techniques. The outcomes of the working group's activities will include automated metadata compilation workflows integrated into user-friendly tools, advanced dataset querying capabilities in PRIDE, and the creation of educational resources for the scientific community. These efforts will enable researchers to efficiently locate and reuse proteomics datasets, facilitating secondary analyses such as AI model training and large-scale reanalysis.
target_proposal_title: Intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data

title: Elucidating genome structure-function relationships in human brain cells
title_norm: elucidating genome structurefunction relationships in human brain cells
abstract_text: "The research domain focuses on single-cell genomics of the human brain, specifically investigating the relationship between three-dimensional chromatin architecture and gene expression in healthy states and Alzheimer's disease. The mechanisms governing gene expression remain poorly understood because current single-modality analyses fail to capture causal relationships and provide only a fragmented view of gene regulatory networks. The primary objective is to develop a transformer-based multimodal generative artificial intelligence model that integrates chromatin accessibility, three-dimensional chromatin organization, and gene expression to determine how chromatin architecture regulates gene activity. This approach synthesizes single-cell Hi-C, single-cell RNA-seq, and bulk ATAC-seq datasets from human brain tissues and supplementary mouse cells by aligning embeddings through contrastive learning and employing tensor decomposition to impute missing data across consensus cell types. By capturing a broader spatial range of regulatory mechanisms than existing methods, this framework will enable the identification of epigenetic drivers and biophysical rules of genome folding underlying normal neural diversity and Alzheimer's disease progression."

abstract_original: Single-cell analysis has profoundly enhanced our understanding of brain tissue by facilitating the examination of gene expression and epigenetic features. However, investigating these modalities independently offers a fragmented view of gene regulation and its relationship to transcriptional activity. To overcome this limitation, we propose developing a multimodal generative AI model that integrates single-cell genomics datasets. This framework seeks to illuminate the interplay between three-dimensional genomic architecture and gene expression, uncovering the physical principles underlying the emergence of cell-type-specific gene expression programs, despite the inherent stochasticity of gene regulation at the single-cell level. Applied to datasets from Alzheimer's patients, this approach has the potential to identify epigenetic drivers of disease progression, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of neurodegenerative processes.

title: MaiTool - LLM-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
title_norm: maitool  llmpowered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain encompasses microbiome and ancient DNA science with a focus on integrating large language models into bioinformatics workflows. While current large language models can extract literature insights and summarize methodologies, they lack the ability to directly analyze datasets, execute robust computational analyses, or dynamically interact with microbiome data repositories. To address this gap, the primary objective is to develop MaiTool, a graphical interface that combines large language models with bioinformatics tools to establish a novel AI-driven standard for seamless natural language literature retrieval and immediate computational data analysis.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves evaluating and fine-tuning existing large language models alongside the development of a unified API and a standalone software application for interactive data analysis. Key methodologies and tools utilized in this project include BioGPT, BioMedLM, GeneGPT, REST APIs, Java, JavaFX, Gluon, and lightweight bioinformatics pipelines. The resulting software will be validated through a dedicated testing phase and usability studies to ensure the tool effectively meets the requirements of researchers.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will utilize datasets and databases including MGnify, MG-RAST, the Human Microbiome Project, the Microbiome Atlas of Mothers and Infants, Integrated Microbial Genomes and Microbiomes, and the Sequence Read Archive. These datasets will be integrated through a unified API that automatically retrieves and processes taxonomic profiles and metadata using sample accessions extracted by the language model. Data limitations involving raw data processing constraints are mitigated by providing generated pipeline descriptions for independent execution, while data quality issues are addressed by integrating measures to flag dataset errors early.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The first year of the project will focus on exploring language models and repositories, designing integration frameworks, developing repository APIs, and refining dataset selection. The second year will involve deploying the large language model REST API, building the MaiTool front-end, conducting comprehensive testing, and completing a public release.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The project team consists of Daniel Huson, Laura Weyrich, Maik Pietzner, and a proposed staff scientist with expertise in large language models, providing the cross-disciplinary collaboration needed for metagenomic algorithms, ancient DNA analysis, and multimodal omics dataset integration. In accordance with open science principles, the research results will be published and the fully functional MaiTool software and integrated system will be released to the public."
}

abstract_original: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and BioGPT have revolutionized how researchers engage with scientific literature, offering capabilities such as extracting insights, summarizing methodologies, and identifying relevant publications. These models have applications in microbiome research, where they can assist in identifying datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST. However, LLMs lack the ability to directly analyze datasets, necessitating integration with bioinformatics tools to enable robust computational analysis. This project aims to develop MaiTool, a graphical interface that combines LLM capabilities with bioinformatics workflows for microbiome and ancient DNA research. MaiTool will enable users to explore publications, access public datasets via APIs, and perform dynamic analyses, integrating quality control measures to enhance reliability. Existing GPT systems (e.g., BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT) will be evaluated and fine-tuned for microbiome applications. We will assess repositories such as HMP, IMG/M, and SRA for their suitability and develop APIs for seamless data access and integration. By addressing queries such as studies involving specific taxa, MaiTool will allow LLMs to retrieve literature while bioinformatics pipelines analyze and visualize dataset profiles. This approach aims to advance interdisciplinary research workflows and establish a new standard for AI-driven bioinformatics.
target_proposal_title: MaiTool - LLM-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis

title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
title_norm: synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
authors: Jeffrey Barrick; Jeremy Schmit
abstract_original: Bacterial cells have evolved to adapt their molecular composition to maximize growth and survival. Our current knowledge of bacterial cell states is fragmented. Researchers often only analyze data they generate themselves—usually for just one strain under a limited number of conditions—because it is difficult to harmonize omics datasets collected with different technologies in different labs. Our NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to create a first-of-its-kind atlas of bacterial cell states. To manageably scale data collection and analysis, we will build from examining model Escherichia coli strains in lab conditions, to adding wild E. coli strains in natural environments such as the human gut, to including diverse bacterial species with additional cell states. We expect to identify distinct foci corresponding to bacterial growth states and lifestyles (e.g., replicating, starving, motile, biofilm, spore, viable but nonculturable) by mapping the organization and occupancy of cell state space with dimensional reduction approaches. We will examine to what extent the gene expression signatures of different cell states and the relationships among them are conserved during bacterial evolution. Finally, we will use this framework to create a classifier that predicts the cell state composition of a bacterial population from metatranscriptomic data. By following open-science practices, we will make our pipelines and datasets reusable and maintainable by the research community. Our project may reveal new bacterial cell states and ways that we can non-genetically reprogram bacteria to prevent them from adopting lifestyles that damage the environment and cause disease.
target_proposal_title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states

title: Energetic Origins of Connectivity within Protein Interaction Networks
title_norm: energetic origins of connectivity within protein interaction networks
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "Current knowledge establishes that protein interaction networks exhibit scale-free topologies, but the role of multiscale biophysical properties in determining network architecture within computational biophysics remains incomplete. It is currently unknown how cells maintain preferred protein-protein interaction network architectures despite continuous protein evolution and how individual biophysical properties constrain overall network topology. The primary objective is to determine how protein stability, binding efficiency, and intrinsic disorder shape these networks, which is significant because it establishes a novel biophysical framework linking physical properties to emergent cellular connectivity and robustness.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves constructing protein interaction networks from existing interactome datasets, computing structural properties of constituent proteins, mapping these features onto network topologies, and simulating evolutionary trajectories using genetic algorithms. Key analytical methods include graph analysis using Python and Cytoscape, network clustering, contextual artificial intelligence models, generative modeling for stability prediction, and disorder prediction tools. Computational predictions and network analyses will be validated using experimental proteolysis-based stability data, proteomic half-life measurements, and protein abundance data.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project utilizes in vivo and high-throughput interactome datasets for yeast, Escherichia coli, Caenorhabditis elegans, Arabidopsis, and humans, alongside single-cell and condition-specific data from the Gene Expression Omnibus, Gene Ontology, and WikiPathways. These diverse datasets will be integrated by combining computational network models with predicted biophysical descriptors and parameterizing them via contextual artificial intelligence models. To address potential experimental biases in the interactome datasets, the synthesis plan utilizes curated, high-quality data and varies analytical thresholds to assess the robustness of the structural and functional correlations.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "Project milestones include constructing interaction networks across multiple species, computing centrality metrics, generating protein stability estimates, annotating specific protein types, conducting enrichment analyses, and developing genetic algorithms. Regarding a specific timeline, the proposal does not specify that information.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The collaborative team comprises the Schlebach, Mukhtar, Serohijos, and Shakhnovich laboratories, along with a requested staff scientist and an assistant. Regarding open science, the proposal does not specify that information."
}

abstract_original: At least 10% of cellular proteins are intrinsically unstable and fold with marginal efficiency. In the cell, these proteins are preferentially engaged by chaperones and quality control proteins that refold or degrade them. Similarly, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) preferentially interact with specific partners that they require for folding and function. Such proteins must exhibit bias in the types of protein-protein interactions they form within the cell. We therefore hypothesize that the emergent scaling properties of protein interaction networks arise, in part, from the promiscuous interactions formed by unstable proteins and the obligate interactions formed by IDPs. To test this hypothesis, we will analyze existing large-scale interactome datasets to explore the context of unstable and disordered proteins within interaction networks. By extending this approach to evaluate how proteins with various conformational properties are distributed across several unicellular and multicellular networks, we aim to uncover generalizable insights into how protein biophysics shapes network architecture. Additionally, by mapping the centrality of proteins involved in various supramolecular organization regimes, we will identify topological niches associated with the occurrence of liquid-liquid phase separation and quinary structure. Finally, to determine the extent to which these biases constrain network evolution, we will utilize genetic algorithms to explore how changes in the stability of the proteome restrict the topologies that are accessible through evolution. Together, these investigations will provide insights into the role of protein stability and binding efficiency in the evolution of PPI networks and how this relates to the molecular mechanisms of evolution.

abstract_original: Messenger RNA molecules are constantly bound by proteins that regulate all aspects of their function, including their processing, localization, translation, and degradation1. These mRNA-protein complexes (mRNPs) can also interact with each other and assemble into higher-order structures that play critical roles in cellular organization and response to environmental stimuli1-3. Despite their importance, we lack a comprehensive map of these cellular RNA-protein interaction networks at both the nano and micro scales. Years of efforts by researchers across the globe have yielded a large, but disjointed, collection of datasets that map different aspects of RNA-protein interactions. Currently, we lack tools to integrate these datasets, preventing their synthesis into a coherent and interpretable interaction map. Here, we propose to develop tools to combine disparate data types to build transcriptome-wide maps of mRNPs, and their higher-order interactions within cells. We will then apply these tools to gain insights into long-standing biological mysteries, including the impacts of synonymous mutations and cell-type specific effects of widely expressed RNAs.

title: Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation
title_norm: oceans of disorder elucidating the role of disordered proteins in cellular adaptation
abstract_text: "Within the domains of protein biophysics and evolutionary biology, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDRs) function and adapt as molecular sensors across diverse marine environments. However, a critical scientific gap remains due to the lack of a systematic understanding regarding the sequence-level, biophysical, and functional mechanisms by which individual IDRs structurally adapt to extreme and fluctuating environmental conditions. To address this, the primary objective is to systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors through a computational approach that combines structural predictions, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations under varying temperature and salinity, and deep learning models to link sequence features to adaptive mechanisms. The data integration strategy annotates metagenomic protein sequences from the Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0 and the OceanDNA database with corresponding environmental and genomic metadata, supplementing standard biophysical predictions with additional simulation-derived labels to overcome prediction limitations in extreme conditions. Ultimately, this research provides the first large-scale systematic mapping of IDR biophysical adaptations to environmental contexts, generating foundational insights for evolutionary biology and enabling the engineering of environmentally resilient proteins for biotechnology."

abstract_original: Intrinsically disordered proteins and protein regions (collectively IDRs) are key regulators of environmental sensing, owing to their ability to undergo conformational changes in response to physicochemical fluctuations. Despite evidence from individual studies, a comprehensive understanding of IDR-driven adaptations across diverse environments remains elusive. The deep sea, characterized by extreme and variable conditions such as temperature, pressure, and salinity, offers a unique opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Over the past decade, large-scale ocean sampling expeditions using shotgun metagenomics have revolutionized our understanding of marine biodiversity, providing access to the genetic diversity of organisms, from microbes to fish, thriving in these extreme habitats. These datasets offer an unprecedented opportunity to explore how IDRs have evolved as molecular sensors to support survival across varied environmental conditions. Here, we will, for the same time, use these metagenomic datasets to systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors. Our multidisciplinary team, with expertise in metagenomics, protein biophysics, cell biology, and deep learning, will integrate bioinformatics, simulations, machine learning, and theoretical approaches to uncover sequence-level and functional adaptations of IDRs across marine environments. The outcomes of this research will produce a comprehensive map of IDR adaptations in marine systems, revealing their emergent properties as molecular sensors and actuators. In addition to advancing fundamental insights into stress adaptation and evolutionary biology, this work will inform biotechnological innovations, including engineering robust systems for extreme environments.

abstract_original: Large-scale consortia like the Dependency Map and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia have generated extensive multi-omics data for over 2000 primary cell lines, including bulk measurements of DNA, chromatin accessibility, RNA, and proteins. Recently, multi-omics single-cell sequencing and imaging data labeling RNA and proteins for these cell lines have become increasingly available. However, these datasets remain fragmented, lacking integration into a unified framework to model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell. While previous efforts have created multimodal benchmark datasets, these often include diverse samples from multiple donors and heterogeneous cell types. In contrast, our project focuses on single model systems, such as commonly used cell lines, which already feature extensive single-cell, bulk sequencing, and imaging data. By eliminating donor and cell type variability, our approach enables robust analyses and precise alignment across modalities, including RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility. This focus on homogenous cell types within a consistent biological context facilitates mechanistic studies of regulatory interactions and perturbation responses, minimizing confounding variability. We aim to develop multimodal frameworks for 7 cell lines and computational pipelines to analyze relationships across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. By incorporating additional multi-omics data, including bulk and single-cell perturbation datasets (e.g., loss-of-function screens and Perturb-seq), we will create a comprehensive benchmarking resource. With expertise in machine learning, network biology, and genomics, and NCEMS support for data wrangling, our team will deliver tools to study regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. These efforts will foster fundamental discoveries, community-driven resource development, and innovation in multi-omics research.

title: From image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
title_norm: from image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
authors: Mary Mirvis; Adriana Dawes
abstract_original: Mesoscale cellular organization emerges from complex interactions among chemical, structural, and physical components. Understanding how mesoscale structures influence local and collective cellular properties remains a significant challenge, often beyond the scope of individual experimental studies. While vast image datasets for cellular components exist, their full potential for deeper secondary analysis and synthesis remains untapped. We propose to synthesize morphological and physico-chemical measurements from cell image, in vitro, and in silico data to unravel the principles of mesoscale cellular organization. Our approach will develop a pipeline using transfer learning and mutual prediction, trained on complete datasets (all components of interest present) and applied to incomplete datasets (missing one or more components). This methodology will uncover relationships between cellular components and enable holistic systems-level predictions. To demonstrate the generalizability and biological relevance of this approach, we will test it on three increasingly complex mesoscale systems centered on the nucleus: (1) nucleus-nucleolus, (2) nucleus-centrosome-microtubules, and (3) nucleus-mitochondria-mitochondrial condensates. These test cases will showcase how our method integrates and predicts complex systems relationships, advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

abstract_original: Allostery—the ability of a perturbation at one site in a protein to control function at a distant site— underlies enzyme catalysis, signaling, and gene regulation. Yet we still lack a general, quantitative way to define how “allosteric” a protein is, to compare that across systems, and to predict how substitutions will strengthen, weaken, or rewire that control. This project develops a physics-informed data science framework to obtain quantitative order parameters of allostery and use them to classify, predict, and ultimately engineer regulatory behavior. We will integrate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets, and evolutionary information (Table 1) to extract dynamic coupling measures that report how a local perturbation propagates through the protein over time. From these data we will derive physically interpretable allosteric order parameters that quantify three key features: (i) strength of long-range communication, (ii) directionality/asymmetry of information flow, and (iii) timescale of propagation. These parameters will form the basis of an “allostery score” that allows us to categorize the degree and mode of allostery across proteins and across species. We will then train machine learning models to predict how specific amino acid substitutions alter these order parameters — i.e., how a mutation changes not just local stability, but global regulatory wiring. Finally, we will apply this framework to design mutations that reprogram allosteric regulation in transcription factors, and experimentally test these designs. The outcome is a generalizable, predictive map from sequence to allosteric control.

  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain is biomolecular modeling, specifically focusing on the integration of temporal protein dynamics and environmental responses to shift from a static sequence-structure paradigm to a dynamic model that predicts enzyme function. Current AI models for protein function prediction rely on static sequence and structural data, while existing language models achieve high accuracy but omit temporal information and the role of dynamic conformational changes. The primary objective is to enhance enzyme function prediction by integrating multi-scale molecular dynamics simulations and biophysical determinants into a multi-modal AI model named MD4PLM.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design consists of curating enzyme function annotations, simulation trajectories, and biophysical determinants, followed by synthesizing these data via the multi-modal MD4PLM AI framework. Key methods and tools include ESM-2, MMseqs2, spatio-temporal GNNs, causal attention, gated fusion, all-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics, AI-driven molecular dynamics, APBS, Frustratometer, and MDtraj. Results will be benchmarked against sequence-based and structure-based models using GO terms, EC numbers, Fmax, and AUPRC metrics, while potential discrepancies will be validated with multiple force fields.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "Datasets and databases utilized for this research include UniProt/SwissProt, the Protein Data Bank, ATLAS, md-CATH, and Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center Anton projects. These datasets will be integrated using a gated fusion module and multi-modal learning techniques to combine multi-scale molecular dynamics simulations and biophysical features into unified embeddings. Limited conformational sampling will be addressed by using coarse-grained and AI-driven models, applying enhanced sampling techniques like replica exchange and umbrella sampling, and validating across multiple force fields.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The twenty-four-month timeline includes data curation and simulation setup during the first two months, molecular dynamics simulations and feature extraction from months three to twelve, biophysical determinants analysis from months thirteen to eighteen, and benchmarking and dissemination from months nineteen to twenty-four. The feasibility of this project relies on a collaboration combining expertise in molecular dynamics simulations, biophysics, AI model development, bioinformatics, and experimental enzyme studies, alongside computational resources and staff from NCEMS.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "All processed trajectories and determinants will be deposited in open repositories including MDRepo, Zenodo, and GitHub, and funds are requested for open-access publication. The research team includes principal investigators Lin, Chen, Shen, and Lagard, supported by an NCEMS staff scientist, a staff scientist assistant, and a program manager."

abstract_original: Recent AI advances have transformed biomolecular research, enabling accurate prediction of biomolecu- lar functions from sequence and structural data. However, the role of dynamic motions and environmental responses in shaping biomolecular function remains underexplored in AI-driven approaches. In this pro- posal, our working group aims to bridge this gap by integrating temporal and physicochemical insights from molecular dynamics (MD) with AI techniques to enhance predictive accuracy in protein function, focusing on enzymes. We will work closely with NCEMS in two phases: (I) Comprehensive data curation of enzyme function annotations, collection of multi-scale simulation trajectories, and biophysical deter- minants causally linked to enzyme activity. (II) Synthesizing simulations and biophysical determinants through a multi-modal AI model to enhance enzyme function predictions. The project integrates comple- mentary expertise across multiple labs and will leverage NCEMS computational resources to generate large-scale data. By synergizing AI and MD, we will advance biomolecular modeling beyond the static sequence-structure paradigm to include temporal resolution, guiding rational design of therapeutic and functional biomolecules.
target_proposal_title: Integrating AI and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Quantitative Prediction of Enzyme Functions

title: Discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
title_norm: discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
abstract_text:
{
  "abstract": "In the domain of microbial systems biology, this research focuses on the distribution, regulation, and diversity of bacterial organelles, encompassing protein-bounded compartments, lipid-bounded compartments, and biomolecular condensates in the human gut microbiome. While the existence of prokaryotic organelles is recognized, there is a lack of systematic assessment for condensate-forming proteins, and the ecological functions, environmental responsiveness, and inter-organelle interactions within complex microbial communities remain largely uncharacterized. The primary objective is to map the prevalence, diversity, and regulatory dynamics of these structures by utilizing computational methods, including Hidden Markov Models and machine learning tools, to analyze gene neighborhoods and co-expression networks across various human phenotypes. To achieve this, metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and metaproteomic datasets from repositories such as GMrepo and the IBD Multi-omics Database will be harmonized and paired at the individual sample level to track functional activity and validate protein expression. This comprehensive analysis is expected to provide fundamental insights into the evolutionary history of cellular compartmentalization and generate foundational data to advance the rational design of synthetic biology and biotechnological applications."

abstract_original: Once considered exclusive to eukaryotes, subcellular organelles are now recognized as common features of prokaryotic cells. Bacterial organelles exhibit remarkable diversity and specialization, falling into three structural classes: protein-bounded compart- ments, lipid-bounded compartments, and biomolecular condensates. While recent model sys- tem studies have uncovered molecular mechanisms controlling the formation and function of several bacterial organelles, their activities in ecological contexts, environmental responsive- ness, and inter-organelle interactions remain poorly characterized. Here, we propose a com- munity synthesis approach to define the landscape of bacterial organelles in the human gut mi- crobiome using publicly available multi-omics data. We have assembled a team of experts on the genetics and biochemistry of bacterial microcompartments, encapsulins, ferrosomes, and biomolecular condensates. With input from NCEMS staff we will enumerate the occurrence of bacterial organelles from metagenomic datasets and examine meta-transcriptomic and meta- proteomic data to characterize their regulation and expression. This framework will allow us to test key hypotheses, such as whether organelles with overlapping functions can co-exist within the same organisms as well as various members of a microbial community and how organelle expression patterns change in response to environmental conditions. We will also examine co- ordinated expression between organelles, which will provide insights into potential inter-orga- nelle interactions. These studies will form the basis for publications on the distribution, co-oc- currence, and functional roles of bacterial organelles. The generated data will guide future hy- potheses, shed light on the evolutionary trajectory of cellular compartmentalization, and enable the rational design of biotechnological applications based on the unique features of bacterial organelles.

title: From Protein Knots to Pierced Lassos: Unraveling the Evolutionary Origin of Complex Topologies
title_norm: from protein knots to pierced lassos unraveling the evolutionary origin of complex topologies
abstract_text:
[
  "In the domains of structural bioinformatics and protein evolution, research focuses on the emergence and functional consequences of complex protein topologies such as knots, slipknots, and lassos. Despite current databases containing sequence and structural annotations, the exact evolutionary branch points where these nontrivial topologies first emerged remain unknown. The primary objective is to integrate structural and phylogenetic databases to reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees for 9 knotted protein superfamilies and 26 lasso protein families, thereby tracking the emergence of entangled topologies. This approach synthesizes data from repositories like UniProt, PDB, and OMA by overlaying functional and evolutionary features onto phylogenetic maps, while utilizing AI sequence models and computational structural modeling to fill information gaps at divergence points. Pinpointing the evolutionary origins of these complex topologies will provide mechanistic insights into protein stability, function, and disease virulence, ultimately enabling the rational design of proteins with specific topological properties."
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain is structural bioinformatics and protein evolution, focusing on the emergence and functional consequences of complex protein topologies such as knots, slipknots, and lassos. The primary objective is to integrate structural and phylogenetic databases to identify the precise evolutionary turning points where topological changes occurred, as current databases do not map these evolutionary branch points. Identifying the evolutionary origins of complex protein topologies will provide mechanistic insights into protein stability, function, and disease virulence, enabling the rational design of proteins with specific topological properties.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study will reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees for nine knotted protein superfamilies and twenty-six lasso protein families by mapping sequence, structure, and functional data to track the emergence of entangled topologies. Key tools and methods include KnotProt 2.0, LassoProt, AlphaProt 2.0, and AlphaLasso for topological predictions, OMA for orthologous clades, TimeTree for divergence estimation, and AI-based structural modeling via GPUs. Results will be validated against manually verified topological annotations and by modeling multiple representatives and seeds at estimated evolutionary branch points to account for potential false positives.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will utilize UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold DB, KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, AlphaLasso, OMA, TimeTree, PhosphoSitePlus, Human Protein Atlas, MobiDb, InterPro, PROSITE, Meltome Atlas, MaveDB, DepMap, Open Targets Platform, DisGeNet, NCBI Virus, and GISAID. Datasets will be synthesized by using UniProt references to overlay functional, evolutionary, and structural features onto reconstructed phylogenetic maps to identify statistically significant patterns. Data limitations regarding missing sequences and a lack of structural information at evolutionary branch points will be addressed by using AI sequence models to fill gaps and generating computational structural models at multiple predicted branch points.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "The twenty-four-month timeline includes data integration for knotted proteins in months one through six, generating trees and structural models in months seven through ten, a first publication in months eleven through fourteen, investigating additional topologies in months fifteen through twenty, and a second publication in months twenty-one through twenty-four. Collaboration is required because integrating large-scale sequence, topological, and evolutionary databases alongside computationally intensive structural modeling exceeds the capacity and domain expertise of any single subgroup.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "Open science plans include publishing at least two primary literature articles and providing an open, data-driven platform for studying protein entanglement. The team includes evolutionary analysis expert Dr. Ryan Cheng, student Virangi Hewage, an existing Working Group, and requested NCEMS personnel comprising a Staff Scientist and a Staff Scientist Assistant."
}

abstract_original: Proteins can adopt intricate three-dimensional structures, including complex topologies such as knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and even more complex structures. These entangled architectures challenge traditional views of protein folding and stability, suggesting that nature may use topological complexity as a mechanism to fine-tune function, regulation, or mechanical resilience. Despite growing structural data, the evolutionary origins and functional consequences of these nontrivial topologies remain largely unexplored. This project aims to leverage existing databases to identify the evolutionary turning points at which topological changes first arose within protein families. By integrating sequence, structural, and phylogenetic data from resources such as UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold, AlphaKnot, and AlphaLasso, we will reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees that map the emergence and diversification of entangled proteins across evolutionary time. We will analyze whether specific sequence motifs, disulfide patterns, or intrinsically disordered regions are associated with the onset of entanglement, and whether such proteins are enriched in pathogenic or stress-adapted organisms. Furthermore, we will assess how topological complexity correlates with functional hotspots, including catalytic or allosteric regions, to reveal possible adaptive advantages. This work will establish a framework to trace, predict, and design protein topologies with distinct structural and functional characteristics. The outcomes will not only deepen our understanding of how topology shapes evolution and biomolecular behavior but also provide an open, data-driven platform for studying entanglement as a functional and evolutionary principle in protein science.

title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
title_norm: deciphering systemic biological networks through aidriven multiomic integration
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain is molecular and cellular biology, focusing specifically on bidirectional organ cross-talk that maintains physiological homeostasis and drives systemic adaptation during endurance exercise. Current knowledge characterizes organ communication primarily at the single-organ level, leaving the molecular architecture, directionality, and temporal regulation of inter-organ signaling at the whole-organism level largely unexplored. To address this limitation, the primary objective is to map molecular responses across omic layers and time to determine inter-organ cross-talk and create an active digital twin rat to simulate systemic adaptation.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study utilizes vertical multi-omic integration within specific organs followed by horizontal integration across organs, employing a bidirectional feedback loop between physical experimental data and a computational digital twin model. Key analytical methods include principal component analysis for dimensionality reduction, a reaction-diffusion equation framework, graph Laplacian operators to encode inter-organ connectivity, and physics-informed neural networks to capture nonlinear biochemical processes. Results will undergo validation through a bidirectional feedback loop where digital twin predictions are iteratively updated and benchmarked against continuous empirical measurements and in vivo experiments from the physical rat.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will use publicly available, large-scale, longitudinal multi-omic datasets derived from eighteen solid tissues of MoTrPAC rats subjected to an eight-week endurance exercise training program. These datasets will be integrated by preprocessing longitudinal multi-omic measurements with principal component analysis, followed by the application of a hybrid framework that models inter-organ connectivity and captures organ-specific regulatory processes. The limitation of using heterogeneous datasets is addressed by analyzing multi-omic data collected from the exact same animals, while challenges of limited data are mitigated by employing a physics-informed loss function that combines mechanistic modeling with data-driven learning.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "Year one milestones include the multi-omic integration of at least one organ, the publication of a proof-of-principle study, and the submission of an NIH-R01 proposal. Year two milestones include completing the map of inter-organ interactions and identifying the molecular drivers of physiological adaptation.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The research team comprises a biological project leader who requires cross-disciplinary collaborators with expertise in computational data sciences, bioinformatics, and machine learning to integrate multi-scale datasets, alongside potentially assigned staff scientists. The proposal does not specify that information."
}

abstract_original: Organ cross-talk refers to the bidirectional communication between different organs that enables the body to maintain physiological homeostasis, respond and adapt during dynamic states. Disturbances to these inter-organ communication networks may result in inappropriate physiological responses, thereby compromising systemic function. This proposal will leverage a unique publicly available large-scale, multi-organ, multi-omic dataset comprising 18 solid tissues from rats subjected to an endurance exercise training program. Our hypothesis is that organ-specific signaling hierarchies will determines the coordinated multiorgan responses that drive systemic adaptation. Following organ-specific multi-omic vertical integration, we will determine 1) the predictors of phenotypic adaptations, and 2) the cross talk between organs via horizontal integration. The computed networks will provide the foundation to generate a digital twin rat which will serve as a valuable tool to model organismal responses to physiological, environmental and pharmacological challenges. This comprehensive, temporally resolved analysis will offer unprecedented insights into how molecular interactions are coordinated across organs and levels of organization to determine whole-organism physiological function.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: conserved disorder learning sequence conservation from functional constraints in intrinsically disordered regions
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "Current knowledge in protein biophysics establishes structure-function relationships for folded domains, but intrinsically disordered regions evolve rapidly, exhibit highly flexible conformations, and lack specific functional annotations mapping sequence features to function. A significant scientific gap remains regarding how these rapidly evolving and sequence-diverse intrinsically disordered regions encode functional specificity. To establish a foundation for functional annotation and provide a framework connecting sequence, structural ensembles, and biological function, the primary objective is to systematically identify and characterize conserved intrinsically disordered regions across proteomes by integrating evolutionary, structural, and functional experimental data.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design synthesizes large-scale evolutionary and structural data by analyzing human and viral proteomes through the integration of sequence motifs, deep mutational scanning data, post-translational modifications, and molecular dynamics simulations. Key analytical methods include all-atom explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations, AIUpred disorder prediction, ELM prediction tools, a machine learning framework, and physicochemical descriptor calculations utilizing fragment windows of five to ten residues. The resulting findings will be validated by utilizing orthologue databases, such as OrthoDB and Ensembl, to provide an independent line of evidence for cross-species sequence conservation.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will utilize diverse datasets and databases, including UniProt, ELM, IDRome, MaveDB, GISAID, MobiDB, ProteinGym, ClinVar, PhosphoSitePlus, OrthoDB, and Ensembl. These datasets will be synthesized by combining experimentally annotated motifs, predicted motifs, deep mutational scanning data, and post-translational modification annotations to construct a proteome-scale map of functionally constrained intrinsically disordered regions. To address the limitation that conservation rarely occurs at the single-residue level in these regions, researchers will calculate averaged sequence features across five to ten residue fragment windows and analyze highly variable viral proteomes to track functional maintenance.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "Project milestones span a two-year timeline, beginning with database curation and shared infrastructure setup in the first six months, followed by establishing quantitative conservation criteria and initiating simulations in months seven through twelve. Cross-disciplinary collaboration integrating molecular biophysics, bioinformatics, data-driven modeling, and experimental expertise will enable the completion of the database and analysis of structural mechanisms by month eighteen, culminating in public release and manuscript submissions by month twenty-four.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The research team is composed of researchers from the Mittal, Soranno, and Zheng laboratories, supported by NCEMS staff scientists including Dr. Daniel Nissley. Open science plans involve building a curated, open-access database of conserved intrinsically disordered regions hosted via CyVerse, developing reproducible computational workflows, and ensuring open-access data dissemination."
}

abstract_original: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins play essential roles in regulation, signaling, and molecular recognition, yet their evolutionary conservation patterns remain poorly understood. While folded domains exhibit clear conservation of structure and function, IDRs evolve rapidly and appear sequence diverse, obscuring how they encode functional specificity. Bridging the sequence function relationship in IDRs and even their reliable functional annotation remains a major challenge. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that subsets of IDRs harbor conserved sequence features such as short linear motifs (SLiMs), charge patterning and aromatic clustering that give rise to transient structural elements and encode critical molecular functions. This project aims to systematically identify and characterize the most conserved IDRs across proteomes by integrating large-scale sequence alignments, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental functional annotations from publicly available databases. By combining resources such as UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM), IDRome, and MaveDB, we will quantify the interplay between evolutionary, structural, and functional signatures of conservation in disordered regions. Our multidisciplinary Working Group unites computational and experimental biophysics to build a curated, open-access database of conserved IDRs. This synthesis effort will reveal how dynamic, flexible protein regions maintain specific and evolvable functions, an emergent property at the mesoscale interface between sequence evolution, molecular structure, and cellular regulation.
target_proposal_title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
title_norm: integrative multiomics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain encompasses mammalian physiology and functional genomics, specifically focusing on the molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms of hibernation across diverse mammalian species. While current research provides insight into lineage-specific hibernation genes, the shared versus lineage-specific transcriptional mechanisms remain largely unresolved because studies lack comparative, phylogenetically-informed analyses that weight evolutionary relatedness. The primary objective is to identify conserved and lineage-specific molecular processes using a phylogenetic framework, which will advance the understanding of mammalian metabolic adaptation and offer potential translational applications for treating human conditions such as ischemia, metabolic disorders, and insulin resistance.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study employs a comparative phylogenetic approach to analyze RNA-sequencing data by testing for convergent gene expression shifts in active states and utilizing a bivariate trait evolution model to compare active and hibernating states. The analytical pipeline integrates FastQC, STAR, and featureCounts for data processing, OrthoFinder and Cactus for genome alignment, and EVE, CAGEE, clusterProfiler, and univariate and bivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models for phylogenetic expression analysis and pathway enrichment. Model performance will be validated using simulation tests, and the relative model fit will be evaluated using the corrected Akaike Information Criterion.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "The project will utilize publicly available RNA-sequencing datasets from the NCBI Short Read Archive that span multiple tissues from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals, along with reference genomes and whole-genome alignments. Datasets will be synthesized by mapping reads to reference genomes, identifying orthologs with OrthoFinder, aligning genomes with Cactus, and analyzing the unified data through phylogenetically-informed trait evolution models. The limitation of sparse datasets lacking uniform tissue representation across species will be addressed by developing novel phylogenetic framework tools that model trait evolution and account for missing data.",

Cross-disciplinary collaboration is required to ensure project feasibility because unifying multi-omics datasets across species demands diverse expertise in cell physiology, molecular biology, bioinformatics, and computational phylogenetics that exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "The project will adhere to open science best practices by utilizing and releasing open-source software and publishing a curated dataset of hibernation-related studies for future research use. abstract_original: Hibernation is a complex physiological strategy that allows certain mammals to withstand prolonged periods of resource scarcity and low temperatures by dramatically suppressing metabolism, while maintaining organ integrity and preserving muscle and bone mass. Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
abstract_text:
{
  "abstract": "Within the domain of protein biophysics and molecular evolution, a critical area of investigation is the phenomenon of allostery in transporter proteins. The primary scientific gap is the lack of understanding regarding the sequence, structural, and dynamic features that distinguish allosterically regulated proteins from non-regulated counterparts, a challenge compounded by existing databases lacking negative examples for effective comparative analysis. To identify the biophysical features and evolutionary origins of allosteric mechanisms, this study compares transporter proteins with and without domain insertions—acting as a proxy for regulation—using molecular dynamics, sequence analysis, and artificial intelligence models. Existing sequence, structural, and mutational data from resources such as the Allosteric Database, Transport Protein Data Base, MAVEdb, InterPro, UniProt, and the Protein Data Bank will be combined, annotated, and labeled to construct a unified augmented allosterome database. Validated through the computational prediction of allosteric residues and regulatory mutations, this research will enable the annotation of novel allosteric systems, improve the interpretation of disease-associated mutations, aid in predicting druggable sites, and support synthetic allosteric system design."

abstract_original: Allostery is a fundamental property of proteins wherein perturbations at one site can influence another distant site. Understanding the sequence, structural, and dynamic determinants of allostery is critical to engineering new biosensors, designing allosteric modulators, and predicting the functional impact of mutations. For many proteins, allostery allows control of protein activity in response to external stimuli, such as ligand binding, protein or nucleic acid interactions, post-translational modifications, light, and redox state. There are proteins, though, that do not clearly exhibit such regulatory mechanisms, and are thus rarely included in publicly available allosteric databases. Consequently, it remains unclear what features distinguish regulated systems and regulatory sites from their non-regulated counterparts. To this end, we will focus our work on a specific class of proteins—namely transporter proteins—and assemble a database that is, on the one hand, very specific—restricted to all such proteins, and broad because it includes proteins for which there is a lack of evidence for allosteric regulation. This augmented allosteric database will provide a basis for identifying the degree of allostery in proteins. Through these databases, and associated computational interrogations, we will reveal the determinants of allostery in transporter proteins, a large and diverse family of membrane proteins comprised of allosteric and non-allosteric members.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
authors: Rajib Saha; Sara Mathieson; Matteo Fumagalli
abstract_original: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.
target_proposal_title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
full_text:
{
  "SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION": "The research domain is proteome homeostasis, specifically focusing on the scientific gap regarding how protein turnover kinetics and half-lives vary or are conserved across different species and domains of life. The primary objective is to harmonize fragmented, publicly available protein turnover datasets across E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens to establish a unified quantitative framework for cross-species meta-analysis. This research is significant because it aims to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles governing protein stability, establishing shared community standards and a comprehensive cross-kingdom database to evaluate how protein lifetimes influence cellular adaptation.",
  "METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH": "The study design involves assembling existing proteomics datasets, re-fitting turnover rates with unified kinetic models, mapping orthologous proteins, and applying multivariate and machine-learning analyses to correlate stability with biophysical properties. Key methods and tools include single- and multi-exponential decay models, non-linear least squares, Bayesian sampling, OrthoDB, UniProt, structural prediction algorithms, protein language models, and deep neural networks using PyTorch. Results will be validated by evaluating multi-target prediction models using reconstruction loss metrics and benchmarking prediction accuracy against baseline models such as existing degron databases.",
  "DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN": "Datasets include dynamic-labeling mass spectrometry data from repositories like PRIDE, structural predictions, and proteome-wide thermodynamic stability measurements from SPROX, TPP, and CETSA. These datasets will be integrated by reanalyzing raw intensity data using consistent computational workflows, standardizing metadata with controlled vocabularies, and combining intrinsic sequence features with structural and extrinsic proteostasis network data. Known data limitations will be addressed by correcting for precursor enrichment kinetics and applying unified models that accommodate multiple degradation phases to resolve incompatible modeling across independent studies.",
  "FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE": "Milestones span a 24-month period, progressing from dataset cataloging, sequential data re-analysis, and ortholog mapping during the first year, to cross-species modeling, database releases, manuscript drafting, and final synthesis in the second year. The project relies on collaboration to integrate distinct expertise in dynamic labeling, quantitative mass spectrometry, data harmonization, large-scale systems modeling, and evolutionary biology that no single laboratory possesses.",
  "OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION": "Open science plans include hosting the Protein Stability Database via NCEMS infrastructure in an archival format, adhering to FAIR principles, releasing all code through CyVerse and GitHub, and publishing open-access manuscripts. The team consists of three Principal Investigators, one Staff Scientist allocated at thirty-three percent effort for twelve months, and one Staff Scientist Assistant allocated at fifty percent effort for twelve months."
}

abstract_original: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.
