title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text:
{
  "abstract": "The research domain of spatial omics focuses on the cross-modal synthesis of spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics at subcellular resolution to investigate cell state and fate. A critical scientific gap exists in understanding how the subcellular spatial organization of RNA and proteins independently predicts cell fate decisions, as current analyses treat these molecules as separate, abundance-centric measurements due to alignment difficulties and a lack of multimodal workflows. The primary objective is to develop a computational synthesis framework that builds a pipeline of image registration, grid harmonization, and multimodal embedding models to align paired spatial data into predictive biophysical fingerprints. Utilizing paired RNA and protein spatial maps from adjacent human cancer sections, the integration strategy corrects for non-rigid tissue distortion via diffeomorphic mapping to register molecular data into a common coordinate framework with shared pixel grids for one-to-one subcellular patch correspondence. This approach is significant because it shifts spatial omics analysis beyond abundance-only baselines by testing whether integrated RNA-protein spatial relationships provide early predictive signals for biophysical sub-states and lineage trajectories."

title: Emergent Phase Separation Grammar: Decoding How Intrinsically Disordered Region Sequence Patterns Drive Mesoscale Condensate Properties
title_norm: emergent phase separation grammar decoding how intrinsically disordered region sequence patterns drive mesoscale condensate properties
abstract_text: In cellular biology, liquid liquid phase separation driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions and multivalent interactions controls the formation, physical properties, and organization of biomolecular condensates. However, how specific molecular sequences, structures, and chemical modifications determine condensate dynamics remains unknown because existing data are scattered across separate databases without systematic integration. To establish predictive rules connecting molecular features to mesoscale condensate properties, this project will compile a feature database, apply deep neural networks, perform automated cell image segmentation, and construct coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations. The study will integrate data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, PhaSePro, and the Human Protein Atlas by creating standardized naming systems and using tensor decomposition to link imaging with molecular profiling. These predictive rules will transition condensate research from observation to prediction, helping to identify therapeutic targets for diseases associated with abnormal protein aggregation like cancer and neurodegenerative disorders.
full_text:
Cellular biology lacks understanding of how molecular sequences determine the formation of biomolecular condensates through liquid phase separation. Disordered protein regions and multivalent interactions drive phase separation but data remain scattered across databases without systematic integration. This project connects molecular features to properties of condensates to identify therapeutic targets for diseases with abnormal protein aggregation.

The study design integrates a database of molecular features with machine learning (ML) and cellular imaging to construct multi scale simulations. Methods include random forests and deep neural networks alongside automated segmentation of cell images and coarse grained simulations of molecular dynamics. The team validates results through cross validation on independent datasets and comparison with literature using Bayesian methods for uncertainty.

The project utilizes structural databases such as the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Database alongside interaction and imaging repositories. Standardized systems of naming map proteins across databases while quality control and tensor decomposition integrate imaging with profiling of molecules. Standardized ontologies and pipelines for filtering of data mitigate heterogeneity while protocols for cross validation prevent leakage of data.

Over a three year timeline the project builds a public database and releases predictive software and develops multi scale simulations. This scope requires multi lab collaboration to combine scientific expertise in biophysics and ML alongside extensive computational resources.

The team shares all code for analysis and datasets publicly under FAIR principles alongside user friendly tools for prediction. The team spans five institutions and trains postdoctoral researchers and undergraduate students through cross laboratory exchanges and public workshops.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) self-organize into membraneless organelles with properties not predictable from individual molecular components. This synthesis project will decode the 'grammar' connecting IDP sequence features to emergent condensate behaviors by integrating multiple public datasets. We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), disorder predictions from MobiDB and DisProt, phase separation propensity scores from PhaSePro and LLPSDB, proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas, and single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas to understand how sequence-encoded information translates to mesoscale organization. The central hypothesis is that specific combinations of sequence motifs—rather than individual features—create emergent interaction networks that dictate condensate material properties, composition, and cellular function. We will employ natural language processing approaches adapted for protein sequences, treating amino acid patterns as a 'language' with grammatical rules governing phase behavior. Machine learning models will identify synergistic motif combinations that predict condensate viscosity, surface tension, and client recruitment capacity. Network analysis will map how these sequence features create emergent interaction topologies at the mesoscale. Graph neural networks will model the collective behavior of multiple IDP chains, predicting how molecular-level interactions scale to condensate-level properties. A key innovation is correlating sequence grammar with cellular phenotypes by integrating GWAS data from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog, connecting IDP variants to disease states through altered mesoscale organization. This project requires transdisciplinary collaboration between computational biophysicists expert in IDP behavior, machine learning specialists in sequence analysis, cell biologists studying condensate function, and statistical geneticists linking variants to phenotypes. The synthesis spans molecular sequence databases, structural repositories, cellular imaging archives, and population genetics resources—a scope impossible for any single laboratory. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for condensate properties from sequence, identification of 'grammatical rules' governing phase separation, and mechanistic insights into how condensate dysregulation causes disease. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and curated datasets will be publicly released following FAIR principles. This work will transform our understanding of how information encoded in linear sequences emerges as three-dimensional mesoscale organization with distinct functional properties.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Ribosome Clustering: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Ribosome Profiling Data to Understand Emergent Translation Factories
title_norm: temporal dynamics of ribosome clustering synthesizing cryoet and ribosome profiling data to understand emergent translation factories
abstract_text: Temporal dynamics and rewiring patterns of protein protein interaction networks regulate critical cellular processes like the cell cycle, circadian rhythms, and stress responses, making their characterization essential for understanding cellular physiology. However, researchers currently lack a systematic understanding of how these networks reorganize over time and cannot integrate static interaction databases with temporal molecular datasets to model dynamic network changes. This project will construct time resolved protein interaction networks and predict cellular phenotypes by applying dynamic time warping, probabilistic interaction modeling, Gaussian process interpolation, frequent subgraph mining, and machine learning with attention mechanisms. The study will integrate diverse datasets from repositories including PRIDE, GEO, BioGRID, and STRING by mapping identifiers to UniProt, correcting batch effects, and combining time series molecular abundance data with static interaction priors. Ultimately, these predictive models and dynamic network representations will transition network analysis from static models to dynamic systems, bridging molecular level changes with system level cellular behaviors.
full_text:
This study investigates the temporal dynamics of networks of protein protein interactions to address how reorganization relates to cellular state transitions. Existing databases contain static interactions and temporal datasets but researchers have not integrated these resources to model dynamic network changes. The objective is to construct dynamic networks to bridge changes at the molecular level with cellular behaviors at the system level.

The design of the study involves harmonizing public datasets to construct probabilistic networks and train models of machine learning. Key methods include dynamic time warping and interpolation of Gaussian processes and decomposition of tensors and machine learning with attention mechanisms. Validation of the models will employ cross validation and statistical randomization with null models and measurements of physical interactions.

The team will obtain datasets from public repositories including the Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Integration involves mapping identifiers to UniProt and aligning temporal scales and combining abundance data of time series with static priors. Because data heterogeneity arises from different designs of experiments, the team will apply standardized preprocessing and correction of batch effects.

Over three years the project will deliver a temporal database and three packages of software and validated models of prediction. This multi lab project requires diverse expertise because the scope spans multiple biological processes and complex computational infrastructure.

The team will support open science by releasing the database and distributing documented packages of software with online tutorials. The cross disciplinary team includes researchers at all stages of careers and offers opportunities for training through mentored research.

abstract_original: Translation occurs not through isolated ribosomes but within dynamic mesoscale clusters called 'translation factories' or polysomes, where emergent properties arise from ribosome cooperation. This synthesis project investigates how ribosome clustering creates emergent translational behaviors—including enhanced processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation—that cannot be predicted from single ribosome properties. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and EMDB revealing in-situ ribosome spatial organization, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data from GEO and GWIPS-viz capturing translation dynamics, structural data from PDB on ribosome-associated factors, and proteomics from PRIDE quantifying translation machinery stoichiometry. The central question is: how do spatial arrangements of ribosomes at the mesoscale (50-500 nm polysome structures) create emergent translational properties distinct from summed individual ribosome activities? Our computational approach combines spatial statistics analysis of cryo-ET reconstructions to characterize ribosome clustering patterns, kinetic modeling of translation dynamics informed by Ribo-seq pausing patterns, and agent-based simulations of polysome behavior. We will develop novel algorithms to segment and classify polysome architectures from tomographic data, then correlate these structures with mRNA-specific translation efficiencies from Ribo-seq. Machine learning will identify features of polysome organization predictive of translation output, protein folding efficiency, and co-translational assembly. Integration with protein-protein interaction networks from STRING and BioGRID will reveal how nascent chain interactions within polysomes enable emergent co-translational complex assembly. This project demands expertise spanning cryo-ET image analysis, translation biology, mathematical modeling, and machine learning—capabilities distributed across specialized laboratories. The data synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural snapshots with dynamic sequencing readouts across different experimental systems. Expected insights include principles governing polysome architecture, quantitative relationships between mesoscale ribosome organization and translation output, and mechanisms of emergent co-translational protein folding. Deliverables include open-source tools for polysome analysis, curated cross-referenced datasets, and predictive models of translation factory behavior. Understanding these emergent translation properties has implications for synthetic biology and diseases involving translation dysregulation.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Biophysical, and Transport Data to Model Collective Gating Behavior
title_norm: emergent mechanics of the nuclear pore complex integrating structural biophysical and transport data to model collective gating behavior
abstract_text: Physical interfaces between mitochondria and other cellular compartments regulate essential cellular functions, and extensive structural, molecular, and genetic data describing these contact sites reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain separated by discipline, preventing researchers from understanding how the nanometer scale physical structure of these contact sites determines their functional roles in signaling and metabolism. This project will establish the structural principles of mitochondrial contact sites by computationally integrating multi omics datasets using AlphaFold, molecular docking, network analysis, and machine learning algorithms to predict functions and map disease mutations. Data from EMPIAR, the Protein Data Bank, ProteomeXchange, and ClinVar will be integrated by fitting protein structures into electron tomography density maps and establishing a unified multi omics data model. These predictive models will define general rules for cellular membrane interfaces, guide future laboratory experiments, and identify disease mechanisms to support therapeutic design.
full_text:
This study investigates physical interfaces of mitochondria with other cellular compartments to resolve how structures at the nanometer scale determine function. Although general functions of contact sites are documented in separate public repositories, these diverse datasets have not been combined. The project seeks to establish structural principles of contact sites to provide predictive models and identify mechanisms of human disease.

The study design relies on computational integration of diverse datasets to generate structural models and train machine learning algorithms. Key methods include pipelines for image segmentation and software for structural prediction alongside neural networks and analysis of molecular networks. The team will validate results using techniques for cross validation across different types of cells and statistical analyses of parameters.

The project will utilize structural and genetic data from the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The team will integrate datasets by fitting structures of proteins into density maps and establishing a unified model for data. To address variability across public datasets, the project will implement uniform pipelines for image segmentation and standardized protocols for analysis.

Over a three year period, the project will launch a public database and create predictive models of contact sites. Collaboration is necessary because the project requires expertise in biology and computational modeling that no single laboratory possesses.

The team will share all findings and analysis code on GitHub while releasing integrated data through a public database. The team includes researchers from multiple career stages across seven institutions and offers training in data integration for students.

abstract_original: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) exemplifies mesoscale emergence: ~500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins create a selective barrier with transport properties unpredictable from individual protein behaviors. This synthesis project will develop comprehensive models of emergent NPC gating by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB capturing NPC architecture, molecular dynamics trajectories from GPCRmd and similar repositories, single-molecule transport kinetics from published studies compiled in curated databases, FG-nup sequence data from UniProt, and nuclear proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas defining cargo flux. The fundamental question is: how do collective FG-nup dynamics create the emergent selective barrier that simultaneously enables rapid transport of specific cargoes while excluding others? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from mesoscale FG-nup network properties—including collective conformational states, transient crosslinks, and cargo-induced reorganization—rather than simple additive binding interactions. Our analytical approach employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics informed by structural data to simulate FG-nup meshwork behavior, network theory to model connectivity patterns, and machine learning to identify collective states from simulation ensembles. We will develop Markov state models capturing transitions between emergent barrier configurations, correlating these with experimental transport rates. Integration of phosphoproteomics data from PhosphoSitePlus will reveal how post-translational modifications tune emergent barrier properties. Cross-species comparative analysis using orthologous NPC data will identify conserved principles of emergent selectivity. This project requires collaboration between structural biologists interpreting NPC architecture, polymer physicists modeling FG-nup behavior, computational chemists running simulations, and cell biologists understanding transport regulation. The synthesis challenge—connecting angstrom-scale structural data to nanometer-scale meshwork organization to micron-scale transport phenotypes—exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent NPC selectivity, identification of collective FG-nup states governing transport, and principles applicable to designing synthetic selective barriers. All simulation protocols, analysis code, and model parameters will be openly shared, enabling community refinement of NPC models.

title: Chromatin Compartmentalization Dynamics: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Model Emergent Nuclear Organization
title_norm: chromatin compartmentalization dynamics synthesizing hic imaging and epigenomic data to model emergent nuclear organization
abstract_text: Cellular biophysics research demonstrates that high macromolecular density within the cytoplasm alters protein folding, diffusion, and phase behavior, which critically influences molecular behaviors and spatial organization at the mesoscale. However, a lack of integrated understanding remains regarding how these molecular scale crowding effects combine to collectively govern larger scale cellular properties and organization. To map density variations and model emergent structures, this project will integrate structural and proteomics data using Voronoi tessellation, train machine learning models on biophysical measurements, and execute agent based simulations. The study will integrate databases including PaxDb, PRIDE, and the Protein Data Bank by standardizing identifiers via UniProt, calculating molecular volumes, and incorporating organelle volume data from electron microscopy. These models will establish a framework linking molecular physics to cellular organization to clarify the mechanisms behind aging, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases associated with protein aggregation.
full_text:
This study in cellular biophysics investigates how cytoplasmic density influences molecular behaviors because organization at the cellular scale remains poorly understood. Databases catalog protein structures and abundances but how cytoplasmic density alters protein folding and governs organization at the cellular scale remains unresolved. The project maps cytoplasmic density variations to link molecular physics with organization at the cellular scale and clarify mechanisms of protein aggregation.

The study design integrates structural and proteomics data to map subcellular density and trains machine learning (ML) models on biophysical measurements. The team applies Voronoi tessellation and calculations of solvent accessible surfaces and Bayesian hierarchical modeling and agent based simulations. Validation of results involves independent datasets and analyses of sensitivity and cross validation across species and experimental testing of predictions.

The project utilizes PaxDb and PRIDE and the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Database and the Human Protein Atlas. The team integrates datasets by standardizing identifiers of proteins and calculating molecular volumes and predicting subcellular localization with machine learning. Because uncertainties of measurements and experimental discrepancies exist, the team uses Bayesian hierarchical models to propagate errors and identify robust predictions.

Over three years the milestones of the project include biannual meetings of working groups and the release of a database and software. This project requires collaboration across multiple laboratories to combine diverse expertise and access computational resources beyond a single laboratory.

The team shares all findings and workflows for analysis publicly through the version controlled repositories of containerized code. The team of biophysicists and computational scientists at various stages of careers provides opportunities for training and research during summer for undergraduates.

abstract_original: Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and nuclear bodies represents emergent mesoscale structure arising from DNA-protein interactions. This synthesis project will integrate multi-modal data to understand how molecular-level chromatin modifications create emergent nuclear compartmentalization with functional consequences. We will synthesize Hi-C contact maps from 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE, super-resolution imaging data from the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library, ChIP-seq for histone modifications and chromatin proteins from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, ATAC-seq accessibility data, and single-cell multi-omics from the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis is that emergent compartmentalization arises from phase separation driven by multivalent interactions among modified histones and reader proteins, creating mesoscale domains (100 nm - 1 μm) with distinct biochemical environments. We will develop integrative computational frameworks combining polymer physics models of chromatin, machine learning for predicting 3D organization from sequence and epigenetic features, and spatial statistics for analyzing imaging data. Novel algorithms will integrate contact frequencies with spatial positions, resolving the relationship between measured interactions and physical distances. Network analysis will identify emergent chromatin communities and their hierarchical organization. We will correlate compartmentalization patterns with transcriptional output using RNA-seq from matched samples, testing whether emergent nuclear organization causally influences gene expression or vice versa. Cross-cell-type analysis will reveal conserved versus cell-specific emergent organizational principles. This project demands expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and genomics—requiring collaboration across traditionally separate fields. The data integration challenge spans contact maps, images, and sequencing data at different resolutions and from different experimental systems. Expected insights include quantitative models of compartmentalization emergence, identification of key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, and understanding of how nuclear structure influences function. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and integrated datasets will be publicly released, establishing resources for the chromosome biology community.

title: Emergent Allostery in Protein Complexes: Mining Structural Databases to Discover Long-Range Communication Networks
title_norm: emergent allostery in protein complexes mining structural databases to discover longrange communication networks
abstract_text: Cellular polarity, driven by the self organization of molecular components to establish spatial asymmetry, is a fundamental biological process that regulates intermediate scale protein clusters and dictates overall cellular organization. Currently, it is not understood how these components function collectively as a system, how observations from different experimental models fit together, or how intermediate scale structures dictate tissue behaviors. To address this, the project will map molecular networks, model intermediate scale physical structures, and predict tissue level outcomes across species using graph neural networks, physical models of diffusion, and machine learning classifiers. The study will integrate diverse databases, including AlphaFold, BioGRID, and the Human Cell Atlas, by mapping structural data onto protein networks and using neural networks to link imaging and proteomics datasets. This multi scale integration framework will establish predictive models of cell polarity, providing critical insights into developmental diseases and cancer associated with polarity defects.
full_text:
This study investigates cellular polarity to resolve how molecular interactions coordinate to establish spatial asymmetry at the intermediate scale. Although specific proteins and lipids regulate polarity, the collective function of these components across different models remains unknown. The project maps molecular networks to predict tissue characteristics, which is novel because it integrates isolated multi scale datasets.

The study uses a three part analytical design to map molecular networks and predict tissue level outcomes across multiple species. Key methods include network analysis software and graph neural networks alongside physical models of diffusion and machine learning classifiers. The team will validate results by generating testable predictions for laboratory experiments and using cross validation for computational models.

The project will utilize databases including BioGRID and AlphaFold and UniProt alongside the Human Cell Atlas and DepMap. The team will integrate datasets by mapping structural data onto protein networks and applying multi modal frameworks to combine transcriptomic data. The proposed study does not address information regarding known data limitations and the corresponding mitigation strategies for this project.

The project spans a three year duration with milestones including three annual collaborative meetings and two summer training workshops. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in cell biology and physics and computational science for data integration.

The team will share all datasets and code publicly using version control and containerized pipelines and a dedicated web portal. The team comprises scientists from six institutions at various career stages and offers training through cross laboratory exchanges and workshops.

abstract_original: Allosteric regulation in multi-subunit protein complexes represents emergent behavior where binding events at one site influence distant sites through collective conformational changes—properties absent in isolated subunits. This synthesis project will systematically discover and characterize emergent allosteric networks by mining structural databases. We will integrate the Protein Data Bank (>200,000 structures), molecular dynamics trajectories from MDAnalysis and related repositories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) data from HDXsite, and mutational fitness landscapes from deep mutational scanning datasets in MaveDB. All databases, analysis tools, and predictive models will be openly released, enabling rational design of allosteric modulators and understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from subunit assembly.

title: Cytoskeletal Crosstalk at the Mesoscale: Integrating Structural and Live-Cell Data to Model Emergent Mechanical Properties
title_norm: cytoskeletal crosstalk at the mesoscale integrating structural and livecell data to model emergent mechanical properties
abstract_text: Intrinsically disordered regions of eukaryotic proteins form dynamic structural ensembles that mediate molecular interactions, phase separation, and post translational modifications, serving as critical regulators of diverse cellular functions. However, because relevant data remain fragmented across isolated databases, the sequence rules governing how these unstructured regions coordinate their diverse physical and functional behaviors remain unresolved and currently unpredictable. To identify these sequence rules, this project will utilize a computational design to train machine learning models and perform graph theoretic network analysis, unsupervised clustering, and statistical regression on aggregated protein data. The study will retrieve data from databases including DisProt, MobiDB, and AlphaFold2, mapping these structural, modification, interaction, and localization attributes directly onto individual protein sequences to align diverse features. Ultimately, these sequence rules will challenge the traditional structure function paradigm of protein biology and provide critical insights into disease mechanisms and synthetic biology design.

This study investigates how amino acid sequences of intrinsically disordered regions of eukaryotic proteins determine interactions but database fragmentation prevents predictions.
Although these unstructured regions mediate molecular interactions and phase separation the rules coordinating these sequence patterns remain unresolved.
The primary research question seeks sequence based rules of unstructured regions to challenge traditional structure function paradigms in protein biology.

The overall study design integrates sequence and structural data to train machine learning models and perform statistical network analyses.
The project applies sequence analysis algorithms and unsupervised clustering alongside supervised machine learning models and statistical regression.
The team will validate machine learning models using cross validation and benchmark new predictive tools against existing software.

The project utilizes diverse databases including DisProt and MobiDB and IDEAL and AlphaFold2 and the Human Protein Atlas.
The team will retrieve these datasets via application programming interfaces and map them directly onto individual protein sequences.
To mitigate the lack of experimental structural data the researchers will substitute computational predictions from molecular dynamics simulations.

Over a two year period the project milestones include establishing a unified database and developing predictive machine learning models.
Integrating molecular sequence data with cellular behaviors requires cross disciplinary expertise in bioinformatics and biophysics and cell biology.

The team will publicly release the integrated database and predictive models and documented version controlled code repositories.
The team includes early career and international researchers across seven institutions and provides cross disciplinary training opportunities.

abstract_original: The cytoskeleton exhibits emergent mechanical properties arising from interactions among actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how cytoskeletal crosstalk creates emergent cellular mechanics by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-ET data from EMPIAR showing cytoskeletal architecture, super-resolution microscopy from the Image Data Resource, mechanical measurements from published atomic force microscopy and optical trap studies, proteomics of cytoskeletal interactomes from BioPlex and hu.MAP, and transcriptomics correlating cytoskeletal gene expression with mechanical phenotypes. The fundamental question is: how do interactions between different cytoskeletal systems at the mesoscale (100 nm - 10 μm) create emergent mechanical properties—stiffness, viscosity, active stress generation—that individual filament types cannot produce? We hypothesize that crosslinker proteins create emergent mechanical coupling by forming dynamic networks whose properties depend on mesoscale organization rather than simple component addition. Our analytical approach combines finite element modeling of cytoskeletal networks informed by structural data, agent-based simulations of crosslinker dynamics, and machine learning to predict mechanical properties from network topology. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cytoskeletal organization from diverse imaging modalities, creating standardized descriptors of mesoscale architecture. Network analysis will identify key nodes (crosslinkers, motors) whose perturbation maximally alters emergent mechanics. Integration with cell migration and morphogenesis datasets will connect mesoscale cytoskeletal organization to cellular behaviors. This project demands expertise in cytoskeletal biology, mechanical engineering, image analysis, and computational modeling—capabilities distributed across different research communities. The synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural data, mechanical measurements, and cellular phenotypes across experimental systems. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent cytoskeletal mechanics, identification of key crosslinkers governing mechanical coupling, and principles for engineering cellular mechanical properties. All analysis tools, simulation code, and curated datasets will be openly shared, advancing both fundamental understanding and mechanobiology applications.

title: Emergent Specificity in Kinase-Substrate Networks: Synthesizing Phosphoproteomics and Structural Data to Decode Signaling Fidelity
title_norm: emergent specificity in kinasesubstrate networks synthesizing phosphoproteomics and structural data to decode signaling fidelity
abstract_text: In cell biology, understanding how the three distinct networks of the cellular skeleton comprising actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments interact and function as a unified system is essential for explaining cellular behavior. However, the physical and functional connections between these networks remain poorly understood, and a comprehensive integrated model of how their interactions generate system level cellular properties is currently lacking. To map these molecular interactions and model their mechanical influence, this project will utilize a computational synthesis approach applying graph theoretic network analysis, AlphaFold2 structural prediction, cross correlation analysis, and machine learning. The study will integrate diverse datasets from the Protein Data Bank, BioGRID, STRING, and the Cell Image Library by establishing standardized vocabularies and weighting interactions using machine learning. Ultimately, this integrated system model will transition the field beyond isolated components, clarifying disease mechanisms in cancer and neurodegeneration while assisting in the engineering of novel synthetic materials.
full_text:
This study of cell biology investigates unknown physical connections among actin and microtubules and intermediate filaments that generate system level properties. Researchers understand individual components of the skeleton and some linking proteins but lack a comprehensive model of coordination among networks. The primary research question examines how these molecular interactions coordinate to model an integrated system that clarifies mechanisms of disease.

The design of the study uses a computational approach that aggregates public data to build models of networks and predict behaviors. Key methods include analysis of networks and algorithms for community detection and structural prediction using AlphaFold2 and machine learning. The team validates these computational results by testing predictions against independent previously unused datasets and published experimental outcomes.

The project utilizes data from the Protein Data Bank and BioGRID and STRING and the Human Protein Atlas. The team integrates these datasets by establishing standardized vocabularies and weighting interactions and using machine learning to resolve conflicts. To mitigate variations in quality of data, the team applies quality based confidence scores and uses machine learning to flag inconsistencies.

The submitted research proposal does not address any information regarding the specific milestones of the project and the overall timeline. Collaboration among laboratories is necessary because expertise in biology of the skeleton and computational modeling exceeds a single laboratory.

The team plans to publish findings in journals with open access and release the compiled database and code for analysis publicly. The team includes researchers in biophysics and computational biology spanning multiple stages of career who offer training through laboratory exchanges.

abstract_original: Cellular signaling networks achieve remarkable specificity despite kinases sharing similar catalytic mechanisms—an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization including scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics. This synthesis project will decode how emergent specificity arises by integrating phosphoproteomics, structural biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize phosphoproteomic data from PhosphoSitePlus and PRIDE (>300,000 phosphosites), kinase-substrate relationships from PhosphoSitePlus and KinaseNET, structural data from PDB on kinase-substrate complexes, protein localization from the Human Protein Atlas, and protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and STRING. The central hypothesis is that signaling specificity emerges from mesoscale organizational features—scaffold-mediated co-localization, compartmentalization, and kinetic proofreading networks—rather than intrinsic kinase-substrate affinity alone. We will develop computational frameworks integrating sequence-based kinase specificity predictions with spatial and temporal context. Machine learning models will predict phosphorylation events by combining kinase motif recognition with localization overlap, scaffold interactions, and network topology. We will construct dynamic models of signaling cascades incorporating mesoscale organization, testing whether emergent specificity requires spatial constraints. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series data will reveal how temporal ordering creates emergent pathway specificity. Integration with disease mutation data from COSMIC and ClinVar will identify how disrupted mesoscale organization causes aberrant signaling. Cross-species comparative analysis will distinguish conserved emergent specificity mechanisms from species-specific adaptations. This project requires collaboration between signaling biologists, structural biologists, computational modelers, and data scientists—expertise distributed across institutions. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, localization, and interaction data at proteome scale exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent signaling specificity, identification of key organizational features enabling fidelity, and principles for predicting signaling outcomes. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released, enabling rational intervention in signaling pathways.

title: Metabolon Assembly and Emergent Metabolic Channeling: Integrating Structural, Metabolomic, and Interactome Data
title_norm: metabolon assembly and emergent metabolic channeling integrating structural metabolomic and interactome data
abstract_text: In cell biology, understanding how combinations of different post translational modifications on proteins interact to regulate cellular processes is essential for deciphering the complex molecular networks that control cellular decisions. However, current research focuses on isolated modifications, leaving the systemic coordination rules of multiple concurrent post translational modifications uncharacterized because existing large scale databases remain disconnected. To determine the structural and temporal rules governing combined post translational modifications, this project will construct multi layered networks and apply graph neural networks with attention mechanisms and temporal association rule mining. The study will integrate data from repositories including UniProt, PhosphoSitePlus, and AlphaFold by establishing a standardized vocabulary, uniform metadata formats, and an evidence based confidence scoring system. These predictive models and coordination rules will explain how molecular events produce complex cellular behaviors, ultimately improving drug design for diseases like cancer and metabolic disorders.
full_text:
This study in cell biology addresses how multiple types of post translational modifications interact systematically to regulate cellular decisions. Databases contain millions of sites of modification and structures of proteins but these datasets lack integration to reveal rules of coordination. This study asks how combined post translational modifications coordinate cellular behaviors to improve the design of drugs for diseases of signaling.

The proposed study uses a computational design to aggregate biological data and build multi layered networks of modification relationships. The team will apply statistical tests and graph neural networks with mechanisms of attention using software for containerization for computational reproducibility. Computational predictions will be validated using techniques of cross validation on independent datasets and shared with external laboratories for physical testing.

The project will use data from PhosphoSitePlus, UniProt, Protein Data Bank (PDB), AlphaFold, BioGRID and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Datasets will be integrated by creating a standardized vocabulary and applying a system to score confidence based on quality of evidence. To mitigate inconsistencies in naming and varying levels of confidence, the team will build a unified ontology and standardize metadata.

Over three years, the project will develop predictive models of machine learning and compile a rulebook for patterns of modification. Integrating massive datasets of molecular structures and cellular behavior requires cross disciplinary expertise that exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

All code for integration of data and predictive models will be publicly available through open source repositories and an online database. The team includes researchers from six institutions and offers opportunities for training such as rotations in laboratories and programs for undergraduates.

abstract_original: Metabolons—transient enzyme assemblies enabling substrate channeling—represent emergent mesoscale organization where metabolic efficiency exceeds predictions from isolated enzyme kinetics. This synthesis project will systematically characterize metabolon organization and emergent channeling by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from PDB on enzyme complexes, metabolomics from MetaboLights and the Human Metabolome Database, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas. The fundamental question is: how does mesoscale enzyme clustering create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced flux, reduced intermediate accumulation, pathway insulation—that isolated enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that metabolon assembly creates microenvironments with emergent kinetic properties determined by enzyme stoichiometry, spatial arrangement, and dynamic association/dissociation. Our computational approach combines constraint-based metabolic modeling incorporating channeling, molecular docking to predict enzyme complex geometries, and kinetic simulations of substrate transfer within assemblies. We will develop algorithms to identify putative metabolons from interaction networks, validating predictions against metabolomic signatures of channeling (reduced free intermediate pools). Machine learning will predict metabolon formation propensity from enzyme properties and cellular conditions. Integration with transcriptomic data will reveal how metabolon assembly responds to metabolic demands. Analysis across organisms will identify conserved metabolon architectures versus species-specific adaptations. This project demands expertise in metabolism, structural biology, systems biology, and computational chemistry—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of interaction, structural, kinetic, and metabolomic data across metabolic pathways exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive metabolon atlas, predictive models of emergent channeling efficiency, and principles governing metabolon assembly. Understanding emergent metabolic organization has implications for metabolic engineering and diseases involving metabolic dysfunction. All databases, models, and analysis tools will be openly released following FAIR principles.

title: Emergent Selectivity of Autophagy Receptors: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode Cargo Recognition Networks
title_norm: emergent selectivity of autophagy receptors synthesizing structural and proteomic data to decode cargo recognition networks
abstract_text: Cellular biology at intermediate scales focuses on stress granules, which are membraneless organelles formed by protein and RNA phase separation that regulate translation and signaling to prevent neurodegenerative diseases. However, existing data remain fragmented across unintegrated public datasets, preventing a unified understanding of stress granule components, their internal spatial organization, and their precise impact on cellular translation and survival. To map stress granule composition and construct three dimensional models of their internal architecture, this project will integrate multiomics data using Bayesian frameworks, machine learning, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and integrative modeling software. The study will synthesize public data from PRIDE, GEO, the Protein Data Bank, and DepMap using constraint based modeling and network analysis to link spatial structure with cellular phenotypes. These structural models and composition maps will establish general principles of membraneless organelle assembly and provide critical insights into pathological protein aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text:
This study investigates cellular biology at intermediate scales to resolve the unknown spatial organization of stress granules (membraneless organelles). Although stress granules regulate translation during stress, existing data on their composition remain fragmented across unintegrated public datasets. The primary objective is to map the composition of stress granules to provide insights into pathological protein aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases.

The study design integrates data from proteomics and transcriptomics to model spatial organization and correlate these models with phenotypic screening data. Key methods include MaxQuant for the processing of proteomics data and Bayesian statistical frameworks and machine learning (ML) algorithms. The team will validate machine learning models using held out datasets and select top predictions for community based experimental validation.

The project will utilize public datasets from PRIDE and MassIVE and ProteomeXchange and GEO and the Protein Data Bank. The team will integrate these datasets using Bayesian frameworks and constraint based modeling and network analysis of cellular phenotypes. To address the lack of standardization across datasets, the team will reprocess raw data using uniform software pipelines.

Over a two year timeline, the project will deliver a searchable database and structural models and reproducible workflows for analysis. This project requires multi lab collaboration to integrate expertise in RNA biology and protein biochemistry and computational integration of data.

The team will host all code in public GitHub repositories and release structural models through open access publications. The team includes researchers across various career stages from seven institutions and provides training opportunities for graduate students.

abstract_original: Selective autophagy achieves remarkable cargo specificity through receptor proteins that bridge substrates to autophagosomes—an emergent property arising from multivalent interactions at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on receptor-cargo and receptor-LC3 complexes, autophagy interactomes from BioGRID and published studies, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, organelle proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas, and autophagy flux measurements from published screens. The central question is: how do autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity at the mesoscale (10-1000 nm cargo structures) through avidity effects, coincidence detection, and cooperative binding that individual receptor-cargo interactions cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from receptor oligomerization, multivalent cargo recognition, and phase separation creating receptor condensates that amplify weak individual interactions. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of receptor-cargo assemblies, network analysis of autophagy interactomes, and machine learning to predict cargo selectivity from receptor and cargo features. We will develop coarse-grained simulations of receptor clustering on cargo surfaces, testing how avidity emerges from receptor density and cargo geometry. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted receptor-cargo recognition to pathological cargo accumulation. Comparative analysis across selective autophagy pathways (mitophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy) will reveal shared versus pathway-specific emergent selectivity mechanisms. This project requires expertise in autophagy biology, structural biology, computational modeling, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and phenotypic data across autophagy pathways exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for engineering selective autophagy. All analysis tools, models, and curated datasets will be openly released, advancing understanding of this therapeutically important pathway.

title: Emergent Timing in Circadian Protein Networks: Integrating Structural Dynamics with Systems-Level Oscillations
title_norm: emergent timing in circadian protein networks integrating structural dynamics with systemslevel oscillations
abstract_text: Cellular metabolism relies on metabolic enzymes temporarily assembling into multi protein complexes called metabolons to directly transfer chemical intermediates between sequential reactions, which improves pathway efficiency and regulation. However, the physical rules governing how these complexes assemble, their detailed physical structures, and the quantitative impacts of this organization on metabolic rates and cellular behavior remain unresolved. To identify these organizational rules across species, this project will model three dimensional structures and quantify metabolic rates using network analysis, machine learning, protein docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and comparative metabolic modeling. The study will integrate structural, interaction, and metabolic data from BioGRID, STRING, the Protein Data Bank, and UniProt into a single unified database schema by mapping enzymes to standardized UniProt classification numbers. These structural models and organizational rules will clarify disease mechanisms, improve metabolic engineering for biotechnology, and establish a model for how temporary molecular groupings generate complex cellular behaviors.
full_text:
This study investigates cellular metabolism and the assembly of enzymes into complexes to address unknown physical rules of molecular organization. Researchers know that temporary complexes improve pathway efficiency but the molecular mechanisms of assembly and physical structures remain unresolved. The primary question asks how these complexes function across species to clarify disease mechanisms and improve metabolic engineering for biotechnology.

The study design compiles biological data to map networks of interactions and constructs mathematical models of metabolic rates. The team will apply machine learning (ML) and software for docking of proteins alongside simulations of molecular dynamics. The team will validate structural models using data from cryo electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and evaluate models through cross validation.

The project will utilize data from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the AlphaFold Database. The team will integrate datasets by mapping enzymes to UniProt numbers and organizing structural data into a unified schema. To address differences in data quality, the project will apply statistical weighting and assign scores of confidence to interactions.

Over three years the project will complete a database of interactions and generate structural models alongside predictive models of metabolism. This work requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in structural biology and biochemistry with systems biology and computational modeling.

The team will make all databases and structural models publicly available while using a shared computational environment for reproducibility. The team features early career scientists across six institutions who will provide workshops and research projects for undergraduate students.

This synthesis project will decode how circadian timing emerges by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and systems biology datasets. Integration with tissue-specific expression data will explain how the same molecular components generate different emergent periods across tissues. Comparative analysis across species will identify conserved emergent timing mechanisms versus species-specific adaptations. This project demands expertise in circadian biology, structural biology, mathematical modeling, and proteomics—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, and systems-level data across circadian networks exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models connecting molecular interactions to emergent periodicity, identification of key mesoscale organizational features determining timing, and principles for modulating circadian rhythms. Understanding emergent circadian timing has implications for chronotherapy and metabolic diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Proton Gradients in Mitochondrial Cristae: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Bioenergetic Data to Model Mesoscale Energy Transduction
title_norm: emergent proton gradients in mitochondrial cristae synthesizing cryoet and bioenergetic data to model mesoscale energy transduction
abstract_text: Translation biology relies on variations in ribosome composition across tissues and conditions to regulate gene expression, making the study of ribosomal protein paralogs and RNA modifications essential for understanding cellular regulation. However, it remains unknown how ribosome compositional diversity is established, how these variations alter ribosome structure and translation dynamics, and how separate structural, proteomic, and functional datasets connect. This project will map ribosome compositional diversity and model its structural and translational impacts using a three phase data synthesis strategy that integrates machine learning, molecular dynamics simulations, and AlphaFold2 structural prediction. The project will integrate proteomic, genomic, and structural data from PRIDE, RMBase, and the Protein Data Bank by linking compositional profiles to structural models and combining ribosome profiling with RNA sequencing. These predictive models will establish a framework for specialized translation regulation, providing critical insights into ribosome dysfunction diseases and identifying novel antibiotic targets.
full_text:
This study investigates translation biology to address how variations in ribosome composition dynamically regulate translation of messenger RNA (mRNA). Although ribosomal proteins and RNA modifications vary across tissues, their structural impacts and connections across separate datasets remain unknown. The proposed study maps ribosome diversity to model structural impacts and test the concept of specialized translation regulation.

This data synthesis project is organized into three phases to map diversity and model structural impacts and predict translational outcomes. The team applies machine learning algorithms and molecular dynamics simulations and structural prediction software such as AlphaFold2 to analyze data. The team validates computational predictions using held out data subsets and published experimental findings from the scientific literature.

The proposed study utilizes datasets from PRIDE and MassIVE and RMBase and MODOMICS and the Protein Data Bank. The team integrates datasets by linking compositional profiles to structural models and combining profiling of ribosomes with proteomics data. The team addresses technical variation in proteomics with pipelines for normalization and resolves missing structures using software for structural prediction.

This project of three years includes milestones such as the creation of a database for ribosome heterogeneity and structural models. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating these diverse datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team releases all data and code through an open access database and registers digital object identifiers for archiving. The team includes researchers from seven institutions and provides training opportunities such as laboratory exchanges for graduate students.

abstract_original: Mitochondrial cristae architecture creates emergent proton gradients that enhance ATP synthesis efficiency beyond predictions from flat membrane models—a mesoscale phenomenon coupling structure to function. This synthesis project will decode how cristae geometry creates emergent bioenergetic properties by integrating structural and functional datasets. We will synthesize cryo-ET data from EMPIAR showing cristae ultrastructure, respiratory chain complex structures from PDB, proteomics of mitochondrial composition from MitoCarta and IMPI, metabolomics from MetaboLights, and bioenergetic measurements from published studies. The central question is: how does cristae morphology at the mesoscale (50-500 nm invaginations) create emergent proton concentration gradients and ATP synthesis rates that flat membranes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that cristae geometry creates microcompartments where local proton concentrations exceed bulk predictions, and that respiratory chain supercomplex organization within cristae optimizes proton delivery to ATP synthase. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of proton diffusion within cristae geometries extracted from tomograms, molecular simulations of supercomplex organization, and systems biology modeling of oxidative phosphorylation incorporating spatial structure. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cristae morphology across cell types and conditions, correlating architecture with bioenergetic output. Integration with disease mutation data will connect cristae morphology defects to mitochondrial dysfunction. Comparative analysis across species and tissues will reveal how emergent bioenergetic optimization adapts to metabolic demands. This project requires expertise in mitochondrial biology, cryo-ET, biophysical modeling, and systems biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and bioenergetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent proton gradients, identification of key architectural features optimizing ATP synthesis, and principles governing cristae-bioenergetics relationships. Understanding emergent mitochondrial function has implications for aging and metabolic diseases. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Antigen Processing in the Immunoproteasome: Integrating Structural and Immunopeptidomic Data to Model Epitope Generation

abstract_text: The physical structure of the nuclear pore complex regulates molecular transport and gene expression, serving as a critical cellular gatekeeper composed of structural scaffold proteins and disordered barrier proteins. However, it remains unknown how this physical structure collectively produces selective transport, because existing structural, kinetic, and functional datasets remain fragmented across separate repositories. This project will determine how protein spatial arrangements generate transport barriers and regulate gene expression by applying coarse grained molecular dynamics, the Integrative Modeling Platform, machine learning, and Bayesian inference. The study will integrate data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, and Gene Expression Omnibus using automated extraction pipelines and the Integrative Modeling Platform to combine physical constraints. These models will establish the mathematical rules governing transport speeds and will explain the physical mechanisms behind genetic diseases, viral infections, and aging.
full_text:
The proposed study investigates the physical structure of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) because its collective transport mechanisms remain unknown. Researchers understand the protein composition of the NPC but separate datasets do not explain the physical mechanisms of transport. The primary question is how the spatial arrangement of NPC proteins regulates transport to identify the physical mechanisms of genetic diseases.

The proposed study uses a computational design for data synthesis to integrate existing datasets into unified physical models of the NPC. The project will apply coarse grained molecular dynamics and the Integrative Modeling Platform alongside machine learning and statistical network analysis. The team will validate the computational models by testing predictions against experimental data and generating hypotheses for future laboratory experiments.

The study will use data from the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Database and the Gene Expression Omnibus. Automated pipelines for extraction and the Integrative Modeling Platform will integrate these datasets using standardized biological ontologies to ensure data compatibility. Because existing datasets are fragmented and inconsistent, the project will use Bayesian inference and quantification of uncertainty within the structural models.

Over a three year period the project will establish collaborative meetings and develop a database to construct models and publish hypotheses. Because combining structural biology and genomics exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory, this project requires cross disciplinary collaboration.

The team will share all code through repositories for version control and publish findings in open access journals for public availability. Computational biologists from six institutions and early career scientists will offer training through rotations of students and workshops.

abstract_original: The immunoproteasome generates MHC-presented peptides through emergent cleavage patterns that differ from constitutive proteasomes—a mesoscale phenomenon where subunit composition alters processing outcomes. This synthesis project will decode how immunoproteasome assembly creates emergent epitope generation by integrating structural biology and immunopeptidomics. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of proteasome variants, immunopeptidomic data from IEDB and SysteMHC Atlas, protein sequence data from UniProt, and transcriptomics correlating proteasome subunit expression with peptide repertoires. The central question is: how does immunoproteasome subunit incorporation create emergent cleavage specificities at the mesoscale (the ~15 nm proteasome barrel) that individual catalytic subunits cannot produce? We hypothesize that emergent cleavage patterns arise from allosteric communication between subunits, altered substrate threading, and cooperative effects among catalytic sites that depend on mesoscale proteasome architecture. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of substrate processing through proteasome channels, machine learning to predict cleavage sites from sequence and proteasome composition, and network analysis of epitope generation pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating proteasome subunit expression patterns with immunopeptidome composition across cell types. Integration with T cell epitope databases will connect emergent cleavage to immune recognition. Analysis across disease states (cancer, infection, autoimmunity) will reveal how altered proteasome composition shifts emergent epitope generation. This project demands expertise in proteasome biology, immunology, structural biology, and machine learning—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, immunopeptidomic, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent epitope generation, identification of key subunit interactions governing cleavage specificity, and principles for modulating antigen processing. Understanding emergent immunoproteasome function has implications for vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Selectivity in Nuclear Export: Synthesizing Structural and Transport Data to Model CRM1-Mediated Cargo Recognition
title_norm: emergent selectivity in nuclear export synthesizing structural and transport data to model crm1mediated cargo recognition
abstract_text: Cellular memory, which enables cells to maintain stable identities across cell divisions despite sharing identical genetic information, is a fundamental biological process regulated by epigenetic modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin structure. However, how these distinct regulatory systems interact as a unified mechanism to integrate transcription factors, chromatin modifications, and three dimensional genome organization to preserve stable yet adaptable cell states remains unknown. To identify epigenetic signatures of cell stability and model cellular memory, this project will synthesize public genomic datasets using chromosome conformation capture processing, chromatin state modeling, network analysis, and deep neural networks. The project will integrate ChIP seq, single cell transcriptomics, DNA methylation, and Hi C datasets from ENCODE, TCGA, and the Human Cell Atlas by aligning genomic coordinates and extracting quantitative features. These predictive models of cell state stability will explain developmental cell fate decisions, inform how memory disruptions drive cancer, and aid in designing cellular reprogramming methods for regenerative medicine.
full_text:
This research of cellular memory addresses how transcription factors and chromatin modifications integrate to maintain stable identities across cell divisions. Although chromatin structure and DNA methylation regulate gene expression, how these systems interact to preserve cell identity remains unknown. The project will construct models of cell stability to explain developmental decisions and understand memory disruptions in cancer.

The study design features a computational synthesis of public genomic datasets using standardized processing pipelines and machine learning models. Key methods include modeling of chromatin states and analysis of pseudotime trajectories alongside machine learning algorithms like deep neural networks. The team will validate results through cross validation across cell types and temporal validation of developmental time series data.

The project utilizes ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and single cell transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas and Hi-C data. The team will integrate datasets by aligning genomic coordinates and mapping epigenetic marks to standardized annotations of the genome. The proposed study does not address information regarding known limitations of the data or specific plans for mitigation.

The project is planned for a duration of three years although the proposal does not specify intermediate milestones. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because integrating diverse datasets requires combined expertise in chromatin biology and computational science.

The project will share findings through open access publications and host the Integrated Cellular Memory Database for public use. The team includes biologists from various career stages and offers training opportunities such as workshops for data analysis.

abstract_original: CRM1-mediated nuclear export achieves selective transport of hundreds of cargoes through a single receptor—emergent selectivity arising from mesoscale complex assembly rather than simple binary interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent export selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and transport kinetics. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on CRM1-cargo complexes, nuclear export signal (NES) sequences from NESdb and ValidNES, proteomics of nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution from the Human Protein Atlas, and transport kinetics from published single-molecule studies. The central question is: how does CRM1 achieve emergent selectivity for diverse cargoes through mesoscale ternary complex formation with RanGTP that binary CRM1-cargo interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from conformational selection, where RanGTP binding creates allosteric changes in CRM1 that differentially stabilize cargo complexes based on NES properties beyond simple affinity. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of CRM1-RanGTP-cargo assemblies, machine learning to predict export efficiency from NES sequence and structure, and kinetic modeling of transport incorporating complex assembly dynamics. We will develop algorithms correlating NES features with export kinetics, identifying sequence and structural determinants of emergent selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted export to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across CRM1 cargoes will reveal shared versus cargo-specific emergent recognition mechanisms. This project requires expertise in nuclear transport, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, sequence, localization, and kinetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent export selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for modulating nuclear export. Understanding emergent transport selectivity has implications for diseases involving mislocalized proteins. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Synthesizing ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data to Model Enhancer Activation
title_norm: emergent cooperativity in transcription factor clusters synthesizing chipseq structural and imaging data to model enhancer activation
abstract_text: Cellular protein quality control relies on the systemic properties of the proteostasis network to maintain proteome stability, a vital process governed by chaperones, degradation pathways, and sequestration mechanisms. However, existing interaction and proteomic datasets remain disconnected, leaving the systems level coordination of these components and their influence on misfolded protein fates uncharacterized. To map the proteostasis network architecture and predict protein fates, this project will employ computational data synthesis combining graph theoretic network analysis, machine learning algorithms, and AlphaFold2 structural modeling. The study will integrate datasets from BioGRID, IntAct, ClinVar, and the Protein Data Bank by mapping entries to UniProt accession numbers to construct multi layer network models representing physical and functional relationships. These predictive models will link network properties to cellular phenotypes, establishing a systems level framework to predict how genetic variants affect cellular health and guide therapies for protein misfolding diseases.
full_text:
This study investigates quality control of cellular proteins to resolve how components of the proteostasis network coordinate to maintain proteome stability. Although individual components are well studied, these sources of data remain disconnected and coordination at the network level is uncharacterized. The project investigates how properties of the network determine protein fates and cellular phenotypes to aid the development of therapies for diseases.

The design of the study uses computational synthesis of data to construct networks with multiple layers and model protein triage. Key methods include analysis of networks using graph theory and algorithms for machine learning (ML) and modeling of structures via AlphaFold2. The team will validate results using cross validation on independent datasets and share predictions of high priority for experimental testing.

The project will utilize data from BioGRID and IntAct and the Protein Data Bank and PRIDE and ProteomeXchange and ClinVar. The team will integrate datasets by mapping entries to accession numbers from UniProt and combining them into multi layer models. To mitigate limitations of data, the team will model missing structures using AlphaFold2 and filter databases of interactions by evidence codes.

The timeline of 24 months includes acquisition of data and construction of networks and modeling of client triage. This project requires collaboration among multiple laboratories because integrating disparate datasets demands expertise in folding of proteins and proteomics.

The team will share all code via GitHub and publish findings in journals with open access to ensure public accessibility. The team includes researchers from seven institutions across various stages of careers and offers opportunities for training of students.
