abstract_original: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers creates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment—mesoscale phenomena where clustered TFs achieve regulatory outcomes impossible for isolated factors. This synthesis project will decode emergent TF cooperativity by integrating genomics, structural biology, and imaging datasets. We will synthesize ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and ReMap, structural data from PDB on TF-DNA complexes, super-resolution imaging of TF clusters from published studies, and transcriptomics correlating TF binding with gene expression. The central question is: how does TF clustering at enhancers (mesoscale assemblies of 10-100 TF molecules) create emergent transcriptional activation that isolated TF binding cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent cooperativity arises from multivalent interactions among TF activation domains, DNA-mediated TF-TF communication, and phase separation creating transcriptional condensates. Our computational approach combines thermodynamic modeling of cooperative DNA binding, machine learning to predict enhancer activity from TF binding patterns, and spatial simulations of TF clustering dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating ChIP-seq occupancy with structural constraints on TF spacing, predicting cooperative binding configurations. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomics will connect TF cluster heterogeneity to transcriptional noise. Integration with GWAS data will link variants affecting emergent cooperativity to disease phenotypes. This project demands expertise in transcriptional regulation, structural biology, imaging analysis, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of genomic, structural, and imaging data across regulatory elements exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent TF cooperativity, identification of key features enabling enhancer activation, and principles for predicting transcriptional output from TF binding. Understanding emergent transcriptional regulation has implications for gene therapy and developmental biology. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Viral Assembly: Synthesizing Cryo-EM and Sequence Data to Model How Capsid Geometry Arises from Protein Interactions
title_norm: emergent viral assembly synthesizing cryoem and sequence data to model how capsid geometry arises from protein interactions
abstract_text: Cellular signaling networks rely on spatial compartmentalization, temporal dynamics, and scaffolding proteins to maintain pathway specificity and prevent crosstalk, which is essential for accurate cellular information processing. However, current research lacks an integrated framework to explain how these mechanisms combine to control signaling specificity because the diverse data remain isolated in incompatible databases. To determine these mechanisms, this project will use a computational synthesis design applying graph theoretic network analysis, community detection, sequence based prediction, and ensemble machine learning models to analyze existing public datasets. The study will integrate databases including BioGRID, IntAct, KEGG, Reactome, Human Protein Atlas, and AlphaFold by mapping subcellular localization and kinetic parameters onto standardized protein protein interaction networks to generate multi modal feature vectors. These predictive models of pathway insulation will clarify basic cellular information processing and identify how disrupted signaling specificity leads to diseases like cancer, metabolic disorders, and developmental abnormalities.
full_text:
Networks of cellular signaling prevent crosstalk but no integrated framework explains how spatial organization and temporal dynamics control specificity. Individual mechanisms of insulation are documented but researchers have not combined these diverse types of data into a unified model. This study investigates how pathways maintain insulation because disrupted specificity of signaling leads to diseases such as cancer and metabolic disorders.

The proposed study uses a design of computational synthesis to analyze existing public datasets and test hypotheses about insulation of pathways. Key methods include algorithms for detection of communities and models of machine learning (ML) such as random forests and neural networks. The team will validate results using computational cross validation and prioritize the resulting biological hypotheses for future experimental testing.

The project utilizes databases of interactions of proteins and pathways including BioGRID and IntAct and KEGG and Reactome and AlphaFold. The team will integrate datasets by mapping localization and kinetic parameters onto networks of interactions of proteins for machine learning. Because quality of databases varies, the team will use a unified system of scoring and estimate missing kinetic parameters.

Over a timeline of three years the project will create a database of signaling specificity and develop predictive models of insulation. This work requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating these diverse datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will release all databases and predictive models and code for analysis under open licenses to ensure public access. The team includes researchers from six institutions at various stages of careers and provides opportunities for training of undergraduate students.

abstract_original: Viral capsid assembly exemplifies emergent mesoscale organization where hundreds of protein subunits self-organize into precise icosahedral structures with properties unpredictable from individual proteins. This synthesis project will decode emergent capsid assembly by integrating structural biology, biophysics, and evolutionary data. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB across viral families, capsid protein sequences from UniProt and NCBI, assembly kinetics from published studies, and evolutionary data on capsid diversification. The central question is: how do local protein-protein interactions create emergent global capsid geometry at the mesoscale (20-200 nm particles) with precise curvature, symmetry, and stability? We hypothesize that emergent geometry arises from conformational switching at quasi-equivalent positions, where identical proteins adopt different local environments to achieve global curvature—a mesoscale organizational principle. Our computational approach combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics of capsid assembly, graph-theoretical analysis of protein interaction networks in capsids, and machine learning to predict assembly outcomes from protein sequences. We will develop algorithms to extract interaction rules from structural data, testing whether minimal rule sets can recapitulate emergent capsid geometries. Evolutionary analysis will reveal how emergent assembly properties constrain capsid protein evolution. Integration with fitness data from deep mutational scanning will connect assembly defects to viral phenotypes. This project requires expertise in virology, structural biology, polymer physics, and evolutionary biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, sequence, kinetic, and evolutionary data across viral families exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include general principles of emergent capsid assembly, predictive models of assembly from sequence, and understanding of how evolution shapes emergent viral architecture. Understanding emergent viral assembly has implications for antiviral design and nanotechnology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

abstract_text: In cell biology, understanding the structural organization, molecular composition, and cell cycle dependent changes of the animal cell centrosome is critical for defining its physical architecture and disease associated genetic variants. However, it remains poorly understood how the spatial organization of centrosomal proteins coordinates functions like microtubule nucleation, and these isolated datasets currently lack a unified structural functional model. To address this, the project will construct an integrated dynamic computational model of the centrosome using coordinate system registration, network community detection, machine learning, and dynamic Bayesian network modeling to link physical architecture to cellular functions. The study will align structural imaging from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Image Data Resource to cryo ET coordinates, combining them with interaction networks, cell cycle timelines, and genetic variants. This dynamic model will establish a novel methodology for synthesizing multi scale data to understand non membrane bound structures, advancing research into centrosome associated diseases like cancer and microcephaly.

To address this, the project will construct an integrated dynamic computational model of the centrosome using coordinate system registration, network community detection, machine learning, and dynamic Bayesian network modeling to link physical architecture to cellular functions. The study will align structural imaging from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Image Data Resource to cryo ET coordinates, combining them with interaction networks, cell cycle timelines, and genetic variants. This dynamic model will establish a novel methodology for synthesizing multi scale data to understand non membrane bound structures, advancing research into centrosome associated diseases like cancer and microcephaly.
abstract_original: BAR domain proteins sense and generate membrane curvature through emergent collective behavior at the mesoscale—properties arising from oligomerization and membrane remodeling that individual proteins cannot achieve. This synthesis project will decode emergent curvature sensing by integrating structural biology, lipidomics, and biophysics datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on BAR domain proteins, lipidomic data from LIPID MAPS and LipidBank, membrane curvature measurements from published studies, and proteomics of membrane-associated proteins from the Human Protein Atlas. The central question is: how do BAR domain proteins create emergent curvature sensitivity and membrane remodeling at the mesoscale (10-100 nm membrane deformations) through collective assembly? We hypothesize that emergent curvature sensing arises from cooperative BAR domain oligomerization on curved membranes, creating positive feedback between protein binding and curvature generation. Our computational approach combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics of BAR domains on membranes, continuum mechanical modeling of membrane deformation, and machine learning to predict curvature preferences from BAR domain structure. We will develop algorithms correlating BAR domain structural features with curvature sensing and generation capabilities. Integration with cellular imaging data will connect in vitro emergent behavior to in vivo membrane remodeling. Analysis across BAR domain families will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent properties. This project demands expertise in membrane biology, structural biology, biophysics, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, lipidomic, and biophysical data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent curvature sensing, identification of key features determining BAR domain function, and principles for engineering membrane-remodeling proteins. Understanding emergent membrane remodeling has implications for endocytosis, cell division, and neurological diseases. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Prion Strain Properties: Synthesizing Cryo-EM Structures with Clinical Data to Model How Fibril Architecture Determines Pathology
title_norm: emergent prion strain properties synthesizing cryoem structures with clinical data to model how fibril architecture determines pathology
abstract_text: Selective autophagy relies on cargo receptor proteins recognizing and binding cellular targets for degradation, a process critical for cellular homeostasis that involves specific receptors, targets, and protein structures. However, it remains poorly understood how these individual molecular interactions scale up to control overall cellular selectivity, function as a system, and compete for substrates. This project will map the global network of receptor target interactions and determine their structural binding rules using a four stage computational workflow that applies machine learning and agent based modeling. The study will integrate data from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, AlphaFold, PhosphoSitePlus, and DepMap by converting diverse protein identifiers to UniProt standards and organizing them into a single unified schema. These results will establish a system wide view of selective autophagy to identify therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases without disrupting general cellular degradation.
full_text:
This study investigates selective autophagy to address how molecular interactions between receptor proteins and targets scale up to regulate pathways. Current studies identify specific receptors but do not explain their regulation by chemical modifications and competition for substrates. This project maps interactions between receptors and targets to model responses to cellular stress and identify therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

The study design uses a four stage computational workflow from collection of data to mathematical modeling of cellular behavior. Key methods include machine learning classifiers and analysis of network topology alongside molecular dynamics simulations and agent based computational modeling. The team will validate results by comparing computational predictions against genetic screens and performing physical tests of binding and mutation.

The project will utilize data from BioGRID and IntAct alongside STRING and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold. The team will integrate datasets by converting identifiers of proteins to UniProt standards and organizing data into a unified schema. The project will use predictions from AlphaFold for missing structures and apply a standardized data cleaning pipeline to resolve inconsistencies.

The 24 month timeline allocates early stages to collection of data and analysis of networks followed by structural modeling and simulations. This project requires multi lab collaboration to combine expertise in cell biology and structural biology alongside proteomics and computational modeling.

The team will share code on GitHub and release findings in open access journals while creating the SelectAuto database. The team includes biologists from six institutions at various career stages and offers training through student exchanges and research internships.

abstract_original: Prion strains exhibit emergent pathological properties—distinct incubation periods, tissue tropisms, and clinical presentations—arising from mesoscale fibril architectures rather than sequence differences. This synthesis project will decode how fibril structure creates emergent strain properties by integrating structural biology, neuropathology, and clinical datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of prion and prion-like fibrils, clinical data from published prion disease cohorts, neuropathological descriptions from brain bank studies, and sequence data from UniProt. The central question is: how does fibril architecture at the mesoscale (fibril cross-sections of ~10 nm, lengths of 100-1000 nm) create emergent strain-specific pathological properties? We hypothesize that emergent strain properties arise from fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and cellular interaction interfaces determined by core architecture. Our computational approach combines structural analysis of fibril polymorphs, machine learning to correlate architectural features with clinical phenotypes, and kinetic modeling of fibril propagation and fragmentation. We will develop algorithms to quantify fibril structural features predictive of strain behavior. Integration with cellular toxicity data will connect fibril properties to emergent pathological mechanisms. Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins (α-synuclein, tau, Aβ) will reveal shared principles of emergent strain determination. This project requires expertise in prion biology, structural biology, neuropathology, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, clinical, and pathological data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models connecting fibril architecture to emergent pathology, identification of key structural features determining strain properties, and principles for predicting disease outcomes from fibril structure. Understanding emergent prion strain properties has implications for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis and therapy. All analysis pipelines, models, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Protein Localization Networks: Synthesizing Imaging and Interactome Data to Model Symmetry Breaking
title_norm: emergent cell polarity from protein localization networks synthesizing imaging and interactome data to model symmetry breaking
abstract_text: Post transcriptional gene regulation, driven by the combinatorial interactions of approximately 1500 RNA binding proteins with messenger RNA, is a fundamental biological process that determines mRNA translation, localization, storage, and degradation. However, the systems level rules governing how these factors collectively dictate mRNA outcomes remain unresolved, and it is currently unknown how multiple proteins cooperatively or competitively determine transcript fate. This project will map the global landscape of protein RNA interactions using a data synthesis design, applying non negative matrix factorization, network analysis, and convolutional and graph neural networks to predict mRNA fate. The study will integrate CLIP seq, ribosome profiling, and structural datasets by mapping all protein binding sites and functional measurements to a unified coordinate system using common transcript identifiers. These predictive models will establish how molecular scale interactions scale up to cellular level organization, advancing basic cell biology and the development of targeted RNA based therapeutics.
full_text:
This study investigates post transcriptional gene regulation to resolve how interactions of RNA binding proteins determine the fate of messenger RNA. Although datasets characterize many of the 1500 human RNA binding proteins, the systems level rules of their interactions remain unresolved. The primary question asks how molecular interactions dictate the fate of messenger RNA to enable the development of targeted therapeutics.

The study uses a design of data synthesis to integrate genomic datasets and train architectures of deep learning that predict outcomes. The team will apply clustering algorithms and multivariate regression and Bayesian networks and convolutional neural networks within Snakemake pipelines. The team will validate computational findings using comparisons of peak calling and evaluate models of machine learning using stratified cross validation.

The project will use CLIP-seq data from ENCODE and annotations of transcripts from GENCODE and metabolic labeling data from SLAM-seq. The team will integrate datasets by mapping binding sites of proteins to a unified coordinate system using common transcript identifiers. To mitigate data heterogeneity and batch effects, the team will use standardized pipelines of quality control and statistical methods.

Although a timeline is not specified, milestones include creating an interaction database and developing models of the fate of messenger RNA. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating massive genomic datasets exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory.

The team will release all software as open source workflows and share the database through an open access portal. The team includes researchers in early career stages from seven institutions and offers training for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers.

abstract_original: Cell polarity emerges from protein localization networks where initially uniform distributions spontaneously break symmetry—a mesoscale phenomenon where spatial organization arises from molecular interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent polarity by integrating imaging, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize protein localization data from the Human Protein Atlas and Cell Image Library, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID, phosphoproteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, and live-cell imaging from published studies capturing polarity establishment. The central question is: how do reaction-diffusion networks of polarity proteins create emergent spatial organization at the mesoscale (1-10 μm polarity domains) from initially homogeneous distributions? We hypothesize that emergent polarity arises from positive feedback loops in membrane-cytoplasm cycling, mutual antagonism between polarity complexes, and scaffolding interactions that amplify initial asymmetries. Our computational approach combines reaction-diffusion modeling of polarity networks, machine learning to predict polarity outcomes from protein expression patterns, and image analysis to quantify polarity establishment dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating interaction networks with spatial localization data, testing which network motifs are necessary and sufficient for emergent symmetry breaking. Integration with single-cell RNA-seq will connect polarity protein expression heterogeneity to polarity establishment variability. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent polarity mechanisms. This project demands expertise in cell polarity, mathematical modeling, image analysis, and systems biology—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, interaction, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent polarity, identification of minimal network requirements for symmetry breaking, and principles for engineering polarized cells. Understanding emergent polarity has implications for development, cancer, and tissue engineering. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Specificity in Ubiquitin Chain Recognition: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode the Ubiquitin Code
title_norm: emergent specificity in ubiquitin chain recognition synthesizing structural and proteomic data to decode the ubiquitin code
abstract_text: In neurobiology, the molecular and spatial organization of proteins within presynaptic and postsynaptic compartments of neuronal synapses is critical for defining synaptic identity and maintaining proper brain function. However, disconnected datasets leave the relationship between protein ratios, spatial distribution, and functional diversity unresolved, obscuring how subcellular protein arrangements produce collective properties like signal strength and plasticity. This project will determine how synaptic molecular composition and spatial architecture dictate functional properties by using weighted gene co expression network analysis, machine learning, and molecular dynamics to computationally synthesize networks and spatial models. The study will integrate data from SynaptomeDB, AlphaFold, and the Allen Brain Atlas by standardizing identifiers, building physical interaction networks, and mapping genetic and physiological data onto super resolution imaging models. These predictive spatial models will provide a structural framework to understand how genetic variations disrupt synaptic organization, explaining how synapses achieve functional diversity in neurological disorders.
full_text:
This study in neurobiology examines the organization of proteins within synapses to resolve how sub cellular arrangements produce collective synaptic properties.
Although researchers have identified proteins of synapses, these disconnected datasets leave the relationship of protein ratios to functional diversity unresolved.
The primary question asks how the architecture of synapses dictates function to provide a framework to understand mechanisms of psychiatric disorders.

The design of the study uses computational synthesis of datasets to map networks of proteins and construct spatial models of synapses.
Tools include weighted analysis of gene coexpression networks and absolute quantification of proteins alongside machine learning (ML) and simulations of molecular dynamics.
The team will validate models using cross validation on data and by comparing results against findings from independent experiments.

The project uses databases including SynaptomeDB and the Protein Data Bank alongside AlphaFold and the Allen Brain Atlas.
The team will integrate datasets by standardizing identifiers and building networks of physical interactions to map genetic data onto spatial models.
Because structures from experiments are incomplete, the project will use computational predictions and standardize identifiers to resolve differences between datasets.

During the three year project the team will host annual meetings and launch an online database and generate structural models of synapses.
This scope requires multi institutional collaboration to combine expertise in proteomics and structural biology with neuroscience and computational modeling across laboratories.

The team will release all code on GitHub and deposit structural models in PDB-Dev and host an open access database.
The team includes researchers from eight institutions to provide training for undergraduates and graduate students and a postdoctoral researcher.

abstract_original: The 'ubiquitin code'—where different polyubiquitin chain types specify distinct cellular outcomes—represents emergent signaling specificity arising from mesoscale chain conformations rather than simple ubiquitin-receptor binding. This synthesis project will decode emergent chain specificity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on ubiquitin chains and receptor complexes, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus and published studies, ubiquitin receptor interactomes from BioGRID, and functional data from published screens. The central question is: how do polyubiquitin chain conformations at the mesoscale (chains of 2-10 ubiquitins spanning 5-50 nm) create emergent signaling specificity that monoubiquitin cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent specificity arises from chain-type-specific conformational ensembles that present distinct binding surfaces, enabling avidity-based discrimination by multivalent receptors. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of polyubiquitin chains, machine learning to predict chain-receptor binding from structural features, and network analysis of ubiquitin signaling pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating chain conformational properties with receptor selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted chain recognition to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across chain types (K48, K63, linear, branched) will reveal principles of emergent specificity. This project requires expertise in ubiquitin biology, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and functional data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models of emergent chain specificity, identification of key conformational features determining receptor selectivity, and principles for predicting ubiquitin signaling outcomes. Understanding the emergent ubiquitin code has implications for targeted protein degradation therapies. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent RNA Localization: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics and RNA Structure Data to Model mRNA Targeting Networks
title_norm: emergent rna localization synthesizing spatial transcriptomics and rna structure data to model mrna targeting networks
abstract_text: The cell surface glycocalyx is a carbohydrate layer whose molecular makeup, physical structure, and biological functions are critical for understanding cellular processes and diseases such as cancer and infections. However, how the diverse molecular components of this cell coat organize and interact to produce collective cellular behaviors remains unresolved because existing datasets are not integrated. This project will integrate public datasets to map cell coat composition, using network analysis, coarse grained physical simulations, and supervised machine learning to model three dimensional structures and predict cellular functions. Data from GlyGen, GlyTouCan, UniCarb DB, the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, Gene Expression Omnibus, and ArrayExpress will be integrated by converting nomenclatures and combining structural and abundance data. This work will establish how molecular level variations scale up to control cellular level processes, providing critical insights into disease mechanisms like tumor spread and viral infection.
full_text:
This study investigates the cell surface carbohydrate layer and the unknown organization of glycocalyx components during collective cellular behaviors. Although individual carbohydrate structures are documented in separate databases, these resources remain unintegrated and the physical organization is unresolved. This project integrates public datasets to model the three dimensional structure of the cell coat and predict molecular control of cellular functions.

The computational design progresses from mapping molecular composition to simulating physical structures and training machine learning models of biological activities. The project applies network analysis, trajectory modeling, coarse grained physical simulations, and supervised machine learning algorithms such as neural networks. Physical models are compared against published biophysical measurements and machine learning predictions are validated using independent test datasets.

The project utilizes data from GlyGen, GlyTouCan, UniCarb DB, the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, and Gene Expression Omnibus. The team integrates these resources by converting carbohydrate nomenclatures into standardized formats and combining structural and abundance data into unified matrices. Inconsistencies in data formats and naming conventions across databases are resolved using automated translation software and standardized metadata guidelines.

Over a three year period, the project will establish collaborative computational workflows, host annual meetings, and deliver a public database. The project requires a multi laboratory effort because the necessary expertise spans carbohydrate chemistry, cell biology, structural biology, and computer science.

All databases, simulation models, and software tools will be made publicly available and code will be shared using containerized packages. The team includes scientists from six institutions representing multiple career stages and will offer training through student rotations and workshops.

abstract_original: mRNA localization creates emergent spatial gene expression patterns through RNA-protein networks operating at the mesoscale—a phenomenon where RNA targeting achieves precision impossible from individual binding events. This synthesis project will decode emergent RNA localization by integrating spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and RNA biology datasets. We will synthesize spatial transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas and published studies, RNA structure data from SHAPE-MaP experiments in public repositories, RNA-binding protein (RBP) interaction data from ENCODE eCLIP, and RBP localization from the Human Protein Atlas. The central question is: how do RBP networks create emergent mRNA targeting at the mesoscale (RNA granules of 100-1000 nm containing multiple mRNAs and RBPs) with subcellular precision? We hypothesize that emergent localization arises from combinatorial RBP binding, RNA secondary structure context, and phase separation into transport granules that integrate multiple weak targeting signals. Our computational approach combines machine learning to predict localization from sequence and structure features, network analysis of RBP-mRNA interactions, and spatial statistics to quantify localization precision. We will develop algorithms integrating RNA structure predictions with RBP binding sites to model targeting complexes. Integration with translation data will connect localization to local protein synthesis. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent targeting mechanisms. This project demands expertise in RNA biology, spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of spatial, structural, and interaction data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent RNA localization, identification of key features determining targeting, and principles for engineering localized gene expression. Understanding emergent RNA targeting has implications for neurological diseases and mRNA therapeutics. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Mechanics of Bacterial Microcompartments: Synthesizing Structural and Metabolic Data to Model Encapsulated Pathway Efficiency
title_norm: emergent mechanics of bacterial microcompartments synthesizing structural and metabolic data to model encapsulated pathway efficiency
abstract_text: Gene regulation relies on enhancers selectively communicating with and activating target gene promoters in three dimensional nuclear space, which is critical for controlling distant gene expression through complex molecular interactions. However, how chromatin looping, transcription factor binding, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and sequence compatibility collectively interact to establish enhancer promoter regulatory specificity remains poorly understood. To determine how enhancer promoter specificity arises, this project will computationally synthesize multi omic data by mapping connections, analyzing molecular features, and training machine learning models, including random forests and neural networks. The study will integrate public genomic and epigenomic datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, GTEx, and GEO by mapping all data to the GRCh38 reference genome to construct unified feature matrices. These predictive models and specificity rules will improve disease risk interpretation, synthetic regulatory circuit design, and predictions of genomic mutation effects in non coding regions.
full_text:
In gene regulation it is unknown how multiple molecular factors interact to determine specificity of communication between enhancers and promoters. Although enhancers regulate distant genes through chromatin looping, understanding of how these components integrate to establish specificity remains incomplete. The primary objective is to determine how specificity arises from integrated features to improve predictions of the effects of mutations.

The proposed study uses a three part computational synthesis of public data to map and predict connections between enhancers and promoters. The team will apply machine learning (ML) models and algorithms for calling interactions (FitHiC2) to analyze features and predict connections. Validation of results will involve a held out test set and external validation using expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data.

The project will use public datasets from ENCODE and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) containing genomic and eQTL data. The team will integrate datasets by mapping all data to the GRCh38 reference genome and extracting features into unified matrices. Because technical variability exists across consortia, the team will implement standardized workflows and apply strict thresholds for quality control.

The three year project will deliver an integrated database of connections alongside predictive models and testable experimental hypotheses. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating massive multi omic datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will publicly release all generated resources including the integrated database of connections and containerized workflows for analysis. The diverse team spans multiple stages of careers and institutions to provide opportunities for training including workshops and research experiences.

abstract_original: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent emergent metabolic organelles where protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways, creating efficiency and selectivity impossible in the cytoplasm. This synthesis project will decode emergent BMC function by integrating structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of BMC shells and encapsulated enzymes, metabolomics from MetaboLights, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and genomic data on BMC operons from NCBI. The central question is: how does BMC shell architecture at the mesoscale (40-200 nm compartments) create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced pathway flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity—that free enzymes cannot achieve? We will develop algorithms correlating shell protein properties with pore selectivity. Integration with fitness data from published studies will connect BMC organization to growth phenotypes. Comparative analysis across BMC types (carboxysomes, metabolosomes) will reveal shared principles of emergent encapsulated metabolism. This project requires expertise in BMC biology, structural biology, metabolic modeling, and biophysics—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, metabolic, and genomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent BMC efficiency, identification of key architectural features determining function, and principles for engineering synthetic compartments. Understanding emergent BMC function has implications for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

abstract_text: Cell biology relies on understanding how the structural organization of endoplasmic reticulum subdomains, including sheets, tubules, and contact sites, regulates essential cellular functions like protein synthesis, lipid metabolism, and calcium signaling. However, researchers do not understand how molecular components self organize into these domains because existing proteomic, lipidomic, structural, and functional datasets remain isolated within separate disciplines. To determine how subdomain molecular composition determines physical structure and collective functions, this project will apply machine learning, cross species orthology mapping, and graph based modeling within a computational data synthesis pipeline. The study will integrate proteomics, lipidomics, cryo electron tomography, and functional datasets from PRIDE, LIPID MAPS, and EMDB by correlating spatial lipidomics with proteomic maps and linking structural measurements to molecular composition. Ultimately, these results will establish general principles of organelle organization and provide predictive models for how structural disruptions in the endoplasmic reticulum cause diseases like neurodegeneration.
full_text:
This study of cell biology addresses how molecular components self organize into domains of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Researchers understand the structures of subdomains of the endoplasmic reticulum but existing datasets remain isolated across separate scientific disciplines. The primary question is how molecular composition of subdomains determines physical structure to establish general principles of organization of organelles.

The study uses a computational pipeline to integrate diverse datasets into Bayesian frameworks and models of multi layer networks. Key methods include machine learning and segmentation of images for cryo electron tomography (cryo-ET) implemented in Python and R. The team will validate results by testing models on held out datasets and comparing predictions with published experimental data.

The study will source datasets of proteomics and lipidomics from public databases including PRIDE and LIPID MAPS and EMDB. The team will integrate datasets by correlating spatial lipidomics with proteomic maps and linking structural measurements to molecular composition. To mitigate heterogeneity of data, the team will apply standards of quality control and use Bayesian frameworks to quantify uncertainty.

Milestones for Year 1 include collection of data while Year 2 milestones focus on construction of the database. The project requires collaboration across disciplines because no single laboratory possesses the diverse expertise needed to integrate multi scale data.

The team will share findings through publications with open access and host code on GitHub to support open science. The team includes faculty in early stages of their careers and will train graduate students in cell biology.

abstract_original: T cell activation emerges from receptor clustering at immune synapses where mesoscale organization determines signaling thresholds—a phenomenon where spatial arrangement creates activation decisions impossible from receptor occupancy alone. This synthesis project will decode emergent T cell activation by integrating imaging, signaling, and structural datasets. We will synthesize super-resolution imaging from published studies and Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics of TCR signaling from PRIDE, structural data from PDB on TCR complexes, and single-cell RNA-seq from the Human Cell Atlas. The central question is: how does receptor clustering at the mesoscale (100-500 nm microclusters) create emergent activation thresholds that determine T cell responses? We hypothesize that emergent thresholds arise from kinetic segregation of phosphatases, cooperative kinase recruitment, and feedback loops operating within receptor clusters. Our computational approach combines spatial stochastic simulations of TCR signaling, machine learning to predict activation from cluster properties, and network analysis of signaling cascades. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cluster properties across activation states. Integration with functional data will connect cluster organization to T cell fate decisions. Comparative analysis across T cell subsets will reveal how emergent thresholds adapt to different immune functions. This project demands expertise in T cell biology, super-resolution imaging, signaling, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent activation thresholds, identification of key cluster features determining T cell responses, and principles for modulating immune activation. Understanding emergent T cell activation has implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Synthesizing Damage Proteomics and Chromatin Data to Model Repair Mechanism Selection
title_norm: emergent dna repair pathway choice synthesizing damage proteomics and chromatin data to model repair mechanism selection
abstract_text: Mechanobiology studies how cells convert physical forces into biochemical signals and downstream behaviors, a process initiated when force sensitive proteins change shape under physical stress to regulate cellular function. However, the complete network connecting force sensors to gene expression remains unmapped, and current methods cannot integrate physical force measurements with structural data or model multi input physical signaling. This project will use a data synthesis approach combining network analysis algorithms, machine learning models, and molecular dynamics simulations to map force induced signaling networks and model physical inputs against gene expression. By integrating structural, interaction, and single molecule force spectroscopy databases, the study will apply confidence scoring and multi layer network modeling to link molecular structures to signaling pathways. These quantitative models will establish a predictive framework for uncharacterized force sensitive proteins, advancing the understanding of physical forces in cell development and diseases like cancer.
full_text:
This project investigates mechanobiology to understand how cells convert physical forces into biochemical signals because pathways of signaling remain unmapped. Force sensitive proteins change shape under physical stress but networks connecting these sensors to expression of genes remain unmapped. The study maps networks of force induced signaling because physical forces influence development of cells and diseases like cancer.

The proposed study uses data synthesis to map networks of signaling and integrate structures of proteins with measurements of force. Key methods include algorithms for analysis of networks and models of machine learning and simulations of molecular dynamics. The team will validate models using held out datasets and published experimental findings that were excluded from development of models.

The project uses data from BioGRID and IntAct and STRING and Reactome and KEGG and the Protein Data Bank. Datasets will be integrated by applying confidence scoring to interactions of proteins and using multi layer modeling of networks. To mitigate data fragmentation and heterogeneity the team will implement standardized schemas and use AlphaFold predictions to fill gaps in structures.

The proposal mentions biannual meetings of working groups and an annual workshop but specific milestones and the timeline are not specified. Collaboration is required because the project spans biophysics and structural biology and cell biology which exceeds capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will release all resources including the Mechanotransduction Integration Database (MechIntDB) and share code publicly using GitHub. The team includes researchers from seven institutions across various career stages and offers training opportunities like experiences of undergraduate research.

abstract_original: DNA repair pathway choice represents emergent decision-making where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively determine repair mechanism—a mesoscale phenomenon integrating multiple inputs into discrete outcomes. This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: A Cross-Cell-Type Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Material States and Their Emergent Control of Gene Expression Noise
title_norm: a crosscelltype atlas of biomolecular condensate material states and their emergent control of gene expression noise
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation organize cellular processes through physical properties like viscosity and elasticity, which are critical for maintaining normal cellular functions and preventing disease phenotypes across species. Currently, the lack of integration between biophysical measurements and large scale datasets leaves it unclear how molecular sequences and interaction networks quantitatively determine condensate physical states and biological outcomes. This project will determine how molecular features predict condensate physical properties across species by extracting features from cellular images and literature to train multimodal machine learning models, including graph neural networks and gradient boosted trees. The study will integrate diverse databases, including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, and the Human Protein Atlas, by standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologs to construct a unified knowledge graph linking molecular and phenotypic data. Ultimately, this research will establish a predictive framework that systematically links molecular scale features to macroscopic physical properties and cellular behaviors, transitioning condensate study from isolated observations to predictive science.
full_text:
This project investigates biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation to address the disconnected relationship between physical states and cellular outcomes. Condensates organize cellular processes through physical properties (such as viscosity) but the influence of molecular sequences on physical states remains unclear. The primary question asks how molecular features predict physical properties to transition the study of condensates into a predictive framework.

This retrospective project of data synthesis compiles public databases and extracts physical features to train multimodal models of machine learning. The team will apply models of deep learning and graph neural networks alongside sparse additive models and gradient boosted trees. Validation involves internal cross validation on held out datasets and replication across independent sources to create public sets of benchmarks.

The project will utilize diverse databases including PhaSepDB and AlphaFold DB alongside the Human Protein Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus. Integration of datasets involves standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologs of species to construct a unified knowledge graph of phenotypic data. Because metrics are inconsistent, the project maps measurements to a latent physical state and corrects batch effects of images.

The twenty four month timeline includes establishing pipelines and extracting features to release the final knowledge graph and modules for training. Collaboration is necessary because the project demands expertise in physics of polymers and computer vision that exceeds any single laboratory.

The team will share findings through a public knowledge graph and open source tools of software alongside open datasets of benchmarks. The team includes physicists and biologists across stages of careers who will provide opportunities for training through workshops led by students.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Analytically, we will build a unified latent-variable model that maps composition/disorder/sequence grammars and imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, coarsening kinetics proxies, FRAP recovery parameters) onto a low-dimensional “material state manifold.” We will then connect that manifold to emergent transcriptional outcomes using hierarchical Bayesian models of bursting (inferring burst size/frequency from scRNA distributions), and causal discovery on perturbation datasets to identify regulators that shift condensates between states. Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Codes: Synthesizing Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics to Predict Organelle Contact Site Morphologies
title_norm: emergent membrane curvature codes synthesizing cryoet proteomics and lipidomics to predict organelle contact site morphologies
abstract_text: In cell biology, membrane contact sites are critical physical junctions where organelles interact to coordinate lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and organelle dynamics, mediated by specific tethering proteins and lipid transporters. However, fragmented data across separate disciplines leave the system level behaviors, redundancy mechanisms, robust network architectures, and stress induced reorganization of these contact sites completely unintegrated and poorly understood. This computational project will integrate public datasets to map a probabilistic network of organelle contact sites, applying hierarchical Bayesian models, similarity network fusion, and dynamic network models to identify robust structural motifs. The project will synthesize data from PRIDE, the Human Protein Atlas, and DepMap by mapping orthologous genes and combining physical, spatial, and functional evidence layers using probabilistic graphical models. Ultimately, this research will establish a system level network model of organelle interactions, enabling the discovery of emergent cellular properties and dynamic behaviors that isolated studies cannot identify.
full_text:
This study in cell biology investigates membrane contact sites to address the unknown network architectures that regulate interactions of organelles. Known tethering proteins and lipid transporters remain unintegrated across separate datasets of proteomics and imaging to explain behaviors at the system level. The primary question asks how a network of contact sites transitions the study from single genes to models at the system level.

This computational study aggregates existing public datasets to build a model of multi layer networks and a queryable knowledge graph. The team will apply hierarchical Bayesian models and fusion of similarity networks alongside algorithms for community detection to analyze the network. Validation of results involves benchmarking against established sets of genes and known complexes of proteins to ensure accuracy.

The project utilizes databases including PRIDE and the Human Protein Atlas alongside green fluorescent protein (GFP) libraries of yeast. The team integrates these datasets by standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologous genes across species to combine layers of evidence. To mitigate data heterogeneity, the team tracks covariates at the study level and applies domain adaptation to align features of images.

The timeline includes holding meetings and virtual sprints to deliver a standardized ontology and reproducible workflows without specific dates. Collaboration across laboratories is necessary because the project requires diverse expertise in biology and statistics alongside large computational resources.

The team will release all code and derived datasets under permissive licenses to provide public access to the workflows. The team includes investigators and researchers in their early career across biology and computer science with training opportunities during collaborative sprints.

abstract_original:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

title: Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Percolation: A Synthesis of Actin/Microtubule Network Architecture and Emergent Intracellular Transport Efficiency
title_norm: mesoscale cytoskeletal percolation a synthesis of actinmicrotubule network architecture and emergent intracellular transport efficiency
abstract_text: In cell biology and biophysics, nanoscale molecular interactions among actin, microtubules, motor proteins, and crosslinkers generate large scale cytoskeletal structures that are essential for cellular organization and function. However, current methods cannot integrate disparate imaging and omics datasets to determine how molecular composition, biochemical regulation, and genetic factors systematically govern physical cytoskeletal organization across diverse cell types. To identify molecular regulators of cytoskeletal patterns and predict structural transitions, this project will utilize a data integrative approach combining image segmentation, variational autoencoders, and active gel biophysical models to extract and align quantitative features. The study will integrate datasets from the Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and DepMap by extracting standardized image features and using joint embeddings to align them with proteomic and genetic perturbation data. Ultimately, these results will establish general physical principles, low dimensional state spaces, and transition rules for cytoskeletal self organization across diverse imaging modalities and biological contexts.
full_text:
This project in cell biology and biophysics investigates how molecular components systematically determine the physical organization of the cytoskeleton. Nanoscale interactions generate mesoscale structures but how to integrate disparate datasets to identify general principles of organization remains unknown. This study seeks to identify regulators of cytoskeletal patterns to establish general physical principles of cytoskeletal self organization.

The retrospective design of the study harmonizes public datasets and uses machine learning to align quantitative structural features with molecular data. The team will apply algorithms for image segmentation (Cellpose) and variational autoencoders and biophysical models of active gels. Validation involves testing on cell lines that are held out and comparing inferred parameters against established facts of biology.

The project utilizes the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library and Broad Institute Cell Painting and datasets of RNAi. The team will integrate these datasets by extracting standardized features from images to align them with proteomic and genetic data. The team will mitigate the limitation of comparing different microscopy modalities by using training that is domain adversarial for batch correction.

The timeline includes virtual sprints on a monthly basis and in person meetings to produce a harmonized table of features. This project of a large scale requires multi lab collaboration because integrating heterogeneous imaging modalities with proteomic data exceeds laboratory capacity.

The team will share all code and workflows that are containerized and the Cytoskeletal Self Organization Atlas through public repositories. The team includes cell biophysicists and graduate students who will receive training through workshops that are hands on and dataset creation.

abstract_original:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation
title_norm: emergent chromatin nanodomain topology integrating hic superresolution imaging and epigenomics to explain celltypespecific gene regulation
abstract_text: Three dimensional chromatin folding regulates the formation of mesoscale genomic structures such as loops and compartments, which are essential for understanding genome organization and cellular function. However, the relative contributions of folding mechanisms remain unresolved, functional relationships are mostly correlative, and conflicting results from siloed, inconsistently processed experimental assays limit mechanistic understanding. This project will identify rules linking one dimensional epigenomic states to three dimensional domains through a retrospective synthesis utilizing attention based machine learning, polymer physics simulations of loop extrusion, and Bayesian optimization. The study will integrate chromosome contact, single cell, and imaging datasets from ENCODE and the 4D Nucleome by standardizing metadata and mapping imaging coordinates to genomic reference builds. These outputs will establish community wide standards for comparing genome organization models and transition correlative observations of chromatin structure into predictive rules for downstream research.
full_text:
This study examines three dimensional chromatin folding to understand how mesoscale genomic structures form and why experimental assays yield conflicting results.
Although genomic datasets and mechanistic models exist, the relative contributions of these mechanisms remain unresolved and data remain inconsistently processed.
The primary research question asks how molecular perturbations affect cellular functions to transition correlative observations into predictive rules of genome organization.

The study design is a retrospective synthesis of public data that integrates metadata harmonization with machine learning and mechanistic model calibration.
Key methods include topological domain calling and polymer physics simulations of loop extrusion calibrated through Bayesian optimization and neural network models.
The team validates models using chromosome level cross validation and posterior predictive checks on an open benchmarking suite with imaging constraints.

The project utilizes public datasets from the Image Data Resource and ENCODE including Hi-C and single cell multi omics data.
The team integrates datasets by standardizing metadata and mapping imaging coordinates to genomic reference builds to constrain genomic contact models.
To mitigate assay heterogeneity, the team categorizes datasets into quality tiers and propagates uncertainty using hierarchical statistical models.

The timeline features monthly virtual sprints to deliver key milestones including a standardized data resource and reproducible workflows.
This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in polymer physics and genomics with high performance computational infrastructure.

The team shares harmonized data matrices and publishes reproducible workflows to open source simulation and machine learning repositories.
The team includes researchers from multiple career stages who train graduate students through reproducibility audits and community outreach.

abstract_original:
Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator: A Pan-Proteome Synthesis of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates
title_norm: protein crowding as an emergent mesoscale regulator a panproteome synthesis of cytoplasmic viscosity diffusion and reaction rates
abstract_text: Cellular biology relies on understanding the stoichiometry, assembly pathways, and dosage regulation of protein complexes, which are fundamental to maintaining cellular homeostasis and organizing molecular interactions at the mesoscale. However, existing data types are analyzed in isolation, and no unified quantitative framework integrates structural, proteomic, and translational data to predict assembly pathways or vulnerability to subunit imbalances. This project will identify global rules governing protein complex stoichiometry and predict subunit imbalance vulnerability by applying hierarchical Bayesian modeling, network flow algorithms, and regularized regression to reconstruct assembly pathways. The study will integrate structural databases like AlphaFold DB and PRIDE proteomics data by mapping proteins to standardized identifiers, extracting structural interface graphs, and calculating translation timing features. These outputs will establish principles of mesoscale cellular organization and identify disease associated vulnerabilities related to dosage imbalances to explain how cells maintain protein complex stability.
full_text:
In cellular biology no unified quantitative framework integrates structural data with proteomic abundance and translation dynamics to predict pathways of assembly. Existing databases provide structural interfaces and protein abundance but isolated analyses leave kinetics and condition specific stoichiometry of protein complexes unknown. This study identifies rules of stoichiometry to explain how cells maintain stability of protein complexes and discover disease associated vulnerabilities.

The proposed study integrates public datasets to build probabilistic models that reconstruct pathways of assembly and predict sensitivity to dosage. Key algorithms include hierarchical Bayesian modeling and Bayesian learning of structure and algorithms for network flow and regularized regression. The team will validate predictions against experimentally characterized protein complexes and perform ablation studies to assess the contribution of each data type.

The study will utilize databases including Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold DB and Complex Portal and DepMap and UniProt. The team will integrate datasets by mapping proteins to standardized identifiers and extracting graphs of structural interfaces for probabilistic priors. To mitigate missing structural data, the team will use AlphaFold predictions and manage batch effects in proteomics with hierarchical Bayesian modeling.

Although the chronological timeline is not specified, milestones include establishing pipelines and developing models and releasing the Complex Assembly Atlas. This cross disciplinary project requires collaboration because integrating structural biology and proteomics exceeds the expertise and infrastructure of any single laboratory.

The team will share all data and code and reproducible pipelines through an open access database called the Complex Assembly Atlas. The cross institutional team includes quantitative scientists and domain experts who will train graduate students and postdocs through modeling sprints.
