abstract_original:
Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties—effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—arising from collective protein/RNA concentrations at 10–1000 nm scales. These properties shape signaling and metabolism but are not predictable from individual macromolecules. This project will test whether crowding-related emergent parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across organisms and conditions.

We will synthesize: (i) quantitative proteomics and absolute protein copy numbers (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB), (ii) subcellular localization and abundance maps (Human Protein Atlas; spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT in PRIDE), (iii) measurements of diffusion and viscosity from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, single-particle tracking, and FRAP compiled from public repositories and literature supplements (IDR/BioImage Archive; curated datasets), (iv) metabolomics that influences osmotic/crowding states (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) structural/biophysical properties of proteins (PDB, AlphaFold DB; predicted disorder from MobiDB; oligomerization from Complex Portal).

We will construct mesoscale “crowding fields” by combining spatial proteomics with protein size/shape estimates (from structures/predictions) to estimate excluded volume and soft interaction potentials in different compartments. We will fit these fields to observed diffusion/viscosity measurements using Bayesian calibration and coarse-grained physical models (e.g., obstruction scaling, fractional Brownian motion). Machine learning models will predict diffusion regimes for probe classes (enzymes, ribosomes, signaling proteins) given local proteome composition and interaction propensity.

Key questions: Do cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints in specific compartments (nucleoplasm vs cytosol) despite large proteome changes? Which protein classes (ribosomal proteins, chaperones, intrinsically disordered proteins) disproportionately control emergent viscosity? Can we predict condition-dependent shifts (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) in mesoscale diffusion landscapes from omics alone?

Expected insights include a quantitative, cross-species map linking proteome composition to emergent physical states, and identification of “crowding hubs” whose abundance changes re-tune global reaction kinetics. The project enables reinterpretation of many phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress) as consequences of mesoscale physical state changes.

This requires team science integrating quantitative proteomics, soft-matter physics, microscopy-based biophysics, and statistical learning, plus substantial data curation across heterogeneous measurement types. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate community standards for reporting diffusion/viscosity, build open databases of calibrated measurements, and deliver reproducible pipelines and training modules for a new generation of data-savvy biophysical cell biologists.

title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness
title_norm: emergent ribosome assembly landscapes integrating cryoem intermediates rrna processing maps and proteomics to explain assembly robustness
abstract_text: In cellular biochemistry and systems biology, the physical clustering of enzymes into localized cellular microdomains regulates metabolic reactions and pathway efficiency, which is critical for coordinating cellular metabolism. However, researchers lack a generalized method to identify metabolic clustering across diverse cell types, leaving the prevalence and quantitative metabolic influence of this spatial organization unknown. This project will determine how pathways organize into spatial clusters by constructing network models and applying Bayesian statistics, network clustering algorithms, constraint based flux simulations, and supervised machine learning. The study will integrate data from the Human Protein Atlas, PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench, and BiGG Models by standardizing identifiers and mapping cellular locations into a single network graph. Ultimately, these spatial metabolic models will resolve long standing errors in metabolic modeling and explain discrepancies between enzyme levels and actual chemical outputs.
full_text:
This study in systems biology examines how the clustering of enzymes into microdomains affects reactions to resolve a methodological gap. Although individual studies show that enzymes associate to coordinate reactions, the prevalence and quantitative influence of this organization remain unknown. The project investigates how stress alters the clustering of enzymes to resolve discrepancies between levels of enzymes and chemical outputs.

The study design integrates public datasets to construct models of networks and uses machine learning (ML) to predict clustering of enzymes. The team will apply Bayesian statistics and supervised machine learning to identify microdomains and to simulate metabolic reactions. Validation involves comparing predictions against groups of controls and testing simulated rates of reactions against experimental data of metabolic flux.

The project utilizes data from the Human Protein Atlas and the PRIDE archive alongside several other public databases. The team will integrate datasets by converting identifiers into standardized formats and combining features into a single network graph. To mitigate missing data and platform specific biases, the researchers will apply metadata normalization and calculate intervals of confidence for locations.

This project of twenty four months includes standardization of data followed by modeling of networks and validation in the final months. This work requires cross disciplinary collaboration because it demands specialized knowledge in imaging and computational modeling and machine learning.

The team will share findings through a public database and release all computational pipelines and code in open source repositories. The team includes senior researchers and trainees from biochemistry and statistics who will receive specialized instruction in modeling of systems.

abstract_original:
Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

We will build a unified “assembly state graph” where nodes are structural intermediates (from cryo-EM) and edges represent transitions constrained by rRNA processing events and factor binding/unbinding. Using probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts, we will infer transition probabilities and identify bottlenecks. Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.

Hypotheses: (1) assembly robustness emerges from redundant, partially ordered modules that buffer factor loss; (2) specific mesoscale nucleolar subcompartments correspond to distinct regions of the assembly state graph; and (3) disease mutations in ribosomopathies disproportionately affect transitions with low redundancy, explaining tissue-specific vulnerability.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

title: Mesoscale Signaling Microclusters as Emergent Computation: A Synthesis of Immune Receptor Imaging, Phosphoproteomics, and Single-Cell Responses
title_norm: mesoscale signaling microclusters as emergent computation a synthesis of immune receptor imaging phosphoproteomics and singlecell responses
abstract_text: Gene regulatory networks maintain cellular stability through feedback and redundancy, making the study of network mechanisms governing cell identity transitions under genetic perturbations essential for understanding cellular robustness. However, existing single cell datasets remain fragmented across protocols, and the exact relationship between network architecture, chromatin state, and cellular robustness remains unresolved without unified cross study analyses. To determine how network architectures and chromatin states control cellular stability, this computational synthesis project will reconstruct causal networks using regularized regression, latent dynamical models, and causal inference frameworks managed via Nextflow or Snakemake pipelines. The study will integrate public perturbation datasets from GEO, ArrayExpress, and scPerturb with ENCODE, BioGRID, and STRING databases, using deep generative models for batch correction and physical interactions as structural constraints. Ultimately, this research will establish causal regulatory relationships rather than mere correlations, explaining how molecular interactions scale up to determine cell level stability across diverse disease states.
full_text:
This study examines gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and the stability of cell identities under genetic perturbations to identify universal network structures. Although GRNs maintain stability through feedback and redundancy, the relationship between architecture of GRNs and chromatin state remains unresolved across datasets. This project asks how architectures of GRNs and chromatin states interact to control cellular stability and establish causal regulatory relationships.

This computational synthesis project integrates public single cell perturbation data with molecular priors to infer and align causal GRNs. The team will use scVI and totalVI for data integration alongside graphical models and latent dynamical models for reconstruction of GRNs. The team will validate results using a framework that evaluates network predictions against held out data from perturbations and reference standards.

The study will utilize datasets of single cell perturbations from GEO and scPerturb alongside epigenomic data from ENCODE and STRING. The team will integrate datasets by standardizing metadata and correcting effects of batch using databases of physical interactions as structural constraints. To mitigate heterogeneity and variable efficacies of perturbations, the team will calculate explicit efficacy scores and use algorithms for batch correction.

The project will release a harmonized atlas and a suite for benchmarking, though the specific chronological timeline is not specified. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in genomics of single cells and statistical causal inference and dynamical systems.

The team will share findings and software tools through open source libraries of code and public repositories with permanent digital identifiers. The diverse team spans multiple stages of careers from students to principal investigators and provides training in causal modeling.

abstract_original:
Immune receptors form mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) at the plasma membrane that act as emergent computational units, integrating ligand binding, mechanical forces, and feedback to produce switch-like or graded activation. The emergent phenomenon is that collective receptor organization and kinase/phosphatase partitioning yields signaling behaviors not predictable from receptor–ligand affinity alone.

We will synthesize: (i) TCR/BCR and Fc receptor super-resolution and TIRF imaging datasets with cluster statistics (IDR, BioImage Archive; published single-molecule localization microscopy datasets), (ii) phosphoproteomics time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) single-cell functional readouts (CyTOF and flow cytometry in ImmPort; scRNA-seq activation time courses in GEO), (iv) ligand affinity/kinetics and epitope data (IEDB; structural complexes in PDB), and (v) perturbation datasets for kinases, phosphatases, and cytoskeletal regulators (DepMap; LINCS small-molecule perturbations).

Analytically, we will develop a multiscale model linking microcluster architecture to downstream phosphorylation and transcription. Computer vision and point-process statistics will quantify cluster size distributions, lifetimes, and nanoscale colocalization of signaling proteins. We will integrate these features with phosphoproteomic trajectories via dynamical systems identification (sparse regression / SINDy) and with single-cell outcomes using mixture models to capture heterogeneous activation states. A key goal is to infer whether there exist universal “microcluster motifs” (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells) that correspond to distinct emergent response modes.

Hypotheses: (1) microcluster morphology encodes a mesoscale “gain control” that determines sensitivity vs specificity; (2) cytoskeletal coupling shifts microcluster systems between excitable and bistable regimes; and (3) disease-associated variants in signaling proteins act by altering partitioning into clusters rather than changing catalytic rates.

Expected insights include predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and functional immune outcomes, a cross-study standardized microcluster feature set, and mechanistic explanations for disparate experimental results in the literature. This requires team science spanning immunology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, plus significant synthesis to harmonize stimulation protocols and imaging modalities.

NCEMS support is essential to convene communities, build open pipelines for microcluster quantification, and create an openly accessible benchmark dataset and modeling toolkit. Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary training in image analysis, omics integration, and reproducible computational immunology.

title: Emergent Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics: Integrating Cryo-ET, Live Imaging, and Proteogenomics to Explain Bioenergetic Plasticity
title_norm: emergent mitochondrial cristae morphodynamics integrating cryoet live imaging and proteogenomics to explain bioenergetic plasticity
abstract_text: Cellular protein quality control, which involves coordinated interactions among chaperones, degradation pathways, and spatial compartments, is essential for regulating protein aggregation, clearance, and cellular survival across diverse organisms and environmental stressors. Currently, no unified framework connects molecular level proteostasis network states to physical protein aggregation outcomes, and it remains unknown how spatial assemblies create non linear thresholds and memory effects. This project will determine how network configurations and spatial assemblies define cellular resilience by using latent state modeling, variational autoencoders, and dynamic Bayesian networks to analyze public multi omics and imaging datasets. The study will integrate data from PRIDE, BioGRID, HuRI, and the Image Data Resource by mapping proteomics assays to a standardized scale and using latent variable models to align molecular and imaging data. These results will establish unifying principles for cellular resilience and explain cell type specific responses to stressors by connecting molecular network configurations to physical mesoscale structures.
full_text:
This project investigates quality control of proteins because no framework connects molecular networks to aggregation of proteins and survival of cells. Researchers understand interactions among chaperones and pathways of degradation but do not know how these elements define discrete states of cells. The primary question is whether cells occupy discrete states of proteostasis to establish principles for resilience against stressors in the environment.

The study uses meta analysis to integrate public datasets and apply modeling of latent states to define regimes of proteostasis. The team will apply factor analysis of data from multiple views and dynamic Bayesian models to analyze the integrated datasets. The team will validate models using cross validation and external validation against known perturbations and benchmarking against randomized networks.

The project will use datasets from PRIDE and BioGRID and HuRI and the Gene Expression Omnibus and AlphaFold. The team will integrate datasets by mapping assays of proteomics to a standardized scale and using models of latent variables. To mitigate inconsistent definitions of the solubility of proteins, the team will establish strict standards for metadata and assays.

Milestones of the project include completing curation of data and releasing the atlas although a chronological timeline is not specified. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating diverse modalities of data exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory.

The team will share findings through an open access atlas and publish reproducible workflows and open source software. The team includes researchers across various stages of careers and disciplines who will provide opportunities for training in analysis.

abstract_original:
Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds (20–100 nm curvature radii; 10–30 nm junctions) whose collective organization determines respiratory efficiency and signaling. The emergent phenomenon is that cristae architecture—junction density, lamellar vs tubular balance, and local protein crowding—produces nonlinear changes in bioenergetic output not predictable from individual OXPHOS complexes.

We will synthesize public datasets: (i) cryo-ET reconstructions and segmentations of cristae across conditions and organisms (EMPIAR, EMDB), (ii) live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics and cristae reporters where available (IDR/BioImage Archive; Mitochondria Dynamics datasets), (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics of mitochondrial fractions and MICOS/OPA1/ATP synthase oligomers (PRIDE), (iv) genomics and transcriptomics for mitochondrial-shaping genes (GTEx, ENCODE; scRNA-seq atlases), and (v) functional readouts of respiration (public Seahorse datasets and compiled literature values; gene perturbation phenotypes in DepMap).

We will quantify mesoscale cristae geometry from cryo-ET via curvature analysis, junction graph extraction, and topology measures (surface genus, connectivity). We will integrate these with proteomic abundance of shaping complexes and with genetic perturbation effects using causal inference and multi-task learning. Physics-informed models of membrane elasticity and protein-induced curvature will be calibrated to explain observed morphotypes and predict transitions.

Central questions: Are there conserved cristae “architectural states” across cell types that correspond to distinct metabolic regimes? Which combinations of MICOS components, ATP synthase dimerization, and OPA1 processing drive state transitions? Can we explain why similar proteomic changes yield different functional outcomes in different tissues as a consequence of mesoscale geometry constraints?

Expected insights include an atlas of cristae architectural states, quantitative links between shaping complex stoichiometry and emergent cristae topology, and mechanistic hypotheses for mitochondrial diseases where morphology and function decouple. Methodological advances will include open-source tools for extracting standardized geometric descriptors from tomograms.

abstract_text: Epithelial cell biology relies on molecular interactions that establish spatial organization and cell polarity across diverse tissues, which is fundamental for maintaining tissue architecture during development and disease. However, current understanding lacks spatial context across diverse species, and no unified quantitative framework exists to connect molecular networks to large scale spatial polarity patterns. This project will determine how molecular networks generate conserved spatial polarity structures by computationally synthesizing multi omic datasets using graph based segmentation, spatial coordinate alignment, and factor modeling constrained by protein interaction networks. The study will integrate public data from the Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, and PRIDE by mapping tissues to standardized ontologies and combining transcript, protein, and imaging features into unified multi omic models. These results will establish a predictive, quantitative model of tissue architecture to clarify how spatial polarity failure drives cancer, inflammation, and infections.
full_text:
This study of the biology of epithelial cells addresses the lack of a quantitative framework for spatial polarity. Although molecular regulators are known, current understanding remains limited by a reliance on single modalities of data without spatial context. The project seeks to model how networks of molecules generate spatial polarity to predict how disruptions of structure drive diverse diseases.

The design of the study is a computational synthesis of public datasets using standardized ontologies and modeling of networks. The team will apply segmentation with Markov random fields and alignment of spatial coordinates via eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian. Validation of results will involve testing for consistency across datasets and performing analyses of sensitivity such as ablation of markers.

The project will utilize public datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus and the database of the Human Cell Atlas. Integration of datasets will involve mapping of cell types to ontologies and converting spatial data into graphs of proximity. To address heterogeneity in resolution of data, the project will implement standardized ontologies and apply analyses of sensitivity.

The timeline includes an initial summit on ontologies and the release of the Polarity Synthesis Atlas and Polarity Scoring Toolkit. Collaboration is required because the project spans diverse platforms of data and demands expertise in the biology of epithelial cells.

The team will publish the Polarity Synthesis Atlas and release the Polarity Scoring Toolkit as open source software. The team includes computational scientists and provides funded opportunities for graduate students to participate in workshops on analysis of data.

abstract_original:
Many viruses create mesoscale replication compartments (100–1000 nm membraneless inclusions or membrane-bound organelles) that concentrate viral and host factors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective compartment organization yields replication efficiencies and immune evasion strategies not predictable from individual viral proteins. This project will ask whether replication compartments share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses.

We will synthesize: (i) viral replication compartment imaging datasets (electron microscopy and fluorescence) from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, spanning RNA viruses (coronaviruses, flaviviruses) and DNA viruses (herpesviruses), (ii) host–virus protein interaction networks (IntAct, BioGRID, VirHostNet), (iii) CRISPR and RNAi screens for host dependency factors (DepMap viral screens; published screens in GEO/SRA), (iv) viral and host transcriptomic responses (GEO; single-cell infection atlases where available), and (v) structural data for viral scaffold proteins and host recruited complexes (PDB, AlphaFold DB).

We will develop a comparative mesoscale compartment feature framework: size distributions, internal subcompartmentalization, proximity to organelles, and dynamics proxies. Using network embedding and community detection on host–virus interactomes, we will identify recurrent host modules (e.g., RNA metabolism, membrane trafficking, stress granule components) recruited into compartments. We will then relate these modules to compartment morphotypes and to replication phenotypes (viral titers/replication markers from public datasets) using multi-level regression and causal graph methods.

Hypotheses: (1) replication compartments implement convergent mesoscale strategies—phase separation, membrane curvature scaffolding, or hybrid forms—to optimize reaction kinetics and shield nucleic acids; (2) the emergent efficiency depends on a small number of host module recruitments that act as “mesoscale organizers”; and (3) antiviral perturbations that disrupt mesoscale organization (rather than single enzymes) provide broad-spectrum leverage.

Expected insights include a cross-virus taxonomy of replication compartment architectures, identification of conserved host mesoscale organizers, and predictive models linking host factor modules to compartment type and replication success. Deliverables will include open compartment feature datasets and interoperable pipelines for image and network integration.

This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.

title: Emergent Cell Wall Nanomechanics: Synthesizing Fungal and Plant Cell Wall Composition, Ultrastructure, and Growth Patterns
title_norm: emergent cell wall nanomechanics synthesizing fungal and plant cell wall composition ultrastructure and growth patterns
abstract_text: In mitochondrial biology, the physical structures and network shapes formed during mitochondrial fission, fusion, transport, and degradation are critical because these morphological states correlate with cellular functions and stress responses. However, existing data remain isolated across diverse experimental methods without standardized metrics, preventing researchers from connecting molecular regulatory processes to consistent mitochondrial network shapes and functional transitions. To identify recurring mitochondrial shapes and model transition dynamics, this project will computationally synthesize public datasets using deep learning image segmentation, variational autoencoders, contrastive learning, and probabilistic state space models. The study will integrate resources including Cell Painting, MitoCarta, and the Gene Expression Omnibus by mapping genes to a common reference and applying multi view statistical models to connect imaging with molecular data. Ultimately, these results will establish a quantitative model of how molecular events scale up to organelle structures, unifying disease observations and providing a computational framework for other organelles.
full_text:
This project investigates network shapes of mitochondria because researchers lack standardized methods to link molecular processes to cellular functions across experiments. Although shapes of mitochondria correlate with cellular functions, existing data remain isolated across methods without standardized metrics for transitions of shapes. This study addresses how molecular processes drive transitions of shapes of mitochondria to model structures of organelles and cellular outcomes.

The overall design uses a computational synthesis of public datasets across four phases of curation and modeling of states of networks. The team will apply deep learning for segmentation of images and variational autoencoders and probabilistic models of state space. The team will validate results using held out datasets and sensitivity analyses and sets of reference data annotated by experts.

The project uses datasets from Cell Painting and the Image Data Resource (IDR) and MitoCarta and the Cancer Dependency Map. The team will integrate datasets by mapping genes to a common mitochondrial reference and standardizing identifiers of cell lines. To mitigate variations in conditions of imaging, the team will use domain adaptation and infer rates from static images.

The timeline includes four sequential milestones to release a registry of datasets and tools for extraction of features. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the scale of data integration exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will share findings through a public atlas and publish open source code and provide educational tutorials. The team includes biologists and experts in machine learning (ML) who will train graduate students through development of sets of annotations.

abstract_original:
Cell walls are mesoscale composite materials (10–500 nm fibril bundles, crosslinks, and pores) whose emergent mechanical properties enable growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polysaccharide architecture produces nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior not predictable from monomer composition. This project will synthesize multi-omics and imaging data to uncover universal principles of cell wall nanocomposite design in plants and fungi.

We will integrate: (i) cell wall compositional datasets (glycomics and carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations from CAZy; polysaccharide composition in Metabolomics Workbench and literature-derived datasets), (ii) solid-state NMR and scattering data where publicly available (BMRB; published SAXS/WAXS datasets), (iii) AFM nanomechanics maps and electron microscopy of wall ultrastructure (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (iv) transcriptomics of wall biosynthesis during growth and stress (GEO; Arabidopsis eFP, fungal expression atlases), and (v) mutant/perturbation phenotypes affecting morphology (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content imaging screens).

Analytically, we will build a mesoscale structure–property model linking polymer composition and enzyme expression to ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation, bundling, pore size distributions) and to mechanical outputs (Young’s modulus maps, viscoelastic parameters). We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Which crosslink motifs (e.g., lignin–cellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) create emergent anisotropic growth? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

title: Mesoscale Proteasome and Autophagy Hub Organization: Integrating Spatial Proteomics, Imaging, and Ubiquitinome Data to Explain Proteostasis Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale proteasome and autophagy hub organization integrating spatial proteomics imaging and ubiquitinome data to explain proteostasis emergence
abstract_text: Cellular signaling pathways regulate diverse functions by reusing a limited set of components, making it critical to understand how network structures, baseline cellular states, and spatial organization determine specific cellular outcomes. However, current understanding remains fragmented because existing analyses are limited to single pathways or single data modalities, lacking a unified framework to integrate diverse multi modal datasets. This project will determine how network motifs, baseline states, and spatial compartmentalization govern signaling dynamics by applying latent variable ordinary differential equation models and neural differential equations constrained by graph neural networks. The study will integrate diverse datasets, including CyTOF, CITE seq, CPTAC, and PhosphoSitePlus, by normalizing protein identifiers, mapping antibody epitopes, standardizing experimental conditions, and implementing a unified metadata schema. Ultimately, these integrated computational models will establish generalizable principles of cellular decision making and predict context specific drug responses through data synthesis without requiring new experiments.
full_text:
This project addresses the lack of a unified framework for explaining how network structures and baseline states determine outcomes of signaling. Although cells reuse limited signaling components and extensive datasets exist, current analyses remain limited to single pathways or modalities of data. The study determines how network motifs govern signaling dynamics to identify generalizable principles of cellular decision making without new experiments.

The study design relies on computational synthesis of public datasets through harmonization of data and graph constrained dynamical modeling. The methodology applies models of ordinary differential equations with latent variables and neural differential equations constrained by neural networks for graphs. The team will validate models by testing predictions of single cell responses and reconstructing held out time points.

The study uses datasets from CyTOF and CITE-seq and CPTAC alongside databases such as PRIDE and PhosphoSitePlus and BioGRID. The team integrates datasets by normalizing identifiers of proteins and mapping epitopes of antibodies under a unified schema of metadata. To mitigate missing data, the team will model missingness during variational inference and use cellular component annotations of gene ontology.

Milestones of the project include releasing a harmonized compendium of data and launching a public atlas with baseline models. This project requires collaboration of multiple laboratories because the scope demands expertise in proteomics and machine learning and network biology.

The team will share harmonized datasets through a public atlas and archive them in repositories for the long term. The team includes researchers from various career stages and provides opportunities for training of graduate students through audits of reproducibility.

abstract_original:
Proteostasis emerges from mesoscale organization of degradation hubs—proteasome-rich microdomains, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation sites (50–1000 nm)—that coordinate substrate selection, sequestration, and clearance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial organization and phase-like sequestration yields system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, not predictable from individual E3 ligases or proteases.

We will synthesize: (i) spatial proteomics identifying proteasome/autophagy component localization (Human Protein Atlas; hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets in PRIDE), (ii) ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover datasets (PRIDE; ubiquitin linkage-specific studies), (iii) bioimaging of aggresomes, p62 bodies, autophagosome markers, and proteasome foci (IDR/BioImage Archive), (iv) genetic perturbation screens for proteostasis regulators (DepMap; CRISPR screens for aggregation/toxicity), and (v) disease datasets with proteostasis failure signatures (AMP-AD proteomics; ALS/FTD proteomics and transcriptomics in GEO).

We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

title: Emergent Bacterial Microcompartment Design Rules: Synthesizing Genomes, Structures, and Metabolic Flux to Predict Organelle-Like Function
title_norm: emergent bacterial microcompartment design rules synthesizing genomes structures and metabolic flux to predict organellelike function
abstract_text: In molecular biology, understanding how variations in ribosome structure, protein composition, and ribosomal RNA modifications regulate selective messenger RNA translation across different tissues is crucial for deciphering cellular regulation. However, existing public datasets remain unintegrated and inconsistently processed, leaving it unclear whether these ribosomal variations causally control translation or merely reflect non functional environmental consequences. This project will computationally synthesize public data to identify consistent ribosome variation patterns and determine if they causally drive selective translation using generalized linear models, multi view factor analysis, and causal inference. The study will integrate data from sources including the Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, and Tabula Sapiens by standardizing profiling metrics and using single cell reference data to adjust for cell mixtures. Ultimately, these findings will challenge the view of the ribosome as a uniform machine and reveal a previously unrecognized layer of gene regulation controlling protein synthesis.
full_text:
Molecular biology lacks clear understanding of whether ribosome variation directly controls the selective translation of specific messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Ribosome variation occurs across tissues but existing public datasets remain unintegrated and lack standardized metadata and consistent processing methods. The project investigates if patterns of ribosome variation causally drive translation to reveal a new layer of gene regulation.

The study design is a computational synthesis of public data organized into five task forces to model ribosome variation. The team will apply generalized linear models and multi view factor analysis and causal inference using genetic perturbation data. Validation of results will use bootstrap resampling and replication across independent datasets and comparison with genetic perturbation outcomes.

The project will use public data from the Gene Expression Omnibus and PRIDE and the Human Cell Atlas. The team will integrate datasets by standardizing data from profiling of ribosomes and mapping of protein isoforms across different databases. Standardized pipelines for data curation will address inconsistent data processing and statistical covariates will control for biological confounding factors.

The proposed study does not address information regarding the specific milestones and the overall timeline of the project. The project requires collaboration of multiple laboratories to combine diverse datasets and expertise across ribosome biology and machine learning.

The team will share all findings and standardized datasets through a public resource and various open access publications. The team includes researchers from multiple disciplines and offers training for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers through workshops.

abstract_original:
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles (50–300 nm) whose emergent permeability and enzyme colocalization enable metabolic pathways that would be inefficient or toxic in the cytosol. The emergent phenomenon is that shell protein assembly and pore organization generate selective transport and reaction microenvironments not predictable from individual enzymes.

We will synthesize: (i) BMC gene clusters across bacterial genomes (NCBI RefSeq, IMG; curated BMC databases), (ii) shell protein and encapsulated enzyme structures (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) metabolomics and flux measurements for BMC-associated pathways (Metabolomics Workbench; published 13C flux studies), (iv) cryo-EM structures of intact BMCs and shells (EMDB/EMPIAR), and (v) environmental metadata and phenotypes for host organisms (GOLD database; literature-derived growth phenotypes).

We will build a comparative framework linking genetic composition to mesoscale shell architecture and emergent function. First, we will annotate shell protein families and predict pore properties (charge, diameter, gating motifs) from structures. Second, we will infer likely shell stoichiometries and tessellation patterns using assembly modeling and constraints from cryo-EM. Third, we will integrate pathway enzyme kinetics (from BRENDA) with predicted permeability to simulate emergent metabolite gradients and flux enhancement using reaction–diffusion models. Machine learning will map gene cluster features to predicted organelle performance metrics (toxicity mitigation, flux gain).

Key questions: Are there universal shell “permeability motifs” that recur across unrelated BMC types? How do small changes in pore composition produce emergent switches between retention vs throughput regimes? Can we predict ecological niches where particular BMC designs confer advantage?

Expected insights include design rules for emergent mesoscale selectivity, a taxonomy of BMC architectures linked to metabolic outcomes, and open tools for predicting BMC function from genomes. While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

title: Mesoscale Vesicle Coat Self-Organization: Integrating Structural Proteomics and Imaging to Explain Cargo Selectivity Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale vesicle coat selforganization integrating structural proteomics and imaging to explain cargo selectivity emergence
abstract_text: In membrane biology, understanding the composition, spatial organization, and functional roles of cell membrane microdomains is critical because these heterogeneous nanoscale structures regulate essential cellular processes and downstream signaling pathways. However, it remains unknown whether membrane microdomains represent reproducible biological states or experimental artifacts, as current methods lack standardized reporting metrics and yield fragmented, poorly reconciled measurements. This project will use hierarchical Bayesian latent variable modeling, spatial statistics, and machine learning in a retrospective meta analysis of public datasets to identify reproducible microdomain signatures and determine how they modulate downstream signaling. The study will integrate data from PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench, Image Data Resource, SwissPalm, BioGRID, GEO, and LINCS by mapping entities to standardized ontologies and applying a hierarchical Bayesian model with modality specific bias terms. These results will establish quantitative, testable models of microdomain states, resolving a long standing debate in membrane biology and providing a generalizable framework for studying other mesoscale biological phenomena.
full_text:
In the biology of membranes the reproducibility of microdomains remains unknown because of fragmented evidence across different experimental techniques. Researchers know that membranes of cells are heterogeneous but do not understand how different measurements correspond or relate to downstream signaling. This project asks if reproducible signatures of microdomains exist to resolve debates by establishing quantitative models of states of membranes.

The study is a retrospective meta analysis of public datasets using a hierarchical Bayesian model to integrate multi omic data. The team will apply spatial statistics and regularized machine learning and models of causal inference to analyze the integrated data. Validation of results will use negative controls and sensitivity analyses and nested cross validation for the predictive models.

The project will use data from PRIDE and SwissPalm and BioGRID and the database of the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The team will integrate these datasets by mapping entities to standardized ontologies and applying a hierarchical Bayesian model. The team will model modality specific biases and propagate measurement uncertainties to mitigate experimental biases and artifacts in imaging.

Milestones of the project include releasing a map of evidence and establishing pipelines but a specific calendar timeline is not specified. Integrating these diverse datasets requires cross disciplinary expertise in biophysics and proteomics and machine learning across multiple laboratories.

The project will share findings through an open access map of evidence and publish standardized workflows for analysis. The team includes biophysicists and statisticians at various stages of careers who will receive training in reproducible meta analysis.

abstract_original:
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. title: Emergent Nuclear Pore Selectivity at the Mesoscale: A Synthesis of FG-Nup Disorder, Transport Kinetics, and NPC Ultrastructure
title_norm: emergent nuclear pore selectivity at the mesoscale a synthesis of fgnup disorder transport kinetics and npc ultrastructure
abstract_text: In cellular biology, establishing how molecular interactions define endosome functional identities and cargo transport pathways is essential for understanding how specific proteins mark and regulate different stages of endocytosis. However, the lack of integration among separate imaging, proteomic, and genetic datasets prevents researchers from understanding how marker proteins overlap during organelle transition and how genetic changes cause transport defects. This project will combine public data using computational analysis, hidden Markov models, state space modeling, multi view learning, and causal discovery algorithms to map endosome states, cargo routing decision points, and perturbation effects. The study will integrate data from the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, BioGRID, and public genomics screens by aligning experimental timelines and applying multi view machine learning to map diverse data types. Ultimately, this research will establish a standardized framework of dynamic transport models, providing a systematic method to identify molecular regulators linked to neurodegeneration and metabolic disorders.
full_text:
Cellular biology lacks integration of separate datasets explaining how molecular interactions dynamically determine the identity of endosomes and routing of cargo. While specific proteins mark stages of endocytosis, researchers do not understand how markers overlap or how genetic changes disrupt transport. This project will integrate public datasets to model dynamics of transport because dynamic models identify molecular regulators of neurodegeneration.

The design of the study relies entirely on computational analysis of public data using statistical modeling to map pathways. The team will apply hidden Markov models and modeling of state spaces alongside multi view learning and automated segmentation of images. Validation involves testing predictions on independent datasets and verifying that molecular groupings replicate across different studies through resampling.

The project will utilize data from the Image Data Resource and the PRIDE database and the Gene Expression Omnibus. Integration will use a standardized framework of metadata and align experimental timelines to map different types of data. Hierarchical statistical models will manage variations between batches, while multi view learning addresses the absence of paired measurements.

The project spans twenty four months with the first year dedicated to collection of data and initial development of models. This scope requires collaboration across disciplines because the project combines specialized knowledge in membrane biology and mathematical modeling.

The team will publish a freely accessible database of trafficking states and deposit code in public repositories with permanent identifiers. The team includes scientists from cell biology and computer science at various stages of careers who will receive training in modeling.

abstract_original:
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.

Key questions: Do different cell types or organisms achieve similar selectivity via distinct FG-Nup sequence grammars (many-to-one mapping)? Are there discrete “barrier states” corresponding to transport regimes (fast/slow, size cutoff shifts) modulated by phosphorylation or composition changes? Can disease-associated mutations be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than loss of specific interactions?

Expected insights include a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars mapped to inferred barrier states, quantitative links between ultrastructure and transport, and open tools for fitting polymer-based NPC models to data.

This effort requires collaboration among polymer physicists, structural biologists, quantitative microscopists, and computational biologists, and hinges on synthesizing diverse public datasets. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, reproducible modeling workflows, and trainee training at the interface of disordered protein science and mesoscale transport phenomena.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in Bacterial Biofilm Matrix Nanostructure: Integrating Omics, Imaging, and Rheology to Predict Community Robustness
title_norm: mesoscale emergence in bacterial biofilm matrix nanostructure integrating omics imaging and rheology to predict community robustness
abstract_text: Eukaryotic cell cycle regulation relies on molecular mechanisms controlling G1/S and G2/M transition irreversibility, where positive feedback, multisite phosphorylation, and ubiquitin mediated degradation generate bistability and hysteresis to ensure directionality. However, it remains unknown how robustness emerges from stochastic molecular components, how regulatory parameters vary across cell types, and how to identify early warning signals of transition failures. To resolve these questions, the study will construct mechanistic and neural ordinary differential equations using latent cyclic manifold inference, optimal transport, and Bayesian model selection to identify transition features and predict failures. The project will integrate public single cell RNA sequencing, imaging, and proteomic datasets from diverse repositories by mapping them to a shared phase coordinate using consensus markers and time warping algorithms. These results will establish a multi omic network level framework that defines general principles of transition robustness, context specific tuning, and early warning signals of cell cycle failure.
full_text:
This study examines eukaryotic cell cycle regulation to resolve how cell to cell variability in timing of transitions arises. Feedback mechanisms ensure directionality of the cell cycle but the emergence of robustness from stochastic molecular components still remains unknown. The primary question asks how networks control robustness of transitions and the study is novel for using multi omic synthesis.

The design of the study integrates public datasets to construct and compare dynamical models of the cell cycle using Bayesian inference. Key methods include latent cyclic manifold inference and optimal transport and neural ordinary differential equations and Bayesian selection of models. The team will validate results using posterior predictive checks and out of sample validation and data from perturbation screens.

The project utilizes public datasets from the Human Cell Atlas and Tabula Sapiens and the Cancer Dependency Map. The team will integrate datasets by mapping of single cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing data to a shared coordinate. To mitigate data heterogeneity and effects of batches, the project will standardize metadata and use consensus based methods for alignment.

Year one milestones focus on curation of data and development of pipelines while year two milestones include completing comparison of models. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in biology of the cell cycle and quantitative imaging and proteomics.

The team will share findings and datasets through the open Cell Cycle Emergence Resource to ensure public access. The diverse team includes researchers from multiple disciplines and provides training opportunities for both graduate students and postdocs.

abstract_original:
Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures (10–500 nm fibers, pores, and crosslinked networks) whose emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers create antibiotic tolerance and spatial metabolic stratification. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polymer and protein assembly yields community-level robustness not predictable from individual ECM components.

We will synthesize: (i) biofilm imaging datasets including confocal, super-resolution, and electron microscopy of ECM architectures (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) metagenomic and transcriptomic profiles of biofilm communities (NCBI SRA; MG-RAST), (iii) proteomics of ECM and secretomes (PRIDE), (iv) publicly available rheology/viscoelastic measurements and diffusion assays (compiled from literature with open data), and (v) antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation datasets (PATRIC; published screens).

We will extract mesoscale structural descriptors from images (fiber thickness distributions, pore size, network connectivity) using segmentation and graph reconstruction. We will integrate these with ECM composition inferred from omics (polysaccharide synthesis genes, amyloid proteins, eDNA abundance proxies) to build predictive models of emergent rheology and diffusional barrier properties. Reaction–diffusion modeling will connect matrix structure to nutrient/antibiotic penetration and to spatial gene expression patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse biofilms converge on a small set of mesoscale ECM architectures that define mechanical and barrier “states”; (2) community composition influences architecture through modular ECM programs; and (3) transitions between ECM states under stress explain abrupt changes in tolerance.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of ECM mesoscale architectures, mechanistic links between matrix nanostructure and emergent tolerance, and open tools for standardized ECM quantification. The work is purely synthesis-based, leveraging existing datasets to unify previously disconnected measurements.

Team science is required across microbiology, materials science, image analysis, and ecological modeling. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous datasets, establish open standards for ECM feature reporting, and train trainees in integrative analysis of microbial communities and mesoscale biomaterials under open science practices.

title: Emergent Spliceosome Nano-Organization: Integrating RNP Structural States, Proximity Proteomics, and Single-Cell Isoform Variability
title_norm: emergent spliceosome nanoorganization integrating rnp structural states proximity proteomics and singlecell isoform variability
abstract_text: In cellular biology, nuclear bodies such as nucleoli and nuclear speckles regulate essential cellular processes, making the characterization of their molecular composition, physical properties, and biological roles critical for understanding cellular organization. However, current research lacks a unified framework to explain how core and peripheral components differ, which RNA features drive localization, and how structural reorganization quantitatively influences cellular processes. This project will computationally analyze public data using random effects meta analysis, Bayesian integration, and graph neural networks to identify core and peripheral components and establish quantitative links to cellular functions. The study will integrate diverse datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, ENCODE, and AlphaFold by mapping entries to standardized ontologies and using Bayesian fusion to construct a unified network graph. Ultimately, these results will establish general organizational principles of nuclear structures and provide a predictive model of how molecular interactions govern downstream cellular functions.
full_text:
This study of cellular biology investigates the molecular composition of nuclear bodies to address the lack of a unified framework. Although general functions of nuclear bodies are documented, understanding of differences between core and peripheral components remains incomplete. The primary research question seeks to identify core elements of nuclear bodies to establish a predictive model of molecular interactions.

This study relies on computational analysis of public data to construct a network based knowledge graph of molecular interactions. Key analytical methods include Bayesian data integration and Leiden community detection algorithms alongside regularized logistic regression and graph neural networks. The team will validate results by calculating scores of probability and testing the predictive models against standardized benchmark datasets.

The project uses data from the Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE) and the Human Protein Atlas and the Image Data Resource. The team will integrate distinct datasets by mapping entries to standardized ontologies and combining multi modal data using Bayesian fusion. To mitigate variations in experimental designs, the team will convert statistics to rank based effect sizes and apply meta analysis.

The project spans an eighteen month period with milestones including development of ontologies and the release of a public database. This study requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the research requires expertise in proteomics and RNA biology and modeling of networks.

The team will publish all findings in a public database and distribute analytical pipelines as reproducible computational workflows. The team includes researchers at various career stages and offers training for graduate students through collaborative events for curation of data.

abstract_original:
Pre-mRNA splicing is executed by spliceosomes and associated nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions (20–200 nm RNP assemblies; 100–500 nm speckle subdomains). The emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of splicing factors into dynamic assemblies produces cell-type-specific isoform distributions and noise, beyond what individual RNA-binding proteins predict.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of spliceosome intermediates (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics of speckles and splicing assemblies (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution imaging of speckle organization and splicing factor puncta (BioImage Archive/IDR), (iv) long-read and single-cell RNA-seq isoform datasets (ENCODE long-read; GEO; Human Cell Atlas where isoform-resolved methods exist), and (v) perturbation screens of splicing factors (DepMap; CRISPR screens; ClinVar variants for splicing genes).

We will build a multiscale model connecting structural intermediate occupancy and speckle mesoscale organization to isoform outcomes. Image-derived features will quantify speckle subdomain size, factor partitioning, and dynamics proxies. Structural states will be represented as a Markov model of assembly intermediates, parameterized by factor availability from proteomics. We will relate these latent variables to isoform variability using hierarchical models and information-theoretic measures of splicing entropy.

Hypotheses: (1) cells regulate splicing by shifting mesoscale partitioning of factors between speckles and nucleoplasm, altering effective assembly kinetics; (2) specific speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) vs high-entropy (diverse) isoform programs; and (3) disease mutations increase isoform noise by destabilizing particular intermediate transitions.

Expected insights include an atlas linking speckle mesoscale states to isoform variability across cell types, identification of key factors controlling emergent splicing entropy, and open pipelines for integrating imaging with isoform-resolved transcriptomics.

This requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, transcriptomics, and statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing disparate data modalities and producing reproducible workflows and training materials enabling trainees to operate across RNP structural biology and single-cell genomics.

title: Mesoscale Organization of Metabolic Enzyme Filaments: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Cytoophidia and Emergent Metabolic Regulation
title_norm: mesoscale organization of metabolic enzyme filaments a crossspecies synthesis of cytoophidia and emergent metabolic regulation
abstract_text: Non genetic antibiotic tolerance and persistence in bacterial populations represent critical survival strategies driven by metabolic deceleration and stress response activation, which are essential for understanding bacterial survival during drug exposure. However, the field lacks a unified framework to integrate disparate public datasets, leaving it unclear whether these survival strategies are organism specific or follow common dynamical and metabolic patterns. To identify conserved physiological states and metabolic constraints across species, this project will utilize retrospective data synthesis applying hierarchical hidden Markov models, multi view factor analysis, and constraint based flux balance simulations. The study will integrate single cell imaging, transcriptomic, and metabolomic data from public repositories by mapping temporal omics profiles to imaging defined physiological phases using probabilistic regression. Ultimately, these results will establish generalizable, system level principles of bacterial survival across species, transitioning the field from cataloging specific mechanisms to identifying novel therapeutic targets.
full_text:
This study investigates non genetic antibiotic tolerance in bacteria to address the lack of a framework for integrating public datasets. Temporary tolerance involves metabolic deceleration and activation of responses to stress but whether these strategies follow common dynamical patterns remains unclear. The primary question asks how conserved physiological states explain bacterial survival to establish generalizable principles at the level of systems.

This retrospective synthesis of data standardizes public datasets using stochastic modeling and metabolic simulations without conducting new experiments in the laboratory. Key methods include hidden Markov models and factor analysis of multiple views alongside analysis of flux balance and containerized managers of workflows. The team will validate predictions using posterior predictive checks and bootstrapping alongside tests of consistency across species and published literature.

The project utilizes public repositories of data from imaging of single cells alongside the Gene Expression Omnibus and the Sequence Read Archive. Integration involves establishing a standardized schema for metadata and mapping temporal data from omics to phases of imaging. To address the lack of direct alignment, the project implements rules for temporal mapping and hierarchical models with shared priors.

Milestones include hosting collaborative meetings and establishing standards for metadata alongside releasing pipelines for analysis and launching an online atlas. Collaboration is necessary because integrating diverse datasets requires expertise in microbiology and biology of systems alongside stochastic modeling and analysis of metabolism.

abstract_original:
Many metabolic enzymes assemble into mesoscale filaments and bundles (50–1000 nm), such as CTP synthase cytoophidia and IMPDH filaments. The emergent phenomenon is that polymerization changes enzyme kinetics, sequestration, and pathway flux in a nonlinear manner not predictable from monomeric enzyme properties. This project will synthesize imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to uncover universal principles of enzyme filament-based regulation.

We will integrate: (i) fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets showing enzyme filaments across organisms and conditions (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) enzyme structures and filament models (PDB; AlphaFold DB; published helical reconstructions), (iii) metabolomics profiling nucleotide pools and related pathways (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) transcriptomics and proteomics for enzyme abundance and PTMs (GEO; PRIDE), and (v) perturbation datasets (LINCS for metabolic inhibitors; genetic screens affecting filament formation).

We will quantify filament morphology (length distributions, bundling, subcellular localization) and link these to metabolic state variables (nucleotide ratios, energy stress markers). Using mechanistic modeling, we will compare alternative hypotheses: polymerization as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir, and determine which best explains cross-study correlations. We will use phylogenetic comparative methods to test whether filament regulation evolved convergently and whether specific sequence motifs predict polymerization propensity.

Key questions: Are there discrete mesoscale filament “states” corresponding to metabolic regimes (growth, stress, differentiation)? Do filaments act as emergent metabolic capacitors that reduce noise in metabolite levels? Can we predict when filamentation will stabilize vs destabilize pathway flux?

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states, quantitative links between filament morphology and metabolite homeostasis, and open tools for filament detection and meta-analysis. This synthesis will unify scattered observations into a coherent framework for mesoscale metabolic regulation.

Team science is required across metabolism, structural biology, imaging analysis, and evolutionary genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation of diverse datasets, development of open pipelines, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale enzyme assemblies and metabolic phenotypes.

abstract_text: Autophagy, specifically the formation, growth, and fusion of autophagosomes and phagophores, is a fundamental cellular process essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and responding to physiological stress. However, the mechanisms governing initiation site selection, the contributions of diverse membrane sources, and the relationship between dynamic states and molecular or lipid composition across species remain unresolved. To identify conserved molecular modules and lipid remodeling signatures controlling autophagosome nucleation, this project will employ a retrospective data driven synthesis utilizing latent factor models, graph based networks, and regularized machine learning. Public datasets from the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, and Metabolomics Workbench will be aligned using hierarchical models and integrated via latent factor modeling to connect imaging with omics data. These results will establish general principles of how molecular networks and membrane lipids interact to form complex cellular structures, distinguishing universal biological mechanisms from species specific adaptations.

Clathrin-mediated endocytosis produces ~100 nm pits whose emergent behavior—variable lifetimes, abortive events, and cargo-dependent maturation—arises from collective assembly of many proteins and membrane mechanics. The emergent phenomenon is nanoscale heterogeneity in pit trajectories that creates cell-to-cell and site-to-site variability in uptake.

We will synthesize: (i) single-molecule and live-cell imaging datasets tracking endocytic proteins and pit lifetimes (IDR/BioImage Archive; published tracking datasets), (ii) proteomics of endocytic complexes and phosphorylation dynamics (PRIDE), (iii) cargo-specific uptake assays and receptor datasets (GEO; literature datasets with quantitative uptake), (iv) membrane lipid composition datasets relevant to endocytosis (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation screens for endocytosis regulators (DepMap; yeast endocytosis screens).

We will standardize pit trajectory extraction and build a probabilistic “pit state machine” model capturing transitions among assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states. We will link state transition probabilities to protein abundance/PTMs and lipid composition using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit “phenotypes” and relate them to cargo classes.

Hypotheses: (1) emergent uptake variability is governed by a small number of mesoscale control parameters (effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane tension proxies) that can be inferred from omics and imaging; (2) different cargos shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes; and (3) cells tune variability (noise) as a functional feature for receptor signaling.

Expected insights include a unified dynamical model explaining why pits with similar molecular parts produce divergent outcomes, and an open atlas of pit phenotypes across conditions. Methodological deliverables will include reproducible pipelines for cross-study trajectory harmonization.

This project requires collaboration among quantitative microscopists, trafficking biologists, proteomics experts, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed for data curation, development of open standards for reporting trajectories and pit features, and training trainees in integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.

abstract_text: In molecular biology and computational genomics, understanding how RNA molecules distribute to specific cellular compartments and organelles is essential for explaining how spatial gene regulation influences overall cell function. However, the field lacks a unified predictive model to explain how diverse RNA sequence elements and protein binding features interact combinatorially to control RNA routing across different cellular states. To establish predictive rules for cellular RNA distribution, this computational synthesis project will utilize regularized generalized linear models, gradient boosted trees, deep multi modal neural networks, and graph neural networks. The study will integrate public spatial transcriptomics, sequencing, and imaging datasets by mapping diverse experimental labels to a standardized compartment ontology and converting raw measurements into probabilistic localization scores. These predictive rules will establish a generalizable framework for spatial gene regulation at a cellular scale, providing a shared resource that prevents redundant experimental efforts.
full_text:
In computational genomics no unified predictive model explains how sequences of RNA and interactions of proteins determine distribution of RNA. Although specific sequence elements and binding proteins are known, combinatorial interactions of these features and cellular adaptations remain poorly understood. The primary research question seeks to establish predictive rules for cellular distribution of RNA to explain spatial gene regulation.

The proposed study utilizes a computational synthesis design to integrate public biological data and build predictive models of RNA distribution. The team will apply regularized generalized linear models, gradient boosted trees, deep multi modal neural networks, and graph neural networks. Models will be validated by testing predictions on independent datasets and comparing results against genetic knockdown or knockout data.

The project will utilize public datasets including APEX-seq, subcellular fractionation RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, eCLIP, and imaging data. To integrate these datasets, the team will establish a standardized vocabulary for cellular compartments and convert raw measurements into probabilistic scores. To mitigate data heterogeneity, the team will implement quality scoring, use probabilistic labels, and share processed summary data.

Proposed milestones include releasing a compartment ontology, establishing baseline models, expanding multi modal integration, and distributing final predictive models. The project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because no single laboratory possesses necessary expertise in RNA biology and machine learning.

The project will share findings through a public database, distribute reproducible data processing pipelines, and establish open reporting standards. The cross disciplinary team includes graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who will receive training in molecular modeling and machine learning.
