abstract_original:
Synaptic active zones contain nanoscale protein nanoclusters (20–200 nm) whose collective arrangement controls neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that mesoscale spatial patterning of channels, scaffolds, and vesicle docking sites produces nonlinear release dynamics not predictable from single protein abundances.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution maps of active zone proteins (STED/PALM datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR), (ii) synaptosome and active zone proteomics across brain regions and conditions (PRIDE; SynProt resources), (iii) electrophysiological and imaging-derived functional measures (paired-pulse ratios, release probability proxies) from public repositories and literature open data, (iv) genetic variant and perturbation data for synaptic proteins (SFARI, ClinVar; mouse phenotyping databases), and (v) developmental single-cell transcriptomics of neuronal types (Allen Brain Atlas; scRNA-seq datasets).

We will quantify nanocluster geometry (cluster size, spacing, co-localization networks) and build spatial point-process models linking organization to release probability. Integrative modeling will connect proteomic stoichiometry to predicted nanoscale architectures using constraints from known structural interactions (PDB/AlphaFold). We will test whether synapses occupy discrete “organizational states” corresponding to functional plasticity modes.

Hypotheses: (1) active zones implement a small set of mesoscale architectures that tune reliability vs flexibility; (2) plasticity involves transitions between these architectures mediated by scaffold phosphorylation and remodeling; and (3) neurodevelopmental disorder variants shift synapses into maladaptive organizational states.

Expected insights include a cross-region atlas of active zone nanoscale architectures, mechanistic links between organization and emergent release dynamics, and open analysis tools for nanocluster quantification and integration with proteomics.

This requires team science across neuroscience, proteomics, quantitative imaging, and spatial statistics, with extensive synthesis across disparate datasets. NCEMS support will enable harmonization, open workflows, and trainee training bridging nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.

title: Emergent Organelle Size Control via Mesoscale Substructure: Integrating Imaging Atlases and Omics to Explain Scaling Laws
title_norm: emergent organelle size control via mesoscale substructure integrating imaging atlases and omics to explain scaling laws
abstract_text: Extracellular vesicle biology relies on understanding multivesicular body biogenesis, vesicle cargo selection, and vesicle size distribution, which are essential processes for cellular communication and the transport of molecular cargo. However, highly heterogeneous and fragmented public datasets leave core molecular signatures unresolved, preventing researchers from distinguishing genuine vesicle cargo from technical contaminants or understanding regulatory cellular networks. This multi institutional data synthesis project will identify reproducible cargo signatures and model vesicle properties by applying hierarchical Bayesian meta regression, latent factor modeling, and multiview integration algorithms to existing public datasets. The project will integrate data from Vesiclepedia, ExoCarta, PRIDE, GEO, SRA, and the Image Data Resource by mapping molecular features to standardized ontologies and applying multiview integration techniques. These results will establish standardized molecular signatures that distinguish biological cargo from technical contaminants, thereby improving biomarker discovery and mapping the systemic mechanisms of vesicle biogenesis.
full_text:
Extracellular vesicle biology lacks consensus on genuine cargo versus technical contaminants and how cellular networks regulate vesicle biogenesis. Although extracellular vesicles transport molecular cargo from multivesicular bodies, fragmented public datasets leave the core molecular signatures of vesicles unresolved. This project will identify reproducible signatures of cargo to distinguish biological cargo from contaminants and map the biogenesis of vesicles.

This multi institutional study will perform hierarchical meta analyses and network integration on existing public datasets without generating new experimental data. The team will apply Bayesian meta regression and modeling of latent factors alongside propagation through networks and machine learning (ML) classifiers. Validation will involve replication across independent datasets and analyses of sensitivity alongside cross validation of predictive models using negative controls.

The project will use databases including Vesiclepedia and ExoCarta and PRIDE and GEO and SRA and BioGRID and IntAct and DepMap. The team will integrate datasets by mapping molecular features to ontologies and linking networks of proteins with profiles of lipids. To mitigate heterogeneity of data, the team will model methods of isolation as fixed effects and use partial pooling.

The project will progress through quarterly milestones to compile curated datasets and develop integrated models and release final guidelines. The scale of public datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires cross disciplinary expertise in cell biology.

The team will share containerized pipelines of analysis and host harmonized datasets on Zenodo alongside publishing in formats of open access. The diverse team spans multiple stages of careers and will train graduate students through workshops on meta analysis and open science.

abstract_original:
Organelle size (nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes) is governed by mesoscale substructures—subcompartments, scaffolds, and assembly intermediates (10–1000 nm)—that create emergent scaling laws with cell size and growth state. The emergent phenomenon is that collective assembly dynamics yield robust organelle size distributions across noisy molecular environments.

We will synthesize: (i) large-scale cell imaging atlases with organelle segmentation (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; IDR high-content datasets; Cell Painting), (ii) single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics capturing cell state (Human Cell Atlas; CITE-seq datasets; PRIDE single-cell proteomics where available), (iii) known organelle biogenesis pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID), (iv) perturbation datasets affecting organelle size (DepMap; LINCS), and (v) ultrastructural datasets for organelle subcompartments (EMPIAR for selected organelles).

We will extract organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture/substructure features from images (granularity, internal puncta, boundary roughness) and relate them to molecular composition and cell size using scaling analysis and stochastic assembly models (nucleation–growth, coalescence, fragmentation). We will test competing mechanistic models (limiting pool, feedback control, coarsening-limited growth) across organelles and cell types.

Key questions: Are there universal mesoscale control motifs that recur across organelles (e.g., scaffold-limited nucleation, fragmentation-mediated size homeostasis)? Which molecular regulators tune variance vs mean size? Do disease states reflect altered control motifs leading to broader distributions (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?

Expected insights include generalized principles of organelle size control grounded in measurable mesoscale features, and open tools for extracting substructure descriptors from public imaging. The project will yield a comparative “organelle scaling atlas” linking size control regimes to molecular networks.

This requires team science across quantitative cell imaging, stochastic modeling, and omics integration. NCEMS support is essential for large-scale data harmonization, development of reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to connect mesoscale organization to emergent cellular-scale phenotypes under open science.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in DNA Damage Repair Foci: Integrating Live Imaging, Proteomics, and 3D Genome Context
title_norm: mesoscale emergence in dna damage repair foci integrating live imaging proteomics and 3d genome context
abstract_text: Nuclear mechanobiology investigates how nuclear physical properties, deformation, and structural failure emerge from interactions between the nuclear lamina, chromatin, and cytoskeleton to regulate critical cellular functions like migration and genome stability. However, existing data remain fragmented across separate imaging, genomic, and mechanical datasets, leaving the generalizable principles and nonlinear interactions that govern nuclear physical behavior across cell types unresolved. This project will integrate public imaging, genomic, and perturbation datasets using image segmentation, multi view latent representation learning, machine learning, physical shell core models, and causal inference to identify factors determining nuclear deformability and structural failure. By establishing unified metadata schemas and ontologies, the study will project features from Cell Painting, the Human Protein Atlas, ENCODE, and other public repositories into a shared latent space. These results will establish a novel computational framework linking nuclear physical states to DNA damage and gene expression, explaining how identical molecular components produce diverse physical behaviors across contexts.
full_text:
In nuclear mechanobiology the principles connecting molecular composition to the physical deformation and structural failure of the nucleus remain unresolved. Although nuclear structures affect migration and stability of the genome, the fragmented nature of existing datasets leaves their nonlinear interactions unresolved. This project investigates how identical molecular components produce different physical behaviors by computationally synthesizing large scale multi modal public datasets.

This retrospective computational study harmonizes public datasets to develop physical proxies and apply predictive and causal modeling to their relationships. The team will apply segmentation of images and multi view representation learning alongside classifiers for machine learning and physical models. Validation will involve nested cross validation across independent datasets and calibration of statistical proxies against direct physical measurements.

The study will utilize public datasets from Cell Painting and the Image Data Resource alongside the Human Protein Atlas. The team will integrate these datasets by establishing a unified schema for metadata and applying multi view statistical methods. To mitigate fragmentation and effects of batches, the project will implement standardized schemas for metadata and apply multilevel models.

The team will complete extraction of features by month 6 and release the final atlas and training materials by month 24. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because it integrates mechanobiology and computer vision alongside epigenomics at a large scale.

The team will share all findings and tools openly through a toolkit for analysis of images and public repositories of code. The diverse team includes researchers across multiple stages of careers and provides training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs.

abstract_original:
DNA damage repair foci are mesoscale assemblies (100–1000 nm) where many proteins and chromatin regions co-localize, often with phase-separation-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.

We will synthesize: (i) live-cell imaging datasets of repair foci dynamics (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) from IDR/BioImage Archive, including time-lapse series, (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of DNA damage response (DDR) time courses (PRIDE), (iii) 3D genome and chromatin context maps (Hi-C/Micro-C from 4DN; ENCODE epigenomics), (iv) CRISPR screens for DDR genes and pathway choice modifiers (DepMap; published DDR screens), and (v) variant datasets for DDR genes in cancer (TCGA; COSMIC).

We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Patterning in Bacterial Division Machinery: A Synthesis of FtsZ Ring Architecture, Dynamics, and Cell Shape Outcomes
title_norm: emergent mesoscale patterning in bacterial division machinery a synthesis of ftsz ring architecture dynamics and cell shape outcomes
abstract_text: In immunology and cell biology, the spatial self organization and signaling dynamics of the immune synapse regulate critical cellular responses driven by membrane mechanics, cytoskeletal dynamics, and receptor ligand kinetics. However, existing data remain fragmented across laboratories, and the field lacks a unified quantitative framework connecting molecular composition, spatial organization, and downstream signaling dynamics across diverse immune cell types. To identify conserved spatial organization motifs and genetic regulators, this retrospective synthesis project will apply graph neural networks, variational multimodal encoders, and causal mediation analysis to extract features and model signaling outcomes. The study will integrate datasets from the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, and the Gene Expression Omnibus by mapping genes to unified identifiers and linking spatial imaging graphs to proteomic time series features. These multimodal models will establish general principles of cellular self organization and improve the design of engineered cell therapies by predicting activation thresholds and toxicity.
full_text:
This study in immunology investigates spatial self organization of the immune synapse to resolve a lack of unified quantitative frameworks. Although membrane mechanics and cytoskeletal dynamics drive spatial patterning of the synapse, data on molecular composition remain fragmented across laboratories. The primary objective is to identify conserved spatial motifs to establish general principles of cellular self organization and improve therapies.

This retrospective synthesis project integrates public datasets through curation of data and extraction of features and modeling of multimodal data. The team will apply ComBat for correction of batch effects and CellProfiler for processing of images alongside graph neural networks. Validation of models will use held out datasets and tests across cell types to evaluate performance with pre registered metrics.

The project will source datasets from the Image Data Resource and PRIDE and Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium databases. Dataset integration involves standardizing metadata with controlled vocabularies and mapping genes to unified identifiers to link data of spatial imaging. To mitigate heterogeneity of data and poor quality of images, the team will apply normalization and weakly supervised segmentation.

Milestones of year one focus on curation of data, while year two includes modeling and release of atlases of data. Integrating diverse datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires expertise across disciplines in immunology and machine learning.

The team will make all code and pipelines for analysis of images publicly available through open source repositories including GitHub. The team includes immunologists and statisticians across stages of careers, providing training for graduate students through workshops and development of tools.

abstract_original:
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. The emergent phenomenon is that collective filament organization and accessory protein patterning produce robust constriction and shape maintenance, not predictable from FtsZ polymerization alone.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution and cryo-ET datasets of divisome architecture across species (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) single-molecule and time-lapse measurements of FtsZ dynamics (published tracking datasets), (iii) proteomics and interaction networks of divisome components (PRIDE; BioGRID), (iv) comparative genomics of division genes across bacteria (NCBI RefSeq), and (v) morphological phenotypes under gene perturbations and antibiotics (BacDive; published high-content imaging screens).

We will quantify ring architecture (bundle thickness, continuity, patchiness) and dynamics (treadmilling speeds, turnover) and relate these to emergent cell shape outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size control). Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Exosome Biogenesis Microdomains: Integrating Endosomal Proteomics, Lipidomics, and Imaging
title_norm: mesoscale emergence of exosome biogenesis microdomains integrating endosomal proteomics lipidomics and imaging
abstract_text: In protein biochemistry and structural biology, allostery is a fundamental process where molecular interactions at one site influence distant sites, regulating diverse cellular functions across individual proteins. However, the field lacks general quantitative rules to predict allosteric residues across diverse protein families because existing datasets remain unharmonized and unintegrated. This project will use computational meta analysis, residue contact graphs, and graph neural networks to identify structural and sequence factors determining allosteric sensitivity across diverse protein classes and evolutionary distances. The study will integrate data from MaveDB, the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, and ClinVar by mapping genetic variants to structural models and overlaying clinical annotations onto residue contact graphs. These predictive models will establish a framework to identify disease causing genetic variants outside active sites, facilitating selective drug design and protein engineering.
full_text:
This study in structural biology investigates allostery to address the lack of quantitative rules for communication over a long range. Current knowledge includes detailed models for individual proteins but these findings are not integrated across families of proteins. The primary question asks how structural factors determine allosteric sensitivity to identify variants that cause disease and design selective drugs.

The design of the study uses a computational meta analysis of structural data to build networks of residue interactions. Key methods include graphs of residue contacts and calculations of network centrality alongside graph neural networks and hierarchical statistical models. The team will validate results using a standardized framework for benchmarking with train test splits and evaluate performance against baselines.

The project uses data from MaveDB and the Protein Data Bank alongside AlphaFold DB and Reactome and ClinVar. The team integrates datasets by mapping genetic variants to canonical sequences of proteins and aligning these sequences to structural models. To mitigate experimental heterogeneity the team will standardize scales of scores and use computational predictions of flexibility for missing structures.

During the first year the team will curate data and then expand the predictive models in the second year. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in structural biology and statistical genetics and machine learning.

The team will release a public database of allosteric mappings and share reproducible workflows alongside standardized datasets for benchmarking. The diverse team includes researchers at various stages of careers and offers training for graduate students through workshops on machine learning.

abstract_original:
Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies, formed in mesoscale endosomal microdomains (50–500 nm) enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids. The emergent phenomenon is that collective microdomain organization yields selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual sorting motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) exosome and endosome proteomics datasets (ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia-linked studies; PRIDE), (ii) lipidomics of extracellular vesicles and endosomal fractions (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), (iii) imaging datasets of ILV formation and endosomal microdomains (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR for EM of MVBs), (iv) RNA cargo profiles (exosomal RNA-seq in GEO), and (v) perturbation screens affecting EV secretion (DepMap; published CRISPR screens).

We will quantify ILV size distributions and microdomain organization from EM and fluorescence images using segmentation and spatial clustering metrics. Multi-omic integration will identify latent microdomain states defined by protein–lipid–RNA composition. Mechanistic modeling will connect ESCRT polymerization and membrane composition to observed ILV size distributions using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models. Predictive models will link microdomain states to cargo enrichment patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) exosome biogenesis proceeds through discrete mesoscale microdomain states that determine cargo classes; (2) lipid composition (ceramides, cholesterol) acts as a mesoscale controller of domain stability and ILV size; and (3) cell-type differences in EV cargo reflect microdomain state occupancy more than expression of individual cargos.

Expected insights include a unified mesoscale model of ILV microdomains, identification of compositional signatures predicting cargo selection, and open resources for EV biogenesis imaging/omics integration.

This requires team science across membrane biology, proteomics/lipidomics, quantitative imaging, and biophysical modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize diverse public datasets and establish open, reproducible pipelines and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale analysis of extracellular vesicle biogenesis.

title: Deciphering the Sequence Grammar of Mesoscale Viscoelasticity in Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: deciphering the sequence grammar of mesoscale viscoelasticity in biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: In molecular and cellular biology, biomolecular condensates form through liquid liquid phase separation of protein and RNA sequences, creating non membrane bound liquid droplets that are essential for cellular organization. Currently, no unified framework explains how sequence variations, environmental conditions, and nanoscale molecular interactions dynamically regulate condensate physical properties and scale up to influence cellular functions. This project will establish a predictive model of phase separation rules by applying machine learning, including graph neural networks, transformer architectures, and convolutional neural networks, to synthesize existing structural, biophysical, genomic, and imaging data. Data from the Protein Data Bank, LLPSDB, Image Data Resource, PhaSePro, UniProt, Gene Expression Omnibus, and PRIDE will be integrated using novel data ontologies and multi omics integration algorithms. The resulting predictive, systems level model will shift the field from descriptive studies to mechanistic insights necessary for understanding cellular organization and designing neurodegenerative disease therapies.
full_text:
Molecular biology lacks a framework to explain how protein and ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequences determine properties of biomolecular condensates.
Proteins form non membrane bound liquid droplets through multivalent interactions but how environmental conditions dynamically regulate these structures remains unknown.
This study establishes a predictive model of phase separation to understand cellular organization and design therapies for neurodegenerative diseases.

The proposed study is a project of data synthesis that applies machine learning (ML) to integrate existing structural and genomic datasets.

abstract_original: This project addresses the emergent phenomenon of viscoelastic transitions within biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). While the ability of proteins to phase separate is well-documented, the mesoscale material properties—such as viscosity, surface tension, and hardening over time—emerge from complex, non-linear interactions that remain poorly understood. We propose to synthesize data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases, combined with structural disorder predictions from AlphaFold (pLDDT scores) and experimental rheology data scattered across literature repositories. The central hypothesis is that specific 'grammars' within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—defined by charge patterning, residue spacing, and aromatic content—deterministically encode the emergent viscoelastic evolution of condensates, distinct from simple phase separation propensity. Our approach involves training deep learning models (specifically Graph Neural Networks) on integrated sequence-rheology datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. We will validate these models by cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) that visualizes condensate morphology in situ. Expected insights include a predictive framework for how pathogenic aggregates (e.g., in neurodegeneration) transition from liquid to solid states, an emergent property not predictable from single-molecule dynamics. This project necessitates NCEMS support to bring together soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning experts to standardize heterogeneous rheological data and develop novel biophysical classifiers.

title: Emergent Chromatin Rheology: Synthesizing 1D Sequence and 3D Topology to Predict Nuclear Stiffness
title_norm: emergent chromatin rheology synthesizing 1d sequence and 3d topology to predict nuclear stiffness
abstract_text: Cellular biomechanics relies on the structural and mechanical interactions between actin filaments and microtubules, which are essential for understanding how local molecular interactions generate global cellular forces. However, existing structural and biophysical datasets remain siloed across disciplines, preventing the development of predictive models that connect molecular level motor kinetics with whole cell morphological changes. This project will determine how nanoscale cytoskeletal interactions coordinate whole cell morphology and force distribution by applying persistent homology, automated data processing pipelines, and agent based machine learning models utilizing reinforcement learning. The study will integrate datasets from EMPIAR, the Protein Data Bank, the Cell Image Library, the BioImage Archive, Zenodo, and Dryad using automated pipelines to create a single queryable database. This work will establish a predictive framework for how molecular mutations affect cellular structure, shifting the analytical focus of cellular biomechanics toward emergent network properties.
full_text:
This study in cellular biomechanics examines interactions between actin filaments and microtubules to address predictive gaps in whole cell morphology. Although individual cytoskeletal components are well characterized, existing datasets remain siloed across disciplines and mechanisms of global force generation remain unresolved. The study investigates how interactions at the nanoscale coordinate morphology of whole cells and distribution of forces to predict properties of networks.

This computational synthesis project uses existing public datasets to model cytoskeletal networks through topological data analysis (TDA) and machine learning (ML). The methodology applies persistent homology within TDA and agent based models of ML alongside pipelines for processing data. The team validates models of ML by comparing simulated topologies against motifs of TDA and testing predictions against datasets of forces.

The project utilizes datasets from EMPIAR and the Protein Data Bank alongside the Cell Image Library and the BioImage Archive. Pipelines integrate these distinct datasets by standardizing metadata and harmonizing scales of space and time into a single queryable database. To mitigate noise in imaging and fragmentation of data, the team applies TDA and pipelines for standardization to identify geometric features.

The proposal does not specify milestones of the project and the overall timeline but schedules biweekly virtual sessions and biannual meetings. Collaboration across multiple laboratories is required because integrating diverse datasets exceeds limits of a single laboratory and demands expertise across disciplines.

The team will share integrated datasets and code for simulations on Zenodo and GitHub and publish findings in open access formats. The team includes physicists and biologists from various career stages to train graduate students in computational modeling and synthesis of data.

abstract_original: This proposal investigates the emergent rheological properties of chromatin at the mesoscale, specifically how local genomic folding patterns dictate the physical stiffness and plasticity of the cell nucleus. The spatial organization of the genome is not merely a packing mechanism but an emergent mechanical scaffold that influences gene expression and nuclear stability. We will synthesize high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data from the 4D Nucleome Project, mechanics data from atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies of isolated nuclei, and transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The novel hypothesis is that specific topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops act as 'mechanical springs' whose collective stiffness emerges from the interplay of epigenetic marks and loop extrusion factors, independent of the underlying DNA sequence length. By employing polymer physics simulations informed by real-world Hi-C contact maps and machine learning regression models, we aim to correlate 3D chromatin architecture with nuclear stiffness measurements. We expect to reveal how changes in mesoscale chromatin folding—driven by differentiation or disease—result in emergent mechanical softening or stiffening, impacting nuclear migration and integrity. This transdisciplinary synthesis requires a team of genomicists, mechanical engineers, and polymer physicists to bridge the gap between sequence-based genomics and physical mechanics.

title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics
title_norm: the emergence of metabolic channeling mapping transient metabolons via integrated interactomics
abstract_text: The three dimensional folding of genomes into topologically associating domains and higher order chromatin structures is a critical biological phenomenon that directly influences gene expression and genomic function. However, because existing genomic and structural datasets are analyzed in isolation, the precise relationship between one dimensional sequences and three dimensional folding patterns remains unresolved. This computational data synthesis project will identify the rules governing how one dimensional features form three dimensional structures by utilizing transformer based deep learning models, graph convolutional networks, and network analysis of chromatin interactions. Public Hi C, ChIP seq, ATAC seq, and RNA seq datasets from ENCODE, the 4D Nucleome, and Gene Expression Omnibus will be aligned and integrated to predict three dimensional spatial graphs. The resulting predictive model will allow researchers to infer three dimensional chromatin structures from one dimensional genomic data, bypassing the need for expensive three dimensional sequencing experiments.
full_text:
This project investigates the three dimensional folding of genomes and how one dimensional genomic sequences determine three dimensional chromatin structures. Existing datasets for genomic sequences and chromatin structures are analyzed in isolation which leaves their structural relationship unresolved. The primary question is how one dimensional features form three dimensional structures to enable prediction without expensive sequencing experiments.

This computational data synthesis project combines data harmonization with deep learning modeling and network analysis of chromatin interactions. The team will apply transformer based deep learning models and graph convolutional networks (GCN) within standardized pipelines for data processing. Validation involves evaluating the accuracy of deep learning models in predicting three dimensional chromatin contact matrices from one dimensional data.

The project utilizes public datasets from the ENCODE Consortium and the 4D Nucleome Project including Hi-C and RNA-seq data. Standardized pipelines will align disparate datasets into a unified coordinate system to predict three dimensional spatial graphs from sequential inputs. To address noise and batch effects in public data, the team will develop a standardized pipeline for data normalization.

The proposed study does not address information regarding the specific milestones and the overall timeline of the project. Integrating large scale multi omics data requires cross disciplinary expertise in computational genomics and biophysics not found in one laboratory.

The team will share all code and trained models in public repositories and publish findings in open access journals. The cross disciplinary team of researchers will train three graduate students and two postdoctoral researchers in genomic data science.

abstract_original: This research focuses on the emergent phenomenon of 'metabolic channeling' arising from the formation of metabolons—transient, mesoscale clusters of sequential enzymes. Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from STRING and BioGRID, enzymatic kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas. Our hypothesis is that low-affinity, transient interactions between metabolic enzymes, often ignored in standard structural biology, create emergent 'super-highways' for substrates that defy diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical strategy involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from PPI networks. We will simulate these models to identify conditions under which channeling emerges as a dominant regulatory mechanism. Insights will likely redefine our understanding of metabolic efficiency, showing how mesoscale organization enables reaction rates impossible in a well-mixed solution. This project requires NCEMS resources to unite enzymologists, systems biologists, and network scientists to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data.

title: Lipid Raft Dynamics and the Emergence of Signal Fidelity in T-Cell Activation
title_norm: lipid raft dynamics and the emergence of signal fidelity in tcell activation
abstract_text: In cell biology, localized mitochondrial membrane fusion and fission events shape the dynamic structural network of the organelle, which is critical for regulating cellular metabolism and maintaining overall physiological homeostasis. However, existing structural, temporal, and metabolic datasets remain unintegrated, and the precise mechanism by which localized membrane interactions cascade to determine global network topology and metabolic output remains unknown. This computational synthesis project will determine how localized molecular interactions generate global network topologies by applying deep learning segmentation, skeletonization, spatial graph analysis, canonical correlation analysis, and reinforcement learning frameworks to existing datasets. The study will integrate data from the OpenOrganelle database, the Image Data Resource, and the Metabolomics Workbench using deep neural networks for canonical correlation analysis and reinforcement learning to model temporal dynamics. These results will establish how physical cellular architectures govern biochemical processes, shifting the paradigm to systems level network dynamics to advance the understanding of aging, neurodegeneration, and metabolic diseases.
full_text:
This cell biology study investigates how localized mitochondrial membrane interactions determine the global topology of the network and cellular metabolism. Although high quality datasets exist for networks driven by GTPases, they remain unintegrated and cascading effects on topology are unknown. This study investigates how localized interactions at the membrane generate global topologies, establishing how physical architectures govern biochemical processes.

The proposed study is a computational synthesis project that integrates existing public datasets without generating new experimental data. The team will apply deep learning for segmentation and skeletonization with analysis of spatial graphs and canonical correlation and reinforcement learning. The reinforcement learning models will be validated by testing their ability to simulate and replicate global topologies in live cell imaging.

The project will use datasets from the OpenOrganelle database and the Image Data Resource and the Metabolomics Workbench. The team will integrate these datasets using deep neural networks for canonical correlation analysis and reinforcement learning for temporal dynamics. To mitigate siloed datasets and high computational demands, the project will use cloud computing with high performance and transdisciplinary collaboration.

The project timeline includes biweekly virtual meetings and biannual intensive hackathons, but a specific multiyear timeline is not specified. Multi lab and cross disciplinary collaboration is required because integrating structural imaging with functional metabolomics requires expertise exceeding any single laboratory.

The team will share synthesized topologies and algorithms on open source platforms and host interactive portals for long term access. The team of biologists and theorists includes investigators and trainees who receive cross training in image processing and multi omics integration.

abstract_original: This proposal examines the emergent role of lipid rafts (mesoscale membrane nanodomains) in generating high-fidelity signaling thresholds in immune cells. T-cell receptor (TCR) triggering exhibits remarkable sensitivity and specificity, an emergent property that cannot be explained by simple ligand-receptor binding affinity. We will synthesize lipidomics datasets, single-molecule tracking data of TCR dynamics from the biological literature, and super-resolution microscopy data (STORM/PALM) available in the BioImage Archive. The central question is how the dynamic clustering of specific lipids (cholesterol, sphingolipids) and proteins creates a mesoscale 'computational engine' that filters noise and amplifies true antigenic signals. We will employ agent-based modeling and molecular dynamics simulations (coarse-grained) to integrate lipid composition data with protein mobility tracks. We expect to demonstrate that lipid rafts function as emergent signal integration hubs that undergo phase transitions to lock in activation states, providing a physical basis for immune decision-making. This synthesis requires a collaborative effort between immunologists, membrane biophysicists, and computational modelers to link compositional lipid data with spatiotemporal signaling outcomes.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Cytoskeleton: From Molecular Motors to Cellular Tensegrity
title_norm: emergent mechanics of the cytoskeleton from molecular motors to cellular tensegrity
abstract_text: Membrane biophysics research focuses on mesoscale lipid domain formation and its role in cellular signaling, which is essential for understanding how transient nanoscale lipid rafts coalesce to regulate cellular communication. However, the biophysical mechanisms transitioning nanoscale lipid protein interactions into stable mesoscale domains remain unresolved because existing computational and imaging methods operate at disconnected spatial and temporal scales. This project will determine the biophysical rules of mesoscale lipid raft assembly and signaling modulation through a retrospective computational synthesis applying hidden Markov models, coarse grained kinetic models, and spatio temporal graph neural networks. The study will integrate molecular dynamics trajectories from MemProtMD, single particle tracking from biophysical databases, and super resolution microscopy from the BioImage Archive into a standardized cloud based data lake. Ultimately, this research will establish a new computational framework and a predictive model of cellular signaling responses to external stimuli, advancing therapeutic insights for cancer and neurodegeneration.
full_text:
This study in the biophysics of membranes addresses how nanoscale interactions of lipids and proteins transition into stable mesoscale domains. Although rafts of lipids are known to be transient structures disconnected scales of observation prevent researchers from understanding their coalescence. The primary question asks how the assembly of rafts of lipids modulates signaling to model cellular responses in cancer and neurodegeneration.

This retrospective study uses a purely computational strategy of data synthesis divided into three phases of integration and pattern recognition. The tools include hidden Markov models anomalous diffusion theories coarse grained kinetic models spatio temporal graph neural networks and deep autoencoders. Validation involves comparing kinetic models from simulations of molecular dynamics against clustering patterns from tracking of single particles and super resolution microscopy.

The team will integrate datasets from MemProtMD the Automated Topology Builder Zenodo the Sequence Read Archive and the BioImage Archive. The team will standardize disparate datasets in a data lake in the cloud to match molecular simulations with cellular microscopy scales. To bridge the spatio temporal gap between simulations and imaging the team will apply machine learning and anomalous diffusion theories.

Although specific calendar dates are not specified, the project proceeds through three sequential phases supported by biannual meetings of the group. Bridging the gap between scales requires cross disciplinary collaboration because no single laboratory possesses expertise in biophysics biology and data science.

The team will share all analytical workflows integrated datasets and predictive models publicly on the open Zenodo and GitHub platforms. The team of biophysicists and data scientists at various stages of their careers will train graduate students in machine learning.

abstract_original: This project investigates how cellular stiffness and shape stability emerge from the stochastic interactions of cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors. The mechanical integrity of a cell is an emergent property of the 'active matter' network of actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, which behave differently than passive polymer networks. We will synthesize data from the Cytoskeleton Registry, cryo-electron tomography of cytoskeletal networks, and traction force microscopy datasets. Our hypothesis is that the cell utilizes a 'tensegrity' (tensional integrity) architecture where emergent mechanical robustness arises specifically from the interplay of compression-bearing microtubules and tension-bearing actin filaments. We will use finite element analysis (FEA) and active gel theory to model whole-cell mechanics based on the integrated structural data. The expected insight is a unified quantitative law describing how local motor activity scales up to global cell deformation and migration capabilities. This project demands a synthesis of cell biology, continuum mechanics, and computational physics, requiring NCEMS support to standardize diverse imaging and force datasets.

title: Viral Capsid Polymorphism: Emergent Geometry from Identical Subunits
title_norm: viral capsid polymorphism emergent geometry from identical subunits
abstract_text: The structural organization of the eukaryotic nucleolus relies on sub compartments that self organize via liquid liquid phase separation, a fundamental process governing cellular compartmentalization and function. Currently, the physical and genetic rules explaining how documented molecular components interact to produce macroscopic, nested nucleolar sub compartments remain unknown, and existing datasets remain unintegrated across disciplines. This project will define sequence level interaction rules to model multi phase nucleolar structure and predict stress induced changes using graph neural networks, transformer based models, Cahn Hilliard equations, and Flory Huggins thermodynamic theory. The study will integrate proteomics, imaging, and genomic data from PRIDE, ENCODE, GEO, and the Human Protein Atlas by normalizing values and building a three layer network of molecular interactions and spatial positions. These predictive models of nucleolar structure will establish a methodological framework for studying other biomolecular condensates and provide insights into diseases linked to abnormal ribosome production like cancer.
full_text:
This study investigates the structural organization of the eukaryotic nucleolus and the unknown physical rules of liquid liquid phase separation. Although molecular nucleolar components are documented, the interactions that produce macroscopic properties remain unknown and unintegrated across disciplines. This project investigates how molecular interactions drive nucleolar structure to provide insights into diseases linked to abnormal ribosome production.

The study uses a computational design that integrates public datasets through modeling of networks with machine learning and thermodynamic simulations. The project will apply graph neural networks and transformer based models alongside Cahn-Hilliard equations and Flory-Huggins thermodynamic theory. The team will validate the computational models by checking if physics based simulations spontaneously generate the three phase nucleolar structure.

The study will utilize the PRIDE database and ENCODE and GEO and the Human Protein Atlas for proteomics and imaging. The team will integrate datasets by normalizing values and mapping them to a reference genome to build three layer networks. To address heterogeneity of data and variations across batches, the team will create a standardized ontology and use automated pipelines.

Although the timeline of the project includes four in person collaborative meetings, the proposal does not specify any chronological milestones. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because integrating genomic data and machine learning requires expertise from biology and physics and computer science.

The project will publish findings in open access journals and host data in the Nucleolar Emergence Atlas database and release code. The team of biologists and physicists and computational scientists will train four postdoctoral researchers and six graduate students through co mentorship.

This structural plasticity is an emergent property of the subunit interaction energy landscape. We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) covering a wide range of viral families, along with thermodynamic stability data from literature. The novel question is: What are the hidden 'assembly codes' within the protein interface sequences that allow for emergent geometric flexibility versus rigidity? We will apply geometric deep learning and symmetry-aware molecular docking simulations to map the energy landscapes of capsid assembly. We expect to discover conserved interfacial motifs that act as 'hinges,' allowing emergent curvature variations that facilitate viral evolution and immune evasion. This study requires a team of structural virologists, geometric topologists, and AI researchers to analyze the vast structural space of viral assemblies.

title: The Emergence of Synaptic Memory: Nanocolumns and PSD Stability
title_norm: the emergence of synaptic memory nanocolumns and psd stability
abstract_text: The spatial organization, clustering, and movement of synaptic vesicles within presynaptic terminals are critical for organizing vesicles into functional pools that regulate neurotransmitter release and synaptic transmission. However, how static physical structures of synaptic vesicle pools relate to dynamic, non linear processes of neurotransmitter release remains unknown because existing structural and functional datasets are unintegrated. To model how three dimensional vesicle pool structures predict neurotransmitter release, this project will synthesize existing datasets using spatial point pattern analysis, computer vision segmentation, Graph Neural Networks, and Recurrent Neural Networks. The study will standardize datasets from EMPIAR, the Allen Brain Atlas, NeuroMorpho, OpenNeuro, and super resolution microscopy into a relational database, combining structural features with functional dynamics. These results will establish a predictive model of presynaptic function and a novel methodology for integrating multi modal biological data without generating new experimental data.
full_text:
This study investigates the spatial organization of synaptic vesicles and how static pools of vesicles relate to dynamic release of neurotransmitters. Scaffolding proteins organize synaptic vesicles into pools but existing datasets remain unintegrated and do not explain dynamics of transition of vesicles. The project models how three dimensional structures of vesicles predict release of neurotransmitters to establish a predictive model of presynaptic function.

The design of the study is a computational synthesis that integrates existing datasets using spatial statistics and computer vision and machine learning. Analytical tools include three dimensional segmentation through computer vision and analysis of spatial point patterns and graph and recurrent neural networks. The models will be validated by comparing predictions against paired data from electrophysiology of synaptic plasticity and release of neurotransmitters.

The project utilizes datasets from EMPIAR and the Allen Brain Atlas and NeuroMorpho and OpenNeuro alongside super resolution microscopy for localization. Datasets will be integrated into a relational database by combining features of structure from graph networks with dynamics from recurrent networks. Fragmentation and differences in formatting of public datasets represent limitations that the team will resolve through standardization and harmonization of databases.

The project is scheduled for a timeline of two years marked by biweekly virtual meetings and three in person hackathons. This project requires collaboration across disciplines because expertise in biophysics and machine learning (ML) is not present in one laboratory.

All datasets and models and code will be made publicly available on GitHub with reproducibility verified by an external consultant. The team includes biophysicists and ML researchers at various stages of career including postdocs who receive co mentorship across disciplines.

abstract_original: This proposal investigates the Post-Synaptic Density (PSD) as a mesoscale storage device, where long-term synaptic plasticity emerges from the trans-synaptic alignment of 'nanocolumns' (clusters of receptors and scaffold proteins). This synthesis requires neurobiologists, biophysicists, and stochastic modelers to bridge the gap between static nanostructure and dynamic neural function.

title: Emergent Selectivity in the Nuclear Pore Complex: A Data-Driven Transport Model
title_norm: emergent selectivity in the nuclear pore complex a datadriven transport model
abstract_text: Cellular mechanobiology relies on the structural maturation and physical dynamics of focal adhesions, which are critical protein complexes that link the extracellular matrix to the actin cytoskeleton to regulate cellular behavior. However, historical divisions between biochemical and biophysical approaches leave it unresolved how nanoscale molecular interactions and protein unfolding events collectively organize into mesoscale structures during cellular mechanosensing. This project will identify spatio temporal network changes during focal adhesion maturation using a computational synthesis that will apply dynamic time warping, spatio temporal graph convolutional networks, topological data analysis, and percolation theory. The study will integrate imaging and proteomic datasets from the Image Data Resource and Proteomics Identifications Database by aligning spatial coordinates, synchronizing temporal data, and constructing dynamic graphs. These findings will establish a predictive systems level model of structural organization, transitioning the study of cellular force sensing from descriptive single molecule observations to a systems biology framework.

Individual components of focal adhesions are characterized but physical principles of their collective assembly remain unresolved due to disciplinary divisions. The project determines how physical forces dictate composition of networks to establish a predictive model of structural organization for biological systems.

This computational project synthesizes data through three phases of harmonization of data and synthesis with machine learning and modeling of networks. The team will apply dynamic time warping and spatio temporal graph convolutional networks and analysis of topological data and theory of percolation. The proposed study does not address the specific methods for the validation or benchmarking of the research results.

The project will use imaging and proteomic datasets from the Image Data Resource and the Proteomics Identifications Database. The team integrates datasets by aligning spatial coordinates and synchronizing temporal data and constructing dynamic graphs of networks of proteins. To mitigate fragmentation of datasets, the team will develop a unified ontology of metadata and normalize spatial coordinates.

The timeline features three sequential phases of harmonization of data and synthesis with machine learning punctuated by meetings of working groups. Cross disciplinary collaboration is required because single laboratories lack the combined expertise to integrate physical and biochemical modalities of data.

The team will share datasets and models and code publicly on GitHub and Zenodo and publish in journals with open access. The team includes scientists from multiple disciplines and stages of career who will receive training in machine learning and development of software.

The NPC acts as a selective gate, an emergent property that functions without energy consumption at the pore itself. We will synthesize structural models of the NPC (PDB-Dev), single-molecule transport kinetics data, and biophysical characterizations of FG-nup phase behavior. The scientific question is how the collective behavior of tethered, disordered proteins creates a 'selective filter' that allows rapid passage of transport factors while excluding inert molecules. We will employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory to model the pore environment based on synthesized structural data. Expected insights include a unified physical model of nucleocytoplasmic transport that explains how mesoscale crowding and weak transient interactions generate emergent gating selectivity. This requires a collaboration between structural biologists, polymer physicists, and computational chemists.

title: Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and the Emergence of Bioenergetic Efficiency
title_norm: mitochondrial cristae morphodynamics and the emergence of bioenergetic efficiency
abstract_text: Stress granules are membrane free protein RNA aggregates that form through phase separation in eukaryotic cells during environmental stress to temporarily store cellular components, representing a critical mechanism for cell survival. However, fragmented data across laboratories leaves the general rules of stress granule assembly, their stress specific molecular composition, and their exact impact on cell survival unclear. This computational synthesis project will identify stress granule assembly rules and predict composition by applying transformer language models, graph neural networks, convolutional networks, vision transformers, and variational autoencoders to existing public datasets. The study will integrate data from the Gene Expression Omnibus, ArrayExpress, BioGRID, STRING, eCLIP, Cell Image Library, and Image Data Resource into a unified relational database using variational autoencoders. Ultimately, establishing these physical and chemical rules of stress granule dynamics will facilitate the identification of novel therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases and cancer drug resistance.
full_text:
This project examines the formation of stress granules to understand how different types of cellular stress dictate their molecular makeup. These aggregates temporarily store proteins and ribonucleic acid (RNA) through phase separation but fragmented data leaves the rules of assembly unclear. The project models the assembly of stress granules to identify therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases and resistance of cancer to drugs.

This computational synthesis project integrates public datasets of genetics and molecular interactions and microscopic imaging without generating new experimental data. The team applies transformer based language models and graph neural networks and convolutional networks and variational autoencoders for analysis. The proposed study does not address the specific methods for the validation or benchmarking of the computational results.

The project utilizes data from the Gene Expression Omnibus and BioGRID and STRING and the Image Data Resource. The team integrates these datasets by building a unified relational database and using variational autoencoders for data projection. To mitigate the limitation of fragmented data from different laboratories, the team creates a database with standardized metadata.

The proposed study does not address the specific milestones or the overall timeline for completing this computational research. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in RNA biology and physical chemistry and computer science.

The team shares all findings and the integrated database and computer code publicly on open source platforms like GitHub. The diverse team includes researchers at various career stages and trains graduate students through joint mentorship and workshops.

The geometry of the cristae at the mesoscale is hypothesized to act as a proton trap, an emergent phenomenon critical for ATP synthesis. We will synthesize electron tomography data of mitochondrial ultrastructure, super-resolution imaging of respiratory chain complexes, and bioenergetic flux data. Our hypothesis is that specific cristae geometries optimize the spatial distance between proton pumps and ATP synthase, creating localized pH gradients (micro-domains) that boost efficiency beyond bulk membrane theory. We will use multiphysics simulations (combining diffusion and electrostatics) on real-world membrane geometries derived from tomography data. Insights will link mesoscale membrane architecture directly to metabolic output, relevant for understanding aging and metabolic diseases. This team science approach needs mitochondrial biologists, image analysis experts, and biophysical modelers.

title: Ribosome Collisions and the Emergence of Translational Quality Control
title_norm: ribosome collisions and the emergence of translational quality control
abstract_text: In cellular biophysics, the selective permeability of the eukaryotic nuclear pore complex regulates transport through a barrier formed by the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins lining its central channel. However, the physical state of this barrier remains disputed because existing experimental methods cannot capture how nanoscale interactions scale to the mesoscale. This project will determine how scaffold spatial arrangement, grafting density, and structural dilations dictate barrier phase behavior by using machine learning guided coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations, topological data analysis, and Bayesian inference. Automated pipelines will integrate static structural coordinates from the Protein Data Bank and Electron Microscopy Data Bank with kinetic and thermodynamic datasets from PRIDE, Zenodo, and Figshare to parameterize these simulations. These results will establish how scaffold properties dictate transport scaling laws, advancing the study of cellular compartmentalization, transport dysregulation diseases, and the design of bio inspired selective filters.
full_text:
Cellular biophysics lacks understanding of how nanoscale interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) scale to form the nuclear pore complex barrier. Although the scaffold regulates transport, the physical state of the barrier is disputed because experimental methods cannot capture structural and dynamic data. This study determines how the structure of the scaffold dictates the phase behavior of the barrier to inform drug delivery.

This computational project integrates existing structural and kinetic datasets through molecular simulations and topological analysis without generating new experimental data. The team will apply machine learning algorithms and coarse grained simulations of molecular dynamics alongside topological analysis and Bayesian inference. The simulation results and topological models will be validated against empirical data on single molecule transport and interactomic binding affinities.

The project will obtain datasets from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank alongside the Protein Data Bank and Zenodo and Figshare. Automated pipelines will standardize diverse data formats to combine static structural coordinates with kinetic data for simulations of molecular dynamics. The team will mitigate limits of resolution in experimental methods by computationally synthesizing static structural data with dynamic kinetic data.

The project features three sequential phases of harmonization of data and molecular simulation and topological analysis punctuated by bi annual summits. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating structural data with transport kinetics exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will publish all datasets and simulation trajectories and analytical code on Zenodo and GitHub in open access formats. The team includes scientists at various career stages to provide cross disciplinary mentorship to two postdocs and two graduate students.

abstract_original: This proposal investigates the emergent phenomenon of 'translational bursting' and quality control arising from ribosome collisions on mRNA. While translation is often modeled as a linear process, ribosomes frequently form 'traffic jams' at the mesoscale, which serve as emergent signals for mRNA degradation or protein folding stress. We will synthesize ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data, cryo-EM structures of colliding ribosomes, and transcriptomic decay rates. The novel hypothesis is that the spatial patterning of ribosome queues acts as a mesoscale sensor for cellular stress, integrating codon usage bias and tRNA availability into a collective decision-making process. We will develop analytical models of traffic flow on mRNA tracks to predict collision probabilities and link them to cellular outcomes found in public datasets. We expect to reveal how the cell utilizes the emergent statistics of ribosome traffic to regulate proteostasis. This requires the synthesis of genomics, structural biology, and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Emergent Synchronization in Ciliary Arrays: Hydrodynamics and Coupling
title_norm: emergent synchronization in ciliary arrays hydrodynamics and coupling
abstract_text: Autophagosome membrane formation at endoplasmic reticulum mitochondria contact sites is a critical biophysical process driven by localized lipid and protein interactions that are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis. Currently, it is unknown how nanoscale lipid transfer and protein scaffolding scale up to generate large scale membrane curvature, as existing biochemical and structural datasets remain unintegrated. This project will determine how lipid composition and protein tethering drive membrane curvature by integrating public imaging and lipidomics data using graph neural networks, 3D U Net architectures, and generative diffusion models. The study will integrate datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench, the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive, and the Image Data Resource by standardizing spatial resolutions and mapping temporal metadata across modalities. These results will establish a predictive biophysical model of organelle formation, providing a critical framework for understanding cellular homeostasis and diseases associated with autophagy dysfunction.
full_text:
This study investigates how nanoscale processes generate larger scale curvature of the membrane at contact sites between endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. Localized interactions initiate autophagosome formation but the physical mechanisms of transition to larger structures are unknown and structural datasets remain unintegrated. The project determines how lipid composition drives curvature of the membrane to build a predictive model of organelle formation.

This computational study integrates public lipidomics and electron tomography and data from imaging of live cells to model dynamics of organelles. The project applies architectures for segmentation of 3D U-Net and analysis of canonical correlation and neural networks on graphs and generative models. Specialists in cellular ultrastructure will validate segmentations of 3D images and test generative models through perturbations of molecules in silico.

The project utilizes datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive and the Image Data Resource. The team integrates datasets by standardizing resolutions and mapping metadata to link data of lipidomics with features of 3D structures. To mitigate complexity of datasets with multiple modes, the team will standardize spatial resolutions and map temporal metadata.

The timeline consists of three sequential phases of curation of data and integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative modeling. This project requires integrating biochemistry of lipids and biophysics and computer vision and imaging of ultrastructure which exceeds any single laboratory.

The team will share all synthesized datasets and models of machine learning and pipelines for analysis publicly on open source platforms. The diverse team includes biologists of lipids and biophysicists and provides training for graduate students and researchers at postdoctoral level.

title: The Extracellular Matrix as a Mechanical Memory: Emergent Reciprocity in Tissue Homeostasis
title_norm: the extracellular matrix as a mechanical memory emergent reciprocity in tissue homeostasis
abstract_text: Extracellular vesicles mediate critical cellular communication by transporting specific molecular cargo, making the biological mechanisms governing cargo sorting and vesicle formation central to understanding cell biology. However, existing datasets remain fragmented, and the biophysical rules translating nanoscale cargo clustering into macroscopic membrane budding and deformation are currently unresolved. To determine these universal principles, this computational study will aggregate public data and apply empirical Bayes methods, graph convolutional networks, variational autoencoders with transformer attention, and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations. The project will integrate data from Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, ExoCarta, PRIDE, GEO, EMPIAR, and PDB by converting formats into a standardized ontology and constructing multi layered networks of molecular interactions. Ultimately, these results will establish a systems level biophysical model of vesicle formation and introduce predictive machine learning tools to advance the field.
full_text:
This cell biology study investigates how the sorting of molecular cargo and the formation of extracellular vesicles (EVs) drive membrane budding.
Although extracellular vesicles carry cargo for communication, datasets are fragmented and biophysical rules of the deformation of membranes remain unresolved.
The study investigates how molecular networks control the budding of vesicles to introduce systems level models and machine learning tools.

This entirely computational study relies on the aggregation and modeling of existing public datasets without generating new experimental data.
The methodology applies empirical Bayes, graph convolutional and attention networks, variational autoencoders with transformer attention and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations.
Computational models and predicted rules of sorting will be validated by domain experts in exosome biology and lipidomics during collaborative workshops.

Data will be obtained from Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, ExoCarta, PRIDE, Gene Expression Omnibus, Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive and Protein Data Bank.
Integration involves converting formats into a standardized ontology, correcting variations between batches and constructing networks of molecular interactions and spatial proximity.
To mitigate heterogeneity of data and variation between batches, the project uses a standardized open source pipeline and empirical Bayes methods.

This study requires multi disciplinary collaboration to integrate membrane biophysics, computational biology, lipidomics and machine learning beyond a single laboratory.

All pipelines of software, processed datasets and models will be shared on GitHub and Zenodo, with papers in open access formats.
The team of biologists, lipidomics specialists and engineers at various career stages will train two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students.

title: The Glycocalyx Code: Emergent Immune Evasion via Bulky Glycan Shields
title_norm: the glycocalyx code emergent immune evasion via bulky glycan shields
abstract_text: In virology and cell biology, understanding the formation and structural organization of viral inclusion bodies within host cells during infection is critical for explaining how microscale molecular interactions scale up to form mesoscale structures. Currently, disconnected data sources prevent a unified understanding of the physical and network based rules governing how viral proteins reorganize host cell cytoplasm into mesoscale compartments. To determine how local molecular interactions drive viral inclusion body assembly and dynamics, this computational data synthesis project will apply graph databases, network propagation, and multimodal deep learning architectures to integrate public datasets. The study will integrate molecular and imaging databases, including BioGRID, STRING, and the Image Data Resource, by standardizing heterogeneous data into a unified graph database and mapping transcriptomic profiles onto protein networks. These results will establish how collective network behaviors drive inclusion body assembly, revealing general principles of cellular organization and identifying broad spectrum therapeutic targets less prone to viral mutation.
full_text:
Cell biology and virology lack a unified understanding of the physical rules that govern the formation of viral inclusion bodies. Although datasets of large scale exist, they remain disconnected and the scaling of microscale interactions to mesoscale structures is unresolved. This project examines how network behaviors drive the assembly of viral inclusion bodies to identify broad spectrum therapeutic targets.

The study uses a design of computational data synthesis to integrate public datasets through network analysis and multimodal machine learning. Key methods include Neo4j graph databases, network propagation, analysis of protein disorder, graph neural networks and architectures of multimodal deep learning. The team will validate predictions of the morphology of viral factories by comparing them with features from databases of cellular imaging.

The project will use datasets from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, Gene Expression Omnibus, ArrayExpress, Image Data Resource and Protein Data Bank. abstract_original: This proposal examines the cell surface glycocalyx—a dense, mesoscale forest of sugars—and its emergent property of regulating immune cell access. title: Symmetry Breaking in the Centrosome: Emergent Spindle Bipolarity
title_norm: symmetry breaking in the centrosome emergent spindle bipolarity
abstract_text: In cellular biophysics, centrosome maturation, pericentriolar material assembly, and microtubule nucleation are critical processes during animal cell division that are driven by protein scaffolding and liquid liquid phase separation. However, fragmented datasets obscure how nanoscale molecular interactions among pericentriolar material components scale up to form the mesoscale structure of the mature centrosome and establish spindle bipolarity. This project will determine the stoichiometric and spatial rules of pericentriolar material condensation using a computational synthesis framework that applies variational autoencoders, graph neural networks, coarse grained molecular dynamics, and agent based simulations. The study will integrate proteomic data from PRIDE, structural maps from EMPIAR, and live cell imaging from the Cell Image Library by mapping them onto a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. These results will establish a reusable computational framework for analyzing mesoscale biological systems, explaining the critical biophysical mechanisms that prevent chromosomal instability and aneuploidy during division.

title: Autophagosome Biogenesis: Emergent Membrane Remodeling from Protein Scaffolds
title_norm: autophagosome biogenesis emergent membrane remodeling from protein scaffolds
abstract_text: Understanding the physical mechanisms governing the structure, self assembly, and transport functions of the Golgi apparatus is essential for resolving how cells coordinate intracellular trafficking and maintain organelle homeostasis. However, the physical rules, molecular ratios, and structural thresholds driving Golgi stacking remain unresolved because existing structural and molecular datasets remain disconnected. This study will identify the geometric rules of Golgi stacking and transport optimization by computationally modeling public biological data using persistent homology, manifold alignment, graph neural networks, and physics informed neural networks. To achieve this, the project will integrate molecular and structural measurements from the Human Protein Atlas, EMPIAR, the Metabolomics Workbench, and the PRIDE database into a shared mathematical framework using topological data analysis. Ultimately, these predictive models of Golgi structure and transport will transition organelle biology from observation to physical prediction, offering critical insights into diseases marked by organelle breakdown.
full_text:
This study investigates the physical mechanisms of the Golgi apparatus and the unknown physical rules that govern its stacked structure.
Although the molecular parts of the Golgi apparatus are documented, existing datasets remain disconnected and their physical integration is unresolved.
The study determines how the shape of the Golgi optimizes transport to explain cellular regulation and diseases of organelle breakdown.

The project uses a computational approach to collect and model existing public biological data without performing new experiments in the laboratory.
The analysis employs persistent homology and manifold alignment in combination with graph neural networks and physics informed neural networks.
The team validates the computational models by restricting parameters to conform to physical laws of thermodynamics and elasticity of membranes.

The study utilizes data from the Human Protein Atlas and EMPIAR alongside the Metabolomics Workbench and the PRIDE database.
The team integrates distinct datasets by mapping molecular and structural measurements onto a shared mathematical framework using topological data analysis.
To manage different data formats and isolated datasets, the team uses metadata standardization and coordinate independent mathematical modeling.
