The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to link structural images with molecular data using expertise from multiple scientific fields.

We will synthesize data on Atg protein interactions, membrane curvature sensing, and lipid composition during starvation responses. The scientific question is how a soluble protein machinery effectively 'wets' and curls a flat membrane into a closed vesicle, an emergent topological transition. We will employ Helfrich bending energy models coupled with protein density fields derived from fluorescence microscopy data. Insights will elucidate the energetic requirements for this mesoscale remodeling and how it is regulated by cellular energy states. This synthesis needs membrane biophysicists, autophagy researchers, and computational geometers.

title: Stress Granules vs. P-Bodies: Emergent Sorting in RNA Phase Separation
title_norm: stress granules vs pbodies emergent sorting in rna phase separation
abstract_text: In plant cell biology, hexameric cellulose synthase complexes assemble and move dynamically along microtubule tracks at the plasma membrane to synthesize cellulose microfibrils, a process essential for cell wall formation. However, the specific protein ratios, temporal interaction networks, environmental responses, and biophysical mechanisms regulating how individual cellulose synthase proteins assemble, transport, and coordinate their activity remain unresolved. This project will determine the biophysical rules governing cellulose synthase assembly and dynamics through a computational synthesis of public multi omics and live cell imaging datasets using graph neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and multi scale simulations. The study will integrate data from the Arabidopsis Information Resource, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, and Image Data Resource by mapping molecular states onto spatial and temporal metrics using a unified multi scale predictive model. Results will establish a predictive model for cellulose synthesis, shifting focus to mesoscale system properties and providing principles of multiprotein complex assembly applicable to other biological systems.
full_text:
In plant cell biology, the biophysical mechanisms regulating the assembly and movement of cellulose synthase complexes remain unresolved.
Although these complexes synthesize cellulose microfibrils along microtubule tracks, the specific protein ratios and environmental responses are unknown.
This study aims to determine the stoichiometric requirements of these complexes to establish predictive models of cell wall synthesis.

The proposed study uses a computational data synthesis design to integrate multi omics and live cell imaging datasets.
The team will apply graph neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and multi scale computational biophysical simulations.
The predictive models will be validated by correlating proteomic abundance data with imaging metrics to ensure biological consistency.

Integrating plant multi omics with biomechanical and imaging data requires diverse expertise exceeding the capacity of a single laboratory.

While both are liquid-like droplets, they maintain distinct compositions. We will synthesize RNA-seq data from isolated granules (RIP-seq), phase diagrams of RNA-binding proteins, and super-resolution imaging of granule coexistence. Insights will reveal the physical rules governing how the cell compartmentalizes RNA processing without membranes. This requires RNA biologists, thermodynamicists, and data scientists.

title: Collapse of the Chaperone Network: Emergent Proteostasis Failure in Aging
title_norm: collapse of the chaperone network emergent proteostasis failure in aging
abstract_text: Bacterial microcompartments are protein based shells that enclose metabolic processes, serving as a critical model for understanding physical self assembly and structural organization in biological systems. However, the specific rules governing how individual proteins organize into multi protein structures remain unknown because existing genomic, structural, and interaction datasets have not been integrated. This project will identify the thermodynamic rules of compartment assembly by using a computational approach that combines structural prediction software, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and phase separation algorithms to simulate assembly pathways. The study will integrate data from the NCBI RefSeq database, the Protein Data Bank, and the PRIDE database by standardizing metadata, mapping genetic sequences to structural models, and parameterizing kinetic simulations. Ultimately, these predictive models will establish computational methods for studying large molecular systems and assist in designing synthetic compartments for biotechnology applications.
full_text:
This project investigates the physical self assembly of bacterial microcompartments because the rules governing mesoscale organization of proteins remain unknown. Although separate databases contain sequences of genes and structures of proteins, these unintegrated data leave assembly pathways and kinetic processes unresolved. The study determines rules of compartment assembly to explain how weak interactions produce stable structures and design synthetic compartments.

The computational design aggregates public data to predict unresolved interactions of proteins and simulate assembly pathways of compartments with kinetic models. The team applies software for structural prediction and graph neural networks alongside reinforcement learning and algorithms for phase separation. Structural biologists on the team evaluate structural predictions, while kinetic simulations are calibrated with existing data from proteomics.

This project utilizes the NCBI RefSeq database and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside the public PRIDE database. The team integrates data by mapping sequences of genes to models of structures and parameterizing kinetic simulations with data from proteomics. Computational tools for prediction estimate missing structural details, while automated pipelines for data cleaning resolve inconsistencies across databases.

Although a chronological timeline is not provided, milestones of the project include creating a unified database and developing predictive models. Combining structural biology and microbiology with biophysics and machine learning exceeds the technical capabilities of any single laboratory.

The team shares all findings and code for software through open access journals and public repositories such as GitHub. Biologists and biophysicists at various career stages train two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students in integration of data.

The chaperone network functions as a collective buffer, but its capacity is finite. We will synthesize proteomics data quantifying chaperone levels across age, protein aggregation datasets, and folding stability data. The novel question is: Is there a sharp 'percolation threshold' where the chaperone network suddenly loses connectivity, leading to systemic collapse? We will model the chaperone system as a flow network where capacity constraints lead to emergent congestion. We expect to define the critical tipping points of proteostasis, providing a theoretical basis for the sudden onset of age-related diseases. This requires systems biologists, network theorists, and gerontologists.

title: Emergent Antibiotic Resistance in Biofilms: The Role of Matrix Architecture
title_norm: emergent antibiotic resistance in biofilms the role of matrix architecture
abstract_text: In cell biology, the biogenesis, spatial distribution, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisome organelle network are critical for regulating lipid metabolism and managing reactive oxygen species. However, it remains unknown how local protein import and membrane lipid sorting at the endoplasmic reticulum scale to determine global network morphology and cellular metabolic states. This project will determine how local protein protein interactions dictate global network morphology by executing a data driven synthesis design that utilizes Cellpose deep learning segmentation, graph neural networks, and Multi Omics Factor Analysis. The study will integrate datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench, Image Data Resource, BioGRID, and STRING by using semantic web technologies and mapping protein interactions onto spatial network models of peroxisomes. These predictive machine learning models will shift organelle research to system wide properties, establishing new computational methods to understand cellular adaptation, aging, and peroxisome biogenesis disorders.
full_text:
In cell biology the regulation of the network of peroxisomes by local processes at the endoplasmic reticulum remains unknown. Peroxisomes form from the endoplasmic reticulum to regulate metabolism but how these local processes scale to global morphology is unknown. The project examines how local interactions of proteins dictate the morphology of the network to understand system wide properties.

The proposed study uses a data driven design of synthesis in four phases to integrate existing public datasets. The team will apply automated pipelines and semantic web ontologies and segmentation with Cellpose and models of factor analysis. Validation of the models will involve forecasting lipidomic profiles of cells using spatial metrics from images of fluorescence microscopy.

The study will use datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench and the Image Data Resource and BioGRID and STRING. The team will integrate these datasets by building a unified database and mapping interactions of proteins onto spatial models of peroxisomes. Because standardization across datasets is lacking, the team will develop automated pipelines of extraction to harmonize the data.

The project will span a two year period with milestones marked by four in person meetings of synthesis. Cross disciplinary collaboration is required because integrating spatial imaging with lipidomics exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

title: GPCR Oligomerization Landscapes: Emergent Signaling Bias via Allostery
title_norm: gpcr oligomerization landscapes emergent signaling bias via allostery
abstract_text: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport system drives essential cellular membrane deformation and severing, a physical process vital for cell division, viral budding, and membrane repair. However, static imaging limitations prevent the real time observation of membrane division, leaving the translation of molecular scale protein lipid interactions into larger scale physical forces poorly understood. This project will identify the physical rules of membrane division by using graph neural networks, topological shape analysis, and coarse grained molecular simulations to integrate structural and biological imaging data into unified computational models. The study will integrate data from the Protein Data Bank, Electron Microscopy Data Bank, BioImage Archive, and Image Data Resource by standardizing spatial coordinates, normalizing signal intensities, and applying uniform metadata labels. These predictive computational models will resolve competing physical theories of membrane division and establish a generalizable framework applicable to other complex cellular protein machines.
full_text:
This project investigates how interactions at the molecular scale within the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) system generate forces. Although protein binding and roles of enzymes are known, static imaging cannot capture continuous physical changes during membrane division. This study models how proteins and lipids generate force to resolve competing physical models of cellular membrane division.

The proposed study uses a computational approach to integrate structural and biological imaging data into unified models of molecular movement. GPCRs often function not as monomers but as mesoscale arrays. We will synthesize FRET/BRET data on receptor proximity, pharmacological response data, and molecular dynamics simulations of receptor interfaces. The central question is how the geometry of the oligomer alters the allosteric pathway of the receptor, creating emergent signaling profiles (e.g., G-protein vs. Arrestin bias) not seen in monomers. We will use statistical thermodynamic models to link oligomer populations to signaling outputs. Insights will guide the design of drugs that target specific oligomeric states, requiring pharmacologists, structural biologists, and computational chemists.

title: Nuclear Speckles as Splicing Hubs: Emergent Amplification of Gene Expression
title_norm: nuclear speckles as splicing hubs emergent amplification of gene expression
abstract_text: The cellular glycocalyx, a surface layer of glycoproteins and glycolipids, forms critical physical barriers, making the study of how its molecular components assemble essential for understanding cell boundary interactions. However, because existing structural, genetic, and imaging datasets remain disconnected, how the microscopic synthesis of individual sugar chains determines overall cell surface physical barrier properties remains unresolved. To determine how molecular sugar linkages dictate physical barrier properties, this project will perform a computational meta analysis utilizing convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and multi modal transformer models. The study will integrate data from GlyTouCan, UniCarbKB, Gene Expression Omnibus, Image Data Resource, and Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive by mapping gene expression to sugar structures and microscopic image features. These predictive physical models will transition cell surface sugar research from descriptive cataloging to predictive modeling, which will clarify how pathogens, cancer cells, and immune cells interact with the cell boundary.
full_text:
This study investigates how the microscopic synthesis of individual sugar chains determines the physical properties of the cell surface barrier. Although biological functions of the glycocalyx are documented, disconnected datasets leave the relationship between molecular synthesis and physical structure unresolved. The project determines how molecular linkages of sugars dictate properties of the cell surface barrier to enable predictive physical modeling.

The project uses a computational meta analysis of public datasets and machine learning to model properties of the cell surface barrier. The team will apply convolutional neural networks for images and graph neural networks for structures and multi modal transformers for integration. The models will be validated by predicting physical properties of the cell surface barrier from expression of genes and molecular structures.

Data sources include GlyTouCan and UniCarbKB and Gene Expression Omnibus and Image Data Resource and Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive. Datasets are integrated by mapping expression of genes to structures of sugars and linking these profiles to features from microscopic images. To address the lack of standardization in public data, the team will develop custom pipelines for the harmonization of data.

The project timeline includes bi weekly virtual meetings and three in person events for collaborative coding across the funding period. This cross disciplinary project requires combined expertise in chemistry of sugars and computer science and molecular biology and physics.

The team will share all code and processed datasets and predictive models on Zenodo and GitHub and in open access journals. Biologists and physicists and computer scientists at various career stages will train researchers in computational biology and data science.

abstract_original: This project examines Nuclear Speckles as mesoscale reaction crucibles that enhance splicing efficiency. We will synthesize spatial transcriptomics data, splicing efficiency metrics (intron retention rates), and imaging of speckle proximity. The hypothesis is that the high local concentration of splicing factors in speckles creates an emergent 'kinetic boost' for specific subsets of genes, regulated by their distance to the speckle. We will correlate 3D genomic distance to speckles with splicing kinetics using integrated datasets. Insights will reveal a spatial code of gene regulation where nuclear position determines processing efficiency. This requires genomicists, cell biologists, and spatial statisticians.

title: Thylakoid Stacking and the Emergence of Photosynthetic Robustness
title_norm: thylakoid stacking and the emergence of photosynthetic robustness
abstract_text: Cellular mechanobiology relies on understanding how non muscle myosin II proteins assemble into contractile structures and interact with actin networks to generate force at the cellular scale from molecular scale functions. However, the intermediate assembly process remains poorly understood because relevant biological data are disconnected, and it is unclear how localized chemical phosphorylation and actin cytoskeleton structure coordinate this assembly. This project will computationally synthesize public data using spatial clustering, topological data analysis, and neural networks to identify phosphorylation thresholds, determine actin guidance mechanisms, and construct mathematical models of cellular force generation. The study will integrate datasets from the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, PeptideAtlas, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, and mechanobiology repositories by creating a standardized metadata framework across spatial and temporal scales. These predictive mathematical models will explain how molecular activities scale up to control cell shape and movement, advancing the understanding of cancer spread, developmental disorders, and heart disease.
full_text:
Cellular mechanobiology lacks understanding of how chemical phosphorylation and the structure of actin networks coordinate assembly of non muscle myosin II. Myosin generates force at the cellular scale from molecular functions but intermediate assembly is poorly understood and data are disconnected. The study determines how phosphorylation levels and shapes of actin networks guide myosin assembly to model movement of cells in disease.

The proposed study uses computational synthesis of public data to progress from data collection and standardization to predictive modeling. The team uses spatial clustering and analysis of topological data and convolutional neural networks (CNN) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The team validates models by comparing predictions of force against physical measurements of forces of traction of cells using explainable artificial intelligence.

The project utilizes the Cell Image Library and PRIDE and PeptideAtlas and BioImage Archive and EMPIAR and various repositories for mechanobiology. The team integrates datasets by creating a standardized framework for metadata that aligns different types of data across spatial and temporal scales. The team resolves disparate formats and locations of data by developing an ontology for metadata and using shared resources for cloud computing.

The timeline includes bi annual meetings and three sequential phases of curation of data and analysis with machine learning and predictive modeling. Multi lab collaboration is required because combining biochemical and structural and mechanical data requires expertise in biology and physics and computer science.

The team shares data and code on public platforms (such as GitHub) and publishes in open access journals and hosts workshops. Biologists and biophysicists and modelers and scientists in data science collaborate at various stages of careers with programs for training of students.

abstract_original: This research investigates the mesoscale stacking of plant thylakoid membranes (grana) and the emergent property of light harvesting robustness. We will synthesize cryo-ET data of thylakoid architecture, spectroscopic data on energy transfer, and environmental stress response data. The question is how the dynamic stacking/unstacking of membranes regulates energy distribution between Photosystem I and II, an emergent mechanism to prevent photodamage. We will use excitonic energy transfer models on realistic membrane geometries. Insights will explain how plants manage fluctuating light environments through mesoscale structural remodeling. This requires plant biologists, quantum biologists, and structural modelers.

title: Exosome Loading and Sorting: Emergent Communication Packets
title_norm: exosome loading and sorting emergent communication packets
abstract_text: The ubiquitin proteasome system regulates cellular homeostasis through the dynamic clustering of proteasomes into membrane less mesoscale condensates during cellular stress and aging, a process critical for maintaining protein quality control. However, the biophysical drivers of this clustering and the mathematical rules governing how spatial organization affects global protein degradation efficiency remain unresolved due to the isolation of existing datasets. This project will identify these biophysical drivers, determine how spatial organization affects degradation kinetics, and develop predictive models of cluster dynamics using graph databases, deep learning segmentation with Cellpose and StarDist, network analysis, and graph neural networks. The study will integrate datasets from the PRIDE database, Image Data Resource, BioGRID, and IntAct into a unified graph database, fusing them using graph neural networks weighted by spatial proximity and colocalization probabilities. These predictive models will provide insights into cellular stress responses and protein misfolding diseases while establishing a generalizable methodological framework for integrating imaging and proteomics data to study other biological condensates.
full_text:
This study investigates the ubiquitin proteasome system to resolve the unknown biophysical drivers of the clustering of proteasomes. Proteasomes reorganize into localized clusters under stress but the physical rules of this transition remain unresolved due to isolated datasets. The primary objective is to model how the clustering of proteasomes affects the kinetics of degradation in diseases of protein misfolding.

This purely computational study synthesizes public data through the harmonization of data and the analysis of networks and predictive modeling. The project applies databases of graphs and algorithms for segmentation (Cellpose and StarDist) and the analysis of networks. Biochemists validate assumptions of interactomics while models are tested on their ability to forecast the dynamics of proteasome networks.

The proposed study utilizes datasets from the PRIDE database and the Image Data Resource and BioGRID and IntAct. The team integrates these datasets into a unified database of graphs where edges of interaction are weighted by proximity in space. To mitigate the isolation and disparity in structure of existing datasets, the team standardizes metadata and harmonizes the data.

The timeline of the project spans three phases in sequence supported by bi weekly virtual meetings and three in person hackathons. Integrating high resolution imaging with functional proteomics requires expertise across disciplines spanning cell biology and biochemistry and the science of data.

The team shares all datasets and models of networks and code for analysis on Zenodo and in open access journals. The team of scientists across various stages of careers provides graduate students with training across disciplines in machine learning.

abstract_original: This proposal focuses on the selective loading of cargo into exosomes, creating mesoscale vectors for intercellular communication. We will synthesize vesicle content databases (ExoCarta), protein-lipid interaction data, and biogenesis pathway data. The hypothesis is that cargo sorting is an emergent property of membrane curvature sensing and microdomain partitioning at the budding site. We will model the sorting thermodynamics to predict cargo enrichment based on molecular properties. Insights will reveal the 'addressing system' of extracellular vesicles, crucial for understanding their role in metastasis and therapy. This requires vesicle biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists.

title: Synthetic Cell Assembly: Predicting Emergent Life-like Behaviors from Component Integration
title_norm: synthetic cell assembly predicting emergent lifelike behaviors from component integration
abstract_text: In nuclear biology and biophysics, the self assembly of the nuclear lamina and its role in organizing the three dimensional genome structure are critical for anchoring heterochromatin and maintaining nuclear integrity. However, it remains unknown how lamin isoforms co assemble at the mesoscale, how genomic regions map to specific lamina environments, and how this meshwork dissipates mechanical stress. This project will identify the physical rules of lamin assembly and genome organization through a computational synthesis that applies persistent homology, graph neural networks, and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations. The study will integrate EMPIAR cryo electron tomography, IDR super resolution microscopy, and 4D Nucleome genomic datasets as spatial and polymer graphs mapped via graph neural networks to constrain molecular dynamics models. Ultimately, these results will establish a novel computational framework that explains how local protein interactions form mesoscale cellular barriers and dictate three dimensional genome organization.
full_text:
This study in nuclear biology and biophysics investigates how lamin protein isoforms co assemble to organize the three dimensional genome. Although researchers know that lamins anchor heterochromatin, the mechanisms of mesoscale self assembly and force dissipation remain completely unknown. The primary objective is to identify the physical rules of lamin assembly to establish a computational framework for cellular barriers.

The proposed study uses a computational synthesis of existing public imaging and genomic datasets to model the nuclear lamina. The team will apply persistent homology for topological data analysis with graph neural networks and simulations of coarse grained molecular dynamics. Collaborating nuclear biologists will evaluate the results while parameters from deep learning will constrain the simulations of molecular dynamics.

The project utilizes imaging datasets from EMPIAR and IDR alongside genomic data such as Hi-C and DamID from 4D Nucleome. The team will use graph neural networks to map interactions between spatial graphs of imaging and polymer graphs of genomic data. To mitigate varying resolutions across imaging datasets, the team will use analysis of topological data to extract scale independent metrics.

The proposed study does not address specific information regarding the milestones and the overall timeline of the project. Cross disciplinary collaboration is required because integrating structural imaging with genomic data requires expertise in nuclear biology and machine learning.

The team will share analytical pipelines and predictive models on GitHub and Zenodo while publishing findings in open access journals. The team includes biophysicists and engineers at various career stages who will train postdoctoral fellows in artificial intelligence and open science.

abstract_original: This final project proposes a meta-synthesis of data from 'bottom-up' synthetic biology to understand the minimal requirements for emergent life-like behaviors (motility, division, homeostasis). We will synthesize data from disparate synthetic cell projects (e.g., liposome encapsulation, minimal genome reconstitution). The goal is to train machine learning models to predict which combinations of modules (energy, information, containment) yield emergent system-level stability vs. collapse. This is the ultimate test of understanding emergence: can we predict the transition from non-living matter to a living system? This requires a broad coalition of synthetic biologists, systems theorists, and AI researchers to define the design rules of life at the mesoscale.
